stem:
A 28-year-old man is brought to a Hunter New England LHD emergency department by police at 2330 after smashing windows at a service station. He paces in cubicle 4, shouts intermittently, refuses to sit, and has clenched fists. He has no known medical history per the brief paramedic handover, no medication list, and no IV access. He answers questions with hostility but is oriented to place and person and is not floridly hallucinating.

The triage nurse offers a quiet area and a drink of water; he kicks the chair away. Security are present at the door. Vital signs from a brief visual check: appears flushed and tachypnoeic, no pallor. He weighs approximately 80 kg. The on-call senior emergency physician asks for your plan for pharmacological management if verbal de-escalation continues to fail.

data_table.Examination: Pacing, clenched fists, raised voice, no obvious head injury, no track marks visible, no medical alert bracelet.
data_table.Investigations: None yet obtainable; refusing observations and venepuncture.

lead_in: After a further attempt at verbal de-escalation, which is the single most appropriate first-line agent for involuntary pharmacological sedation in this scenario?

options.text: Diazepam 10 mg orally
Olanzapine 10 mg intramuscularly
Droperidol 10 mg intramuscularly combined with midazolam 5 mg intramuscularly
Haloperidol 5 mg intramuscularly without a baseline ECG
Ketamine 4 mg/kg intramuscularly

subtopic_detail: First-line IM sedation choice for severe agitation without IV access

stem:
A 41-year-old woman is brought to a Central Coast LHD emergency department by her sister, who reports two weeks of escalating belief that the neighbours are pumping gas through the wall vents. She has barricaded her bedroom door, has not slept for three nights, and tonight threatened her sister with a kitchen knife before being talked down. She has no past psychiatric admission, no substance use history, and takes no medications.

On arrival she is calm but adamant she will leave as soon as she has used the toilet because 'the gas will be worse here'. She refuses voluntary admission, refuses bloods and refuses any medication. There is no immediate physical threat, but the ED registrar judges her at significant risk of harm to herself or others if she leaves now. The on-call psychiatry registrar is 40 minutes away.

data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented, thought disorder absent, persecutory delusion fixed, no command hallucinations elicited, no suicidal ideation, no current aggression.
data_table.Investigations: Refused.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate legal mechanism to detain her in the emergency department under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007?

options.text: Detain under a Schedule 1 Form completed by the ED medical officer as a mentally ill or mentally disordered person
Wait for the psychiatry registrar to attend and authorise detention
Apply common-law restraint without a Schedule 1 because the situation is an emergency
Request police invoke section 22 of the Mental Health Act 2007 to detain her
Apply for a Community Treatment Order to compel her to remain

subtopic_detail: Schedule 1 detention under NSW Mental Health Act 2007

stem:
A 36-year-old man with chronic schizophrenia attends a regional NSW emergency department in acute paranoid agitation after running out of his depot two weeks ago. He weighs 95 kg. He accepts oral lorazepam 2 mg but remains threatening 30 minutes later. The team plans IM sedation. His regular outpatient ECG from last month shows sinus rhythm at 78 bpm with a QTc of 470 ms (Bazett).

He takes no other QT-prolonging medication. He has a known family history of sudden cardiac death in his father at age 48 of unknown cause. His electrolytes from a clinic visit a week ago: K 4.0 mmol/L, Mg 0.85 mmol/L (both within reference). He is now refusing further oral therapy and is pacing.

data_table.Examination: Agitated, no acute medical distress, alert, no focal neurology, BP 145/88, HR 110, SpO2 98% room air.
data_table.Investigations: ECG QTc 470 ms one month ago; current ECG not obtainable due to non-cooperation.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: IM droperidol 10 mg
IM olanzapine 10 mg
IM haloperidol 5 mg plus IM promethazine 25 mg
IM midazolam 10 mg
IM ziprasidone 20 mg

subtopic_detail: Sedation choice when QTc is borderline and SCD family history is positive

stem: An 84 kg man receives IM olanzapine 10 mg in the resus bay of a Hunter New England LHD ED after pharmacological sedation became necessary for severe agitation. He was placed in supine four-point physical restraint by trained staff for the procedure. He is now drowsy but rousable. The bedside nurse asks what specific monitoring and reassessment cadence is required in the first hour.

data_table.Examination: Drowsy, eyes open to voice, GCS 13, no obvious trauma.
data_table.Investigations: Initial vitals post-sedation: HR 96, BP 132/78, RR 14, SpO2 95% on room air, temp 36.8.

lead_in: Which monitoring and re-evaluation plan most closely matches NSW Health guidance for the first hour after IM sedation in a restrained patient?

options.text: Continuous SpO2 and cardiac monitoring; HR, BP, RR, SpO2 and sedation score every 10 minutes for at least 1 hour; restraint reviewed and released as soon as clinically safe; documented review of restraint by a senior clinician within 4 hours
Hourly vitals for 4 hours; restraint maintained for at least 4 hours regardless of sedation level
Vitals every 30 minutes for 2 hours; no requirement for continuous SpO2 if initial saturation is at least 94%
ECG every 15 minutes for the first hour; vitals every 30 minutes; restraint maintained until oral medication is accepted
Vitals every 5 minutes for the first hour; full restraint maintained throughout; no documentation required until the patient is medically cleared

subtopic_detail: Post-sedation monitoring cadence and restraint release per NSW Health

stem:
A 22-year-old woman with a known diagnosis of borderline personality disorder presents to the mental health short-stay unit after deliberate self-harm by superficial cutting. On arrival she is tearful, increasingly loud, and shouting at the nurse that nobody listens. She has not yet been physically aggressive. She refuses to sit in the assessment room and is pacing the corridor near the exit.

Her file notes a previous adverse reaction to IM olanzapine (acute extrapyramidal symptoms) and a recent admission where physical restraint precipitated a flashback to a childhood assault. She is not currently intoxicated.

data_table.Examination: Tearful, loud, pacing, no current threats of harm to self or others beyond the existing cuts which have been dressed; alert and oriented.
data_table.Investigations: Nil acute.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first intervention?

options.text: Offer a low-stimulus space, a named clinician to sit with her, a clear acknowledgement of her distress, and the option of a PRN oral lorazepam if she wishes
Administer IM olanzapine 10 mg now to prevent escalation
Initiate four-point physical restraint and call security
Discharge her with a follow-up appointment to reduce iatrogenic dependence on the unit
Apply for involuntary admission under the Mental Health Act for treatment of personality disorder

subtopic_detail: Trauma-informed de-escalation for distressed BPD patient with documented adverse reactions

stem:
A 30-year-old man is brought into the resus bay at midnight by police. He was found shouting in traffic, was sweating profusely, and was 'fighting things in the air'. Vital signs on arrival: HR 138 sinus tachycardia, BP 178/104, RR 24, SpO2 99% on room air, temp 38.9 C. He is grossly diaphoretic, jaw is clenched, pupils 6 mm bilaterally and reactive.

He has multiple small abrasions on his arms. He weighs about 75 kg. He continues to shout that 'the lizards' are inside the resus bay. Two security staff are required to keep him on the trolley.

data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, dilated pupils, clenched jaw, hyperreflexia in lower limbs, no focal neurology, no obvious head injury, no track marks.
data_table.Investigations: VBG pending; finger-prick glucose 6.4 mmol/L. ECG sinus tachycardia, QTc 420 ms, no ischaemia.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial pharmacological intervention?

options.text: IV diazepam 5 mg titrated to effect with airway support standby
IM droperidol 10 mg
IV beta-blocker (metoprolol 5 mg) for the hypertension
Active cooling alone and observe without sedation
IV haloperidol 5 mg

stem: A 27-year-old patient on a NSW acute mental health inpatient unit becomes acutely aggressive on the ward, throws furniture and threatens to kill the nurse-in-charge. He has been offered de-escalation, oral medication and a quiet area, all of which he has rejected. He is now placed in the seclusion room with a closed door. He weighs 90 kg and has had IM olanzapine 10 mg administered just before entering seclusion.

data_table.Examination: Hostile, no acute medical distress.
data_table.Investigations: Pre-event observations: HR 110, BP 140/85, RR 18, SpO2 98%, temp 37.0.

lead_in: Which observation and review schedule is the minimum required under NSW Health policy while he remains in seclusion?

options.text: Continuous direct visual observation, vital sign checks every 15 minutes, medical review within 1 hour, and senior psychiatrist review within 4 hours
Intermittent observation every 30 minutes, no requirement for medical review unless requested by the nursing team
Continuous CCTV observation alone is sufficient without in-person checks
Vital signs once at entry to seclusion, then again at release
Seclusion can continue for a minimum of 4 hours regardless of clinical state to ensure full sedation

subtopic_detail: Seclusion observation and review minimum standards

stem: A 55-year-old homeless man is brought to a regional NSW ED at 0200 with acute agitation. He smells strongly of alcohol, is unsteady on his feet, and is shouting incoherently. He has a known history of alcohol use disorder and previous severe alcohol withdrawal, and was last admitted 4 weeks ago. He weighs 70 kg. The team is considering IM sedation because he is intermittently swinging at staff. He has accepted no oral medication.

data_table.Examination: Smell of alcohol, ataxic gait, slurred speech, no obvious head injury, no focal neurology, GCS 14.
data_table.Investigations: Awaiting bloods; finger-prick glucose 5.0 mmol/L; ETOH on breath analyzer 0.18%.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step in pharmacological management?

options.text: IM olanzapine 5 mg now
IM midazolam 10 mg
IM diazepam 10 mg
Wait for blood alcohol to fall and avoid all medication
IM droperidol 10 mg plus IM lorazepam 2 mg

subtopic_detail: Avoiding compounded sedation with parenteral benzodiazepines in alcohol intoxication

stem: A 38-year-old man with no past psychiatric history attends a Hunter New England LHD ED following a workplace incident. He is angry that he has been waiting 3 hours, has raised his voice once, but has not been physically aggressive. He paces the waiting area. The triage nurse asks for your approach to verbal de-escalation.

data_table.Examination: Raised voice, pacing, no clenched fists, no current threat.
data_table.Investigations: Nil.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first action?

options.text: Approach with one clinician, maintain a calm voice, acknowledge his frustration, offer a quiet space and an update on wait time
Approach with three security staff to demonstrate the consequences of further escalation
Tell him he will be discharged without assessment if he raises his voice again
Offer oral diazepam 10 mg as a first step
Apply a Schedule 1 form to detain him under the Mental Health Act

stem: A 14-year-old boy with a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability and ADHD is brought to ED by his foster carer. He has been escalating over 48 hours, including hitting his foster sister and breaking furniture. On arrival to ED he is shouting, hitting himself in the head, and trying to bite staff. He weighs 50 kg. He takes risperidone 1 mg daily and methylphenidate XR 36 mg in the morning. Verbal de-escalation by his carer and a familiar paediatric nurse has not worked. He refuses oral medication.

data_table.Examination: Striking himself, attempting to bite, no acute medical distress.
data_table.Investigations: Nil immediately available.

lead_in: If pharmacological sedation becomes necessary, which is the single most appropriate first-line IM agent and dose?

options.text: IM olanzapine 5 mg
IM droperidol 10 mg
IM diazepam 10 mg
IM ketamine 4 mg/kg
IM risperidone 2 mg

subtopic_detail: Adolescent IM sedation choice in autism with ADHD

stem: A 78-year-old woman is admitted to a general medical ward with community-acquired pneumonia. Overnight she becomes acutely agitated, attempts to climb out of bed, removes her IV cannula, and shouts at imaginary visitors. She is normally living independently with mild memory impairment but no formal dementia diagnosis. Her vital signs: HR 102, BP 110/70, RR 24, SpO2 93% on 2 L/min nasal prongs, temp 38.4 C. She is non-cooperative with cognitive assessment. The night cover registrar is considering pharmacological sedation. Verbal de-escalation and reorientation have not settled her.

data_table.Examination: Agitated, picking at sheets, eyes darting, no focal neurology, mucous membranes dry, mildly tachypnoeic.
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.32, lactate 2.1 mmol/L. WCC 16, CRP 130 mg/L, Na 132 mmol/L, K 4.0, creatinine 110 micromol/L.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Address reversible precipitants (oxygenation, analgesia, hydration, bladder, environment), and if pharmacological treatment is required for safety, give haloperidol 0.5 mg orally (or IM if oral declined)
Administer intramuscular olanzapine 5 mg as the first-line pharmacological sedation without first optimising oxygen, hydration, pain control and environmental factors
Administer intramuscular midazolam 5 mg as the first-line pharmacological sedation despite the absence of alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal features
Apply four-point physical restraint to prevent further intravenous line removal and behavioural escalation while the medical team completes their assessment
Administer quetiapine 100 mg orally as the first-line antipsychotic for hyperactive delirium without addressing reversible precipitants or starting at a lower dose

subtopic_detail: Hyperactive delirium in elderly - first-line low-dose haloperidol after non-pharm

stem: A 26-year-old woman who is 32 weeks pregnant with her first child is brought to a Central Coast LHD ED with acute psychosis. She is shouting that the fetus has been replaced. She had escalating symptoms for 2 weeks. She has refused oral medication. She is becoming physically aggressive towards her partner. She has no medical history. Weight today 75 kg. Verbal de-escalation has failed.

data_table.Examination: Agitated, no obstetric concerns reported, fetal movements felt today; obstetric review en route.
data_table.Investigations: Nil immediately.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate IM agent for pharmacological sedation?

options.text: IM olanzapine 10 mg
IM diazepam 10 mg
IM haloperidol 10 mg
IM droperidol 10 mg
Wait for obstetric review before any pharmacological intervention

subtopic_detail: IM sedation choice in late pregnancy

stem: A 35-year-old man received IM droperidol 10 mg in a Hunter New England LHD ED for acute behavioural disturbance 45 minutes ago. The nurse calls you to review. His SpO2 has dropped from 98% on room air to 88%, RR 8, HR 110, BP 95/55. He is unrousable to voice but groans to sternal rub. Pupils 3 mm, equal and reactive. Capillary glucose 5.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Examination: GCS 7 (E1 V2 M4), shallow respirations, jaw soft, no obvious head injury.
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia 110, QTc 470 ms (was 420 pre-sedation). VBG: pH 7.28, pCO2 60 mmHg, lactate 1.8 mmol/L.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Open the airway with a jaw thrust, apply high-flow oxygen, provide bag-valve-mask ventilation if RR remains low, and prepare for definitive airway support
Administer intravenous flumazenil 200 micrograms over 15 seconds as the immediate reversal agent for the over-sedation event in the resus bay
Administer intravenous naloxone 400 micrograms as the immediate reversal agent for the post-sedation respiratory depression in the resus bay
Administer intravenous crystalloid fluid resuscitation as the sole immediate intervention and observe without airway support or assisted ventilation
Administer a repeat intramuscular droperidol 5 mg dose for ongoing sedation needs during the resuscitation period in the bay

stem: A 19-year-old man is brought to ED by friends from a music festival. He is severely agitated, sweating, with dilated pupils, hyperthermic at 39.5 C, hyponatraemic on a stat sodium of 122 mmol/L, and has had a witnessed brief generalised tonic-clonic seizure on arrival. Friends report he took 'three caps' of an unknown white powder and has been drinking water continuously to 'stay hydrated'. HR 130, BP 150/95, SpO2 99% room air.

data_table.Examination: Hyperthermic, diaphoretic, mydriasis, post-ictal, jaw clenched, GCS 13.
data_table.Investigations: Na 122 mmol/L (135-145), K 3.6 mmol/L, finger-prick glucose 5.6 mmol/L, urine ketones negative.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Restrict free water, give IV hypertonic saline (e.g. 150 mL of 3% saline bolus) to raise serum sodium and prevent further seizures; titrate IV benzodiazepines for ongoing agitation/seizure prevention; active cooling

Administer aggressive intravenous normal saline 2 litre bolus over 1 hour to support blood pressure and maintain perfusion in this agitated hyperthermic patient with a stat sodium of 122 mmol/L and ongoing free-water intake history

Administer intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg as primary management for the severe agitation, reassess after 20 minutes for further sedation needs, and defer specific management of the hyponatraemia, hyperthermia and seizure risk

Administer intravenous furosemide 40 mg to enhance renal sodium and water excretion and reduce the severe hyponatraemia in this overdose, with consideration of a repeat dose 4 hours later if sodium remains below 125 mmol/L

Aim for rapid correction of serum sodium to >140 mmol/L within the first 6 hours using repeated hypertonic saline boluses, without symptom-based stopping rules or restriction of correction rate, and without ICU input

stem: A 26-year-old Aboriginal man from a remote community attends a regional NSW ED with acute distress and behavioural escalation after the unexpected death of a family member earlier that day. He is pacing the corridor, intermittently weeping, then yelling. He is not currently aggressive towards staff but has thrown a chair. He has no past mental health diagnosis. He has a strong distrust of clinical staff. His older cousin and an Aboriginal Health Worker who knows him well are present in the waiting room. He has refused oral medication.

data_table.Examination: Distressed, tearful, intermittently shouting, no overt threat to staff, no signs of substance use.
data_table.Investigations: Nil acute.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first action?

options.text: Invite the Aboriginal Health Worker and cousin in to provide a culturally safe space, low stimulus environment, and time for grief; involve the local Aboriginal Mental Health team early
Administer intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg without prior cultural engagement, despite the absence of psychosis or aggression and the cultural context of acute grief
Apply Schedule 1 of the NSW Mental Health Act 2007 to detain him on the basis of behavioural escalation and chair-throwing in the ED corridor
Discharge him home with a sedative prescription (diazepam 5 mg PRN) and a community mental health referral form for follow-up in business hours
Refuse any involvement from family or the Aboriginal Health Worker present, on the basis of maintaining a private clinical assessment environment in the ED

subtopic_detail: Culturally safe response to acute grief in Aboriginal patient

stem: A 50-year-old man with a long history of schizophrenia presents to a Central Coast LHD ED in acute relapse: paranoid, irritable, refusing to engage. He is well known to the local community team. Today he is calm enough to talk but refuses any medication, stating 'it's all poison'. He believes the staff are trying to murder him. He is not currently aggressive but is at risk of leaving the unit. His consultant is on the way. Capacity is being assessed.

data_table.Examination: Alert, calm, paranoid, no current aggression, no acute medical issue.
data_table.Investigations: Nil acute.

lead_in: Which of the following best describes the relationship between capacity, the NSW Mental Health Act 2007, and the decision to administer treatment without consent?

options.text: Lack of capacity is not a prerequisite for involuntary treatment under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007; treatment may be given to a detained patient if the criteria of the Act are met, irrespective of capacity status
Capacity assessment must demonstrate lack of capacity before any involuntary treatment can be given under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007
Consent is required from the next of kin before treatment of a detained mentally ill person
ECT can be given to any detained patient without further authorisation
A patient detained under the NSW MHA must give written consent to each medication dose

subtopic_detail: Capacity vs NSW MHA 2007 treatment authority

stem: A 24-year-old woman in a Central Coast LHD ED receives IM olanzapine 10 mg for severe behavioural disturbance. Twenty minutes later, the nurse calls you: she is profoundly hypotensive (BP 70/40), bradycardic (HR 42), GCS 9, with no urticaria, no wheeze, and warm dry skin. She remains afebrile. She has had no other medication in the last 12 hours per her partner. The team is asking whether this is anaphylaxis.

data_table.Examination: Pale, peripheries warm, no rash, lungs clear, abdomen soft, no focal neurology.
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus bradycardia at 42, no ischaemia, QTc 430 ms. VBG: pH 7.34, lactate 2.5 mmol/L.

lead_in: Which is the single most likely mechanism and most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Alpha-1 blockade and vasovagal-type bradycardia from IM olanzapine; manage with IV fluids, atropine 600 micrograms IV if symptomatic bradycardia, and supportive care; reserve adrenaline only if anaphylaxis features develop

Administer intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg into the lateral thigh as for anaphylaxis, despite the absence of urticaria, wheeze, angio-oedema or tachycardia in this hypotensive bradycardic patient with warm dry skin and afebrile observations

Treat as neuroleptic malignant syndrome with intravenous fluids, supportive cooling, withdrawal of all antipsychotic agents, and consideration of bromocriptine or dantrolene under intensive-care and toxicology input, with continuous monitoring of CK and temperature

Treat as serotonin syndrome with intravenous benzodiazepines, supportive cooling, consideration of cyproheptadine, and ICU admission for cardiovascular monitoring, despite the absence of recent serotonergic drug exposure or hyperreflexia

Administer a repeat intramuscular dose of olanzapine 5 mg for ongoing behavioural disturbance and to maintain sedation while the team completes assessment, alongside intravenous fluids and continuous cardiac monitoring in the resus bay

subtopic_detail: Recognising IM olanzapine alpha-1-mediated hypotensive bradycardia vs anaphylaxis

stem: Following a successful de-escalation in which a patient was placed in brief seclusion and given IM sedation, the ED team is preparing for the post-event debrief.

data_table.Examination: Patient resting, vitals stable.
data_table.Investigations: Nil.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate component of post-event practice mandated by NSW Health policy?

options.text: A patient debrief once the patient is awake and able to engage, and a staff debrief to review what worked and what did not
No debrief is required if the event was resolved without injury
Only the consultant attends the debrief
Debriefs occur 2 weeks after the event for emotional distance
Debriefs are only for restraint events involving security

subtopic_detail: Mandatory patient and staff debrief after restrictive practice

stem: A 31-year-old woman attends a Central Coast LHD GP practice with 8 months of persistent worry about her finances, her partner's health, her children's safety at school, and her own performance at work. She reports muscle tension, sleep-onset insomnia, restlessness and irritability most days. She occasionally feels her heart racing during the day when worry intensifies but has never had a discrete episode lasting under 10 minutes with peak fear, dyspnoea and depersonalisation. She avoids no specific situations and has no intrusive obsessions. She has had two normal thyroid function tests in the past 6 months.

data_table.Examination: Anxious-appearing; resting HR 88, BP 122/78; otherwise unremarkable.
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.8 mU/L (RR 0.4-4.0); B12 350 pmol/L; ECG sinus rhythm.

lead_in: Which is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD)
Panic disorder
Social anxiety disorder
Obsessive-compulsive disorder
Hyperthyroidism

subtopic_detail: GAD diagnostic discrimination from panic, social anxiety, OCD

stem: A 34-year-old man with newly diagnosed generalised anxiety disorder presents to his GP at a Hunter New England LHD community practice. Symptoms have persisted despite 6 months of attempted self-help and a course of CBT through MindSpot, with PHQ-9 7 and GAD-7 16. He has no past psychiatric admission, no substance use, no QT-prolonging drugs, and no contraindications to standard antidepressants. He works as a construction supervisor and asks for an effective but non-sedating option.

data_table.Examination: Anxious, HR 92, BP 128/80, otherwise unremarkable.
data_table.Investigations: TFT, U&E, FBC normal; ECG sinus rhythm with QTc 410 ms.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial pharmacological choice?

options.text: Escitalopram 10 mg daily, titrating after 2 weeks if tolerated
Diazepam 5 mg twice daily long-term
Quetiapine 50 mg nocte
Propranolol 40 mg twice daily
Pregabalin 75 mg twice daily

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents to a Central Coast LHD ED with a 25-minute episode of acute chest tightness, palpitations, dyspnoea, perioral paraesthesia, depersonalisation and a fear of dying that began suddenly while at her desk at work. She has had three similar episodes in the last 2 months and now avoids meetings. ECG is normal, troponin negative, D-dimer negative. She is calm by the time she is reviewed.

data_table.Examination: Now settled, HR 76, BP 118/72, no chest wall tenderness.
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus rhythm, troponin negative, D-dimer negative, TSH 2.1 mU/L.

lead_in: Which intervention has the strongest evidence base for long-term reduction in panic disorder symptoms?

options.text: Cognitive behavioural therapy with interoceptive exposure
Long-term diazepam 5 mg twice daily
Beta-blocker as monotherapy
Avoidance of all situations that have triggered attacks
Reassurance alone after normal cardiac workup

subtopic_detail: Long-term first-line management of panic disorder

stem: A 24-year-old violinist preparing for a major audition presents to her GP at a Central Coast LHD primary care clinic. She becomes severely tremulous and tachycardic during performances, which interferes with her bowing. She does not have generalised social anxiety, does not avoid social situations outside of performance, and is otherwise well. She asks for a non-sedating option that she can take an hour before the audition.

data_table.Examination: Anxious-appearing about audition; otherwise unremarkable. Resting HR 76, BP 118/72.
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus rhythm, no QT prolongation; no asthma history.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate medication?

options.text: Propranolol 20-40 mg orally one hour before the audition
Sertraline 50 mg daily ongoing
Diazepam 5 mg orally one hour before the audition
Quetiapine 25 mg one hour before
Mirtazapine 15 mg the night before

stem: A 19-year-old university student presents to her GP at a Hunter New England LHD student health clinic. She describes 2 hours per day of intrusive thoughts that she might have left the stove on, the door unlocked, or contaminated her hands. She returns home repeatedly to check the stove (typically 3-4 times before being able to leave) and washes her hands until they are raw. She finds the thoughts distressing, recognises them as her own and excessive, and tries to resist them without success.

data_table.Examination: Hands erythematous from over-washing; otherwise unremarkable.
data_table.Investigations: Nil acute required.

lead_in: Which feature most strongly supports a diagnosis of obsessive-compulsive disorder over an anxious worry pattern?

options.text: The thoughts are ego-dystonic, recognised as excessive, and accompanied by compulsive rituals performed to neutralise them
Hand erythema from over-washing
The duration of symptoms (less than 6 months)
The young age at presentation
The presence of intrusive worries about realistic risks (stove, door)

stem: A 28-year-old man with OCD (contamination subtype with 4-hour daily washing) attends a Hunter New England LHD outpatient psychology service. His Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) score is 24 (severe). He asks what the most effective psychological treatment will involve.

data_table.Examination: Erythematous excoriated hands.
data_table.Investigations: Nil acute.

lead_in: Which description most accurately describes the first-line psychological intervention?

options.text: Exposure and response prevention: graded exposure to feared stimuli while refraining from compulsive rituals, allowing habituation and disconfirmation of feared outcomes
Supportive psychotherapy with focus on insight into childhood origins
Generic CBT focused on thought monitoring without behavioural exposure
Acceptance and commitment therapy as monotherapy
EMDR targeting initial onset of compulsions

subtopic_detail: ERP as first-line psychological therapy for OCD

stem: A 35-year-old woman with OCD (Y-BOCS 26) has been on sertraline 100 mg daily for 10 weeks with minimal response. She is engaged with ERP weekly with a clinical psychologist. The treating psychiatrist is considering dose adjustment.

data_table.Examination: Persistent contamination obsessions with washing rituals; minimal change from baseline.
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus rhythm with QTc 420 ms; no medical contraindications.

lead_in: Which adjustment most aligns with evidence-based OCD pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Increase sertraline progressively toward 200 mg daily, allowing 10-12 weeks at the higher dose before judging response
Switch to amitriptyline 75 mg nocte
Add diazepam 5 mg twice daily
Switch to a benzodiazepine and reassess in 2 weeks
Discontinue sertraline and rely on ERP alone

subtopic_detail: OCD SSRI dose optimisation and trial duration

stem: A 32-year-old veteran presents to a Hunter New England LHD GP 8 months after returning from deployment. He reports intrusive memories of an IED incident triggered by sudden loud noises, vivid nightmares occurring 3-4 nights a week, avoidance of car parks (where the incident occurred), persistent negative beliefs that 'I should have died with them', hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, and sleep disturbance. Symptoms have been present since deployment and have not improved.

data_table.Examination: Mood low, hyperalert, startles at door slam, no perceptual abnormality.
data_table.Investigations: TFT, FBC normal; urine drug screen negative.

lead_in: Which DSM-5 criterion cluster set is most clearly met in this presentation?

options.text: Intrusion + avoidance + negative cognitions and mood + altered arousal and reactivity, persisting more than 1 month after exposure
Persistent hallucinations without insight
Dissociative identity states without trauma exposure
Discrete panic attacks with anticipatory worry only
Compulsive checking rituals without obsessions

stem: A 28-year-old woman with PTSD following sexual assault 18 months ago is referred to a Central Coast LHD psychology service. She is engaged, not currently using alcohol or other substances, and is asking for the most effective psychological treatment.

data_table.Examination: PCL-5 score 52; no current self-harm; no active substance use.
data_table.Investigations: Nil.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first-line psychological treatment per Australian and international guidelines?

options.text: Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy (TF-CBT), such as Cognitive Processing Therapy or Prolonged Exposure
Supportive counselling without trauma processing, with weekly sessions for 12 weeks via a registered psychologist under Better Access
Critical incident stress debriefing in a single session targeting the index event, delivered within 6 weeks of the original assault
Long-term psychodynamic psychotherapy as monotherapy with fortnightly sessions for 12 months without structured trauma-focused techniques

stem: A 35-year-old woman has been on clozapine 400 mg daily for 18 months without complication. Her last weekly FBC for the first 18 weeks was normal; she then moved to monthly monitoring at month 6 onwards. Today's routine ANC is 1.4 x10^9/L (reference 2.0-7.5).

stem: A 38-year-old man on clozapine 500 mg daily (level 450 ng/mL at steady state) has been a heavy smoker (25/day) for 20 years. data_table.Examination: Drowsy, slurred speech, hypersalivation, no focal neurology, GCS 13.

Nicotine itself directly inhibits hepatic CYP1A2; cessation of smoking removes this inhibition, increases enzyme activity, and so accelerates clozapine clearance rather than slowing it, producing a steady-state level fall not the observed rise

Reduction of caffeine intake during hospital admission increases clozapine clearance because caffeine and clozapine compete for the same CYP1A2 catalytic site, so caffeine withdrawal removes competitive inhibition and accelerates metabolism

Tobacco smoke inhibits CYP3A4 metabolism of clozapine and cessation of smoking restores normal CYP3A4 activity, leading to a fall in clozapine plasma level over days through the major contribution of CYP3A4 to overall clearance

Nicotine replacement therapy patches release nicotine that directly raises clozapine plasma levels through a pharmacodynamic interaction at central nicotinic receptors, independent of any change in hepatic metabolism or smoking cessation effects
