subtopic_detail: Anorexia nervosa - MARSIPAN-AU medical admission criteria
stem:
A 16-year-old girl is brought to a regional NSW emergency department by her parents after six months of progressive food restriction and excessive exercise. She is 162 cm tall and weighs 41.0 kg (BMI 15.6, less than the third percentile for age). Her parents report she now eats only steamed vegetables and skips breakfast and lunch. She insists she is fine and walks 2 hours daily despite cold weather.

She has not menstruated for four months. On examination she is wearing layered clothing, looks gaunt, and is cooperative but minimises her food restriction. Heart rate is 38 beats per minute supine, blood pressure 84/52 mmHg supine dropping to 70/40 mmHg on standing with a 28 beat per minute rise in heart rate. Temperature is 35.2 degrees Celsius. Capillary refill is 4 seconds.

She is alert and oriented. Bedside investigations show a venous glucose of 3.0 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L, phosphate 0.62 mmol/L, magnesium 0.68 mmol/L, and an ECG showing sinus bradycardia with a corrected QT interval of 470 ms.

data_table.Vitals: HR 38 supine, BP 84/52 supine to 70/40 standing (postural drop with HR rise 28), Temp 35.2 C, capillary refill 4 sec
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 3.0 mmol/L, K 3.1, PO4 0.62, Mg 0.68, ECG QTc 470 ms

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate disposition?

options.text: Discharge home with urgent community eating disorder service follow-up within 48 hours
Admit to a paediatric medical ward for cardiac monitoring, slow refeeding, and electrolyte correction under MARSIPAN-AU pathway
Admit directly to an adolescent inpatient psychiatric unit for behavioural therapy, mealtime supervision, and weight restoration
Observe in the emergency short-stay unit overnight for serial vitals only
Commence high-calorie oral refeeding at 2500 kcal/day immediately in the emergency department

stem:
A 19-year-old woman with a 3-year history of severe restrictive anorexia nervosa is admitted to a metropolitan tertiary hospital with BMI 13.4 after several weeks of minimal oral intake (estimated <500 kcal per day for at least 14 days). Admission electrolytes showed potassium 3.4 mmol/L, phosphate 0.81 mmol/L, magnesium 0.74 mmol/L, sodium 137 mmol/L, and corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L. The team commenced supervised oral refeeding at 1200 kcal/day with prophylactic oral thiamine 300 mg daily, oral phosphate supplements, and a multivitamin per the NSW Health Eating Disorders Toolkit refeeding pathway.

After 72 hours of advancing intake to 1800 kcal/day, she develops new bilateral lower limb pitting oedema extending to the mid-calf, generalised fatigue, and mild dyspnoea on exertion. She has no chest pain and no orthopnoea. Repeat bloods show potassium 2.8 mmol/L, phosphate 0.38 mmol/L, magnesium 0.58 mmol/L, sodium 136 mmol/L, urea 2.1 mmol/L, creatinine 48 micromol/L, glucose 5.9 mmol/L, and corrected calcium 2.18 mmol/L.

data_table.Bloods (day 3): K 2.8 mmol/L, PO4 0.38 mmol/L, Mg 0.58 mmol/L, Na 136, urea 2.1, creatinine 48, corrected Ca 2.18, glucose 5.9
data_table.Examination: Bilateral pitting oedema to mid-calf, mild exertional dyspnoea, clear chest

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Increase caloric intake to 2200 kcal/day to keep up with rising energy demands and continue oral phosphate supplementation alone without intravenous electrolyte replacement
Commence furosemide 40 mg orally daily for the lower limb oedema and continue caloric advancement as planned
Hold caloric advancement, replace intravenous phosphate, potassium, and magnesium, and continue thiamine; treat refeeding oedema conservatively
Cease all oral intake for 48 hours to allow electrolytes to normalise, then restart at 1200 kcal/day
Transfuse 4 units of 20 percent albumin to address the lower limb oedema

subtopic_detail: Family-Based Treatment (Maudsley) for adolescent anorexia nervosa
stem:
A 14-year-old girl is reviewed at the John Hunter Children's Hospital outpatient adolescent eating disorders clinic (Hunter New England LHD). Over the past 8 months she has restricted intake and lost weight from 52 kg to 42 kg (current BMI 16.1, BMI z-score -1.8). She is medically stable with normal electrolytes, HR 58, BP 102/64 mmHg, no postural drop, and no QTc prolongation.

She lives at home with both parents and a younger sister, is engaged in Year 9 schoolwork, and has supportive parents who can take leave from work to be involved in treatment. There is no history of self-harm, no suicidality, and no comorbid substance use. Her parents ask what evidence-based outpatient treatment is most likely to lead to weight restoration and recovery.

She is reluctant but agrees to attend treatment if her parents are involved. The InsideOut Institute and the RANZCP eating disorders clinical practice guidelines both inform local pathways.

data_table.Anthropometry: BMI 16.1, BMI z-score -1.8, weight loss 10 kg over 8 months
data_table.Medical status: HR 58, BP 102/64 mmHg, no postural drop, QTc 410 ms, normal electrolytes
data_table.Psychosocial: Lives with both parents and sister, parents able to be involved, no self-harm or suicidality

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first-line outpatient treatment?

options.text: Family-Based Treatment (Maudsley FBT) with parents taking initial control of refeeding
Individual cognitive behavioural therapy for eating disorders (CBT-ED) with the adolescent alone
Olanzapine 2.5 mg orally nightly as monotherapy to address eating disorder cognitions
Inpatient psychiatric admission for behavioural weight restoration
Supportive counselling from a school counsellor without family involvement

stem:
A 22-year-old university student presents to her general practitioner in Newcastle (Hunter New England LHD) with a 2-year history of episodes she describes as eating very large amounts in a discrete period (often a packet of biscuits, a tub of ice cream, and leftover meals) accompanied by a sense of loss of control. Following these episodes she induces vomiting by manual stimulation.

The episodes have been occurring on average 4 times per week for the past 6 months. She is preoccupied with body shape and weight, and her self-evaluation is heavily influenced by these. Her BMI is 22.4. She denies food restriction outside binge episodes. She has no suicidal ideation, no significant depressive features, and no substance use. Bloods show potassium 3.2 mmol/L, chloride 92 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, bicarbonate 32 mmol/L, urea 5.0 mmol/L, and creatinine 64 micromol/L. ECG is normal sinus rhythm with QTc 415 ms. She is keen to engage in treatment.

data_table.Binge-purge pattern: Binge then self-induced vomiting, 4 episodes/week for 6 months
data_table.Bloods: K 3.2, Cl 92, Na 138, HCO3 32, urea 5.0, Cr 64

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg orally daily as monotherapy without structured psychotherapy
Olanzapine 5 mg orally nightly to reduce binge urges
Inpatient psychiatric admission for behavioural disruption of the binge-purge cycle with mealtime supervision and group therapy
Enhanced cognitive behavioural therapy for eating disorders (CBT-ED) over approximately 20 sessions with oral potassium replacement
Topiramate 100 mg orally daily as first-line monotherapy

stem:
A 38-year-old man is referred to a community mental health team at Gosford Hospital (Central Coast LHD) with binge episodes occurring on average 3 days per week for the past 14 months. Episodes involve eating unusually large amounts in under 2 hours, with a sense of loss of control, eating until uncomfortably full, eating alone because of embarrassment, and feeling disgusted afterwards.

He does not vomit, use laxatives, fast, or exercise excessively after episodes. His BMI is 34. He has tried two 12-session courses of guided self-help cognitive behavioural therapy for eating disorders (CBT-ED) over the past year with only modest reduction in binge frequency, and he has completed a 16-session full CBT-ED course without remission. He has hypertension (treated with perindopril 5 mg daily, BP 128/78 mmHg), no history of cardiovascular disease, no arrhythmia, no glaucoma, no substance use disorder, no past psychosis, and no family history of sudden cardiac death.

ECG shows sinus rhythm with QTc 410 ms. He asks about pharmacological options to augment further psychotherapy. The Therapeutic Goods Administration has registered one stimulant for adult binge eating disorder in Australia.

data_table.Binge pattern: Binge without compensatory behaviour, 3 days/week for 14 months, DSM-5 BED moderate-severe
data_table.Prior treatment: Guided self-help CBT-ED x2 courses and full CBT-ED 16 sessions, modest response only
data_table.Comorbidities: Hypertension on perindopril, BP 128/78, no CV disease/arrhythmia/glaucoma/SUD/psychosis

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate pharmacological augmentation?

options.text: Olanzapine 5 mg orally nightly as monotherapy
Fluoxetine 20 mg orally daily as binge-suppressing monotherapy without ongoing structured psychotherapy
Diazepam 5 mg orally as needed before high-risk binge times
Quetiapine 50 mg orally nightly for binge urges and sleep
Lisdexamfetamine starting at 30 mg orally daily and titrated, in conjunction with ongoing CBT-ED

stem:
A 26-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner in Maitland (Hunter New England LHD) with a 4-month history of fatigue, muscle weakness, and occasional palpitations. She is reluctant to discuss eating but eventually discloses, after rapport-building, that she binges 3 to 4 times per week followed by self-induced vomiting. She also occasionally takes stimulant laxatives after large meals. She has not used diuretics.

Her BMI is 23.1. Vital signs are HR 92 regular, BP 104/64 mmHg supine with no postural drop, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius. Examination shows parotid swelling bilaterally, scarring on the dorsum of her right hand (Russell sign), and dental enamel erosion on the lingual surface of upper incisors. There is no peripheral oedema. ECG shows sinus rhythm with U waves and a QTc of 472 ms.

Bloods show sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 2.9 mmol/L, chloride 90 mmol/L, bicarbonate 34 mmol/L, urea 4.8 mmol/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L, magnesium 0.78 mmol/L, and glucose 5.1 mmol/L. Urine chloride is 8 mmol/L.

data_table.Examination signs: Parotid swelling, Russell sign on right hand, lingual dental erosion

lead_in: Which is the single most likely underlying acid-base and electrolyte mechanism?

options.text: Renal tubular acidosis type 1 with hypokalaemic non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis
Self-induced vomiting causing hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic, chloride-responsive metabolic alkalosis with secondary hyperaldosteronism
Surreptitious thiazide diuretic abuse causing hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with high urine chloride and secondary hyperaldosteronism
Primary hyperaldosteronism causing hypokalaemic alkalosis with hypertension
Laxative abuse alone causing hypokalaemic non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis

subtopic_detail: ARFID vs picky eating - DSM-5 differentiation
stem:
An 11-year-old boy is brought to a paediatric eating disorders clinic at Tamworth Hospital (Hunter New England LHD) by his mother. Since age 4 he has eaten an extremely restricted range of foods, accepting only plain pasta, white bread, banana, and one specific brand of crackers. He refuses foods of certain textures or colours and gags or vomits when pressured to try new foods.

He has never expressed concern about body weight, shape, or fear of fatness, and he does not engage in any compensatory behaviours. Over the past 18 months his weight has dropped from the 25th to the 3rd percentile, his linear growth has slowed, and his last iron studies showed ferritin 8 micrograms per litre with microcytic anaemia (Hb 102 g/L, MCV 72 fL).

His vitamin D is 28 nmol/L. He has missed multiple school excursions because he refuses to eat unfamiliar food and has lost two friendships over lunchtime exclusion. There is no history of trauma, no obsessive-compulsive disorder, no autism diagnosis (though he is awaiting assessment), and no medical cause for food refusal on prior gastroenterology workup including coeliac serology, endoscopy, and pH probe.

data_table.Eating pattern: Lifelong restriction to 4 foods, refusal based on texture/colour, no weight/shape concern
data_table.Growth: Weight dropped 25th to 3rd percentile, slowed linear growth
data_table.Bloods: Ferritin 8 mcg/L, Hb 102 g/L, MCV 72 fL, Vit D 28 nmol/L
data_table.Psychosocial: Excursion avoidance, social withdrawal at meals

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate diagnosis?

options.text: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) - sensory-based selective intake without weight/shape concern
Anorexia nervosa, restricting subtype - driven by weight/shape concern and body image disturbance
Picky eating within normal developmental range - transient, no nutritional or functional impact
Specific phobia of food (cibophobia) - circumscribed fear of choking or contamination with avoidance
Pica - persistent ingestion of non-nutritive non-food substances inappropriate to developmental level

stem:
A 24-year-old man in Sydney is referred to psychiatry distressed about the appearance of his nose. He spends >=4 hours daily checking his nose in mirrors, takes repeated comparison photos, avoids social outings and dating, and is convinced his nose looks deformed though objectively it is unremarkable. He has consulted two plastic surgeons for rhinoplasty; both declined. Weight, eating and shape concerns are absent.

He has no delusions of reference and no auditory hallucinations. He has tried to stop the checking but feels driven to perform it to reduce anxiety. BDD-YBOCS is 28 (severe). He has no current suicidal ideation but past passive ideation when preoccupation peaks. He has no substance use, no psychotic features, K-10 22, no past medication trials and no medical comorbidities. He is keen to start treatment now and has private health cover.

data_table.Preoccupation: Nose appearance, 4+ hours/day, repetitive checking and comparison
data_table.Insight: Recognises behaviours as excessive, feels driven
data_table.Risk: Past passive SI when preoccupation peaks, no current plan

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first-line treatment plan for severe body dysmorphic disorder?

options.text: Refer for a third rhinoplasty consultation, expecting that successful surgery will resolve the preoccupation
Olanzapine 5 mg nocte as first-line monotherapy
BDD-tailored CBT with exposure and response prevention plus an SSRI titrated to the higher end of the dose range over 12-16 weeks before declaring non-response
Diazepam 5 mg PRN for distress with no other intervention
Reassurance that the nose looks normal, with no further intervention

subtopic_detail: Postpartum psychosis vs PND vs baby blues
stem:
A 28-year-old woman, G1P1, delivered her first child by uncomplicated vaginal birth 8 days ago. Her mother brings her to the emergency department at John Hunter Hospital (Hunter New England LHD) because over the past 36 hours she has slept barely 2 hours per night, has been moving rapidly between activities, and tonight told her partner she could hear the baby's deceased grandmother whispering instructions about the baby's safety.

She has shifting beliefs that the baby is in danger from neighbours, and she has refused to let her partner near the infant. Examination shows pressured speech, labile affect alternating between elated and tearful, mild thought disorder, and stated auditory hallucinations. She has fleeting thoughts that the baby would be safer elsewhere. She has no prior psychiatric history. Her mother had a hospital admission for a 'breakdown' after her own first child.

She is not taking any medications, breastfeeds occasionally, and otherwise the baby is feeding well. Vitals are normal, no infection signs, no fever, basic bloods including TSH, FBC, UEC, LFTs, calcium, and CRP are normal.

data_table.Mental state: Pressured speech, labile affect (elated to tearful), thought disorder, AH commanding (deceased relative), persecutory delusions, fleeting thoughts baby safer elsewhere
data_table.Investigations: TSH, FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, CRP all normal
data_table.Family history: Mother psychiatric admission post first child

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Reassurance that this is the postpartum 'baby blues' and discharge home with sleep advice
Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily as outpatient with general practitioner follow-up in 1 week
Reassure that postpartum hormonal fluctuations cause hallucinations and arrange community mental health team review in 72 hours
Urgent psychiatric admission, ideally to a mother-baby unit, for inpatient stabilisation with antipsychotic treatment and infant safety planning
Diazepam 5 mg orally and overnight ED observation with discharge in the morning if calmer

subtopic_detail: Lithium and Ebstein anomaly - pregnancy planning in bipolar disorder
stem:
A 32-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, stable for 4 years on lithium carbonate 900 mg orally nightly with steady-state 12-hour trough level 0.8 mmol/L, presents to her psychiatrist at Calvary Mater Newcastle (Hunter New England LHD) because she and her male partner are planning a pregnancy within the next 6 months. She has had three previous severe manic episodes (two requiring involuntary inpatient admission with psychotic features) and one severe depressive episode with active suicidal ideation requiring electroconvulsive therapy.

Trials of sodium valproate (discontinued due to substantial weight gain of 14 kg over 6 months), olanzapine (discontinued due to metabolic syndrome with HbA1c rising to 50 mmol/mol), and quetiapine (discontinued due to inadequate prophylaxis with breakthrough mania despite a dose of 600 mg daily) have all been documented in her psychiatric file. Lithium has been the only mood stabiliser to achieve sustained euthymia.

She has a family history of bipolar disorder (her mother, who also required lithium maintenance) and a maternal aunt with completed suicide. Her renal function is normal (eGFR 95 mL/min/1.73 m squared, urinary albumin-creatinine ratio normal), thyroid function is normal on no replacement (TSH 1.6 mIU/L), and she has no cardiac, renal, or thyroid disease.

data_table.Current regimen: Lithium 900 mg nocte, level 0.8 mmol/L, euthymic 4 years
data_table.Prior trials: Valproate (weight gain), olanzapine (metabolic syndrome), quetiapine (breakthrough mania)
data_table.History: 3 severe manic episodes (2 inpatient), 1 severe depressive with ECT and SI

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Discontinue lithium abruptly preconception and continue with no mood stabiliser through pregnancy given TGA category D rating
Switch from lithium to sodium valproate immediately as a safer alternative through pregnancy, citing the TGA category D rating of lithium and concerns about Ebstein anomaly

Switch to carbamazepine immediately as a safer alternative with a more favourable teratogenicity profile than both lithium and valproate, continue without further fetal surveillance, and avoid fetal echocardiography given the absence of lithium exposure during the planned conception
Stop lithium for the first trimester only, then restart in trimester 2

Continue lithium at the lowest effective dose with twice-monthly level monitoring (more frequent peripartum), arrange a fetal echocardiogram at 18-20 weeks for Ebstein anomaly screening, and plan delivery with peripartum lithium reduction and neonatal monitoring

stem:
A 31-year-old woman attends her 6-week postnatal check at a community general practice in Maitland (Hunter New England LHD). She delivered her second child by lower segment caesarean for breech presentation at 39 weeks. The baby is breastfeeding well and gaining weight along the 50th percentile. The general practitioner administers the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) as part of routine COPE-aligned perinatal mental health screening.

The patient scores 14 in total. Her response to question 10 of the EPDS (which asks about self-harm thoughts) is scored 1, corresponding to the response 'Hardly ever'. She reports feeling tearful several days per week, not enjoying activities she previously enjoyed, occasional anxiety about the baby's safety that is manageable, and sleep that is broken but appropriate to a newborn.

She denies any plan or intent to harm herself or the baby and describes a supportive partner and engaged extended family. She has no past psychiatric history, no substance use, and no obstetric complications. Her thyroid function tested 2 weeks ago was normal (TSH 1.8 mIU/L). She has no medication allergies. She is not currently taking any medications and is exclusively breastfeeding.

data_table.Mental state: Tearful, anhedonia, manageable anxiety, no active SI/intent
data_table.Obstetric: G2P2, 6 weeks postpartum, LSCS at 39 weeks, breech

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step according to the COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline?

options.text: Conduct a structured clinical interview to confirm a depressive episode, offer psychological therapy as first-line, and consider sertraline if symptoms warrant pharmacotherapy

Reassure her that an EPDS score of 14 is within the normal postnatal range for a woman with a newborn, attribute her symptoms to sleep deprivation, and rescreen with the EPDS in 3 months without further action
Refer urgently to the emergency department because of the item 10 score
Commence venlafaxine 75 mg orally daily without further assessment because of EPDS >=13
Reassure that the EPDS is unreliable in the first 12 weeks postpartum and defer screening until 3 months

stem:
A 29-year-old woman is 8 weeks postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding her first child. She has moderate postnatal MDD confirmed after structured interview following EPDS 16; 6 weeks of CBT has produced limited improvement and she wishes to add an SSRI while continuing to breastfeed. She has no past medication trials, no allergies, normal renal and hepatic function, no QTc prolongation (resting ECG QTc 410 ms) and no concerning interactions.

The infant was term, is feeding well and gaining weight on the 50th percentile, with no congenital heart disease, no liver dysfunction and no prematurity. The TGA, AMH lactation appendix, and COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline provide concordant guidance. She specifically asks why fluoxetine is not the first choice given a friend was started on it.
lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first-line SSRI for this scenario, and why is it preferred over the listed alternatives?

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg orally daily
Sertraline 50 mg orally daily
Citalopram 20 mg orally daily
Venlafaxine 75 mg orally daily
Doxepin 25 mg orally nightly

stem:
A neonate is born at 39 weeks gestation by spontaneous vaginal delivery to a 30-year-old G2P2 woman with a history of recurrent major depressive disorder, treated throughout pregnancy with paroxetine 20 mg orally daily after specialist advice in her first trimester. The pregnancy was otherwise uncomplicated; antenatal screening was unremarkable; the morphology scan at 20 weeks showed no structural anomalies.

Birthweight is 3.4 kg, Apgars 8 and 9, cord pH 7.32. In the first 12 hours of life the neonate develops jitteriness, mild hypertonia, tremor, an irritable cry, and feeding difficulty with poor latch. Temperature, blood glucose (3.5 mmol/L), oxygen saturation (98 percent room air), and respiratory rate (52 breaths per minute) are all within normal ranges. Septic screen including FBC, CRP, blood culture is negative; cranial ultrasound is normal; no maternal opioid or other substance exposure is reported.

The mother did not have gestational diabetes. There is no family history of metabolic disease. The neonatologist explains the most likely diagnosis to the mother.

data_table.Neonate: Jittery, hypertonic, tremulous, irritable cry, poor feeding from 12 hours of life
data_table.Vitals: T normal, glucose 3.5 mmol/L, SpO2 98%, RR 52
data_table.Workup: Septic screen negative, cranial USS normal, no substance exposure

lead_in: Which is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Neonatal hypoglycaemia
Early-onset neonatal sepsis with maternal chorioamnionitis as the underlying source
Neonatal adaptation syndrome (poor neonatal adaptation) from late-trimester SSRI exposure
Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy
Neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome

stem:
A 25-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is maintained on sodium valproate 1000 mg orally daily and attends a Maitland community mental health clinic (Hunter New England LHD) for routine review. She has been euthymic for 18 months on valproate after two prior manic admissions; lithium was discontinued for tremor and polyuria with insufficient response, and olanzapine for metabolic side effects.

She uses condoms inconsistently as her only contraception, is uncertain whether she wants children and has not actively planned a pregnancy. She has no other medications, normal renal and hepatic function, normal cycles and is not currently pregnant (LMP 10 days ago, urine beta-hCG negative). The TGA introduced the Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program in 2023 with mandatory annual acknowledgement, including documentation of pregnancy status, contraception adequacy, and risk acknowledgement.

data_table.Diagnosis: Bipolar I, euthymic 18 months on valproate 1000 mg daily
data_table.Pregnancy status: Not pregnant (beta-hCG negative, LMP 10 days ago)

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate plan under the TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program?

options.text: Continue current valproate unchanged because she is mood-stable today; document verbal acknowledgement of teratogenicity at her next routine visit
Cease valproate abruptly today with no replacement mood stabiliser, relying on her current stability until she returns when ready to actively conceive
Switch immediately to topiramate as the safest pregnancy-compatible alternative without formal shared decision-making or PPP enrolment paperwork
In-clinic pregnancy test, counsel on the ~10% major malformation and IQ risks of valproate, ensure LARC, complete TGA risk acknowledgement annually, and formally review valproate vs alternatives
Recommend tubal ligation as the only acceptable option to continue valproate without formal pregnancy prevention program enrolment paperwork now

stem: A 32-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium carbonate 500 mg orally bd for the past 18 months. Her last lithium level 10 weeks ago was 0.7 mmol/L (taken 12 hours post-dose). Her TSH, creatinine, weight and HbA1c have been stable. She attends her GP for a routine review and asks how often these tests need to be repeated long-term.

data_table.Examination: Well, BMI 24, no signs of toxicity or hypothyroidism.
data_table.Investigations: Most recent (10 weeks ago): lithium 0.7 mmol/L, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, creatinine 70 micromol/L, eGFR >90, calcium corrected 2.35 mmol/L.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate ongoing monitoring schedule consistent with eTG and RANZCP guidance for a stable patient on long-term lithium?

options.text: Lithium level every 3 months; UEC, TSH and calcium every 6 months; weight and HbA1c annually; eGFR annually
Lithium level annually if asymptomatic; UEC and TSH only if symptoms develop
Lithium level weekly indefinitely
Lithium level every 12 months; calcium not routinely monitored
Lithium level every 3 months; no need for renal or thyroid follow-up once 5 years have passed without abnormality

stem: A 48-year-old woman on lithium 750 mg orally daily for 12 years presents to her GP feeling unwell. She has had gastroenteritis for the past 4 days with reduced oral intake and ongoing vomiting. Her routine outpatient lithium level taken yesterday is 1.6 mmol/L (usually 0.8). She has mild tremor that her partner describes as 'coarser than usual', and feels a bit unsteady walking. She is alert, oriented and conversational. Her usual ACE inhibitor for hypertension was continued through the illness.

data_table.Examination: Alert, dry mucous membranes, coarse tremor of outstretched hands, mild ataxic gait, no nystagmus, no clonus.
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 1.6 mmol/L (12 h trough), creatinine 130 micromol/L (baseline 80), eGFR 48 (baseline >90), TSH 2.0 mIU/L.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Withhold lithium and ACE inhibitor immediately, refer to ED for IV rehydration with isotonic saline, repeat lithium and renal function 6-hourly, and contact NSW Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26 for advice

Continue lithium at the usual 750 mg dose, advise ongoing oral fluids at home, and arrange repeat outpatient lithium and renal function in 1 week, without immediate intravenous rehydration, drug withholding or hospital review

Reduce lithium to 250 mg daily, continue the ACE inhibitor at the usual dose, and review at the GP clinic in 48 hours with repeat lithium level and renal function, without intravenous rehydration or hospital assessment

Commence haemodialysis immediately on the basis that the lithium level is above 1.5 mmol/L, irrespective of chronicity, clinical severity or response to intravenous rehydration, with no prior fluid resuscitation or specialist input

Administer activated charcoal 50 g orally as gastrointestinal decontamination for the elevated lithium level, continue lithium and the ACE inhibitor unchanged, and review with outpatient bloods in 1 week without intravenous rehydration

subtopic_detail: Chronic lithium toxicity precipitated by gastroenteritis + ACE inhibitor

stem: A 28-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, well-controlled on lithium 750 mg daily for 4 years, attends pre-conception counselling. She has had two severe manic episodes in the past, both requiring inpatient admission. She wants to start trying to conceive within the next 3 months. Her partner is supportive. She asks about lithium during pregnancy.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic. Weight 68 kg.
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.7 mmol/L, TSH 1.6 mIU/L, eGFR >90.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate counselling and management plan?

options.text: Continue lithium through pregnancy with multidisciplinary perinatal psychiatry, maternal-fetal medicine and obstetric involvement; fetal echocardiogram at 18-20 weeks; monitor lithium levels at least monthly with dose adjustment for increased renal clearance; plan delivery in a tertiary centre

Stop lithium immediately and substitute sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily for mood stabilisation through pregnancy, with valproate levels at 4 weeks and a fetal anomaly scan at 18-20 weeks given valproate is preferred to lithium in women planning conception

Stop lithium at least 3 months pre-conception with antenatal observation only and resume lithium 750 mg daily postpartum once breastfeeding decisions are made, accepting the relapse risk given that her two manic episodes occurred during medication-free periods

Continue lithium 750 mg daily without dose adjustment through pregnancy with no fetal cardiac imaging required because the absolute teratogenic risk of Ebstein anomaly is low and routine third-trimester anatomy scanning captures any clinically significant anomaly

Switch to carbamazepine 400 mg twice daily because of its lower teratogenic risk than lithium, with carbamazepine level monitoring monthly and a fetal anomaly scan at 18-20 weeks, accepting carbamazepine may be less effective for her predominantly manic illness

subtopic_detail: Pre-conception counselling for bipolar I on lithium

stem: A 31-year-old woman delivered a healthy term baby 5 days ago. She has bipolar I disorder and resumed her pre-pregnancy lithium 750 mg daily after delivery. She would like to breastfeed. She is feeling well and her mood is stable. The baby is feeding well, vitals normal, weight tracking the 50th centile.

data_table.Examination: Mother well, lactating, no postnatal complications. Baby vigorous, normal exam.
data_table.Investigations: Mother lithium 0.8 mmol/L, eGFR >90, TSH 1.4.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate counselling regarding lithium and breastfeeding?

options.text: Breastfeeding while on lithium is permissible only with close monitoring of the infant (clinical review, lithium level if any concern, thyroid function); shared decision with the mother weighing relapse-prevention benefits against potential infant exposure, and consideration of formula supplementation

Lithium is absolutely contraindicated during breastfeeding; counsel that formula feeding is mandatory and arrange lactation support to suppress milk supply using bromocriptine or cabergoline while maintaining the maternal 750 mg lithium dose for relapse prevention

Breastfeeding is safe without any additional monitoring beyond routine postnatal care; continue maternal lithium 750 mg daily and follow the standard newborn schedule of weight, feeding and jaundice checks at the routine community child-health visits

Switch the mother to sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily to allow safer breastfeeding, with valproate level and LFTs at 2 weeks and a postnatal mood review at 4 weeks for relapse, given lithium transfers more readily into breast milk than valproate

Pump and discard breast milk for the first 6 weeks while taking lithium, then commence direct breastfeeding once infant renal maturation is more complete, with an infant lithium level and TSH at 6 weeks before starting feeds at the breast

subtopic_detail: Lithium and breastfeeding - shared decision framework

stem: A 45-year-old man on stable lithium 800 mg daily (level 0.7 mmol/L 2 months ago) develops acute back pain and is started by another clinician on ibuprofen 400 mg orally tds for a week. Five days later he attends his GP with new-onset tremor, mild confusion, and 1 kg of weight loss. His repeat lithium level today is 1.4 mmol/L.

data_table.Examination: Mild coarse tremor, drowsy, slight ataxia, no nystagmus, no clonus.
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 1.4 mmol/L, creatinine 110 micromol/L (baseline 70), eGFR 60 (baseline >90), TSH 2.0.

lead_in: Which mechanism most accurately explains the rise in lithium level?

options.text: NSAID-induced reduction in prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilation, decreased GFR, and increased proximal tubular sodium reabsorption, which together reduce lithium clearance
NSAID induction of CYP3A4 increasing lithium metabolism
Displacement of lithium from plasma protein binding
Increase in lithium oral bioavailability through enhanced gastric absorption
Hepatic enzyme inhibition increasing free lithium concentration

stem: A 39-year-old woman on lithium for 8 years for bipolar I disorder attends her annual review. She has noticed increasing fatigue, weight gain of 3 kg over 6 months, and constipation. Her current dose is 750 mg orally daily. Her last lithium level 3 months ago was 0.7 mmol/L. She has no goitre on examination.

data_table.Examination: Well-looking, no goitre, normal reflexes.
data_table.Investigations: TSH 8.5 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free T4 9 pmol/L (10-22), TPO antibodies positive, eGFR 75, lithium 0.7 mmol/L.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue lithium at the current dose and commence levothyroxine titrated to a euthyroid TSH; review TSH at 6-8 weeks
Stop lithium immediately and refer to an endocrinologist
Switch to sodium valproate to avoid the thyroid effect
Halve the lithium dose to reduce thyroid suppression
Treat with carbimazole to suppress autoimmune thyroiditis

subtopic_detail: Lithium-induced hypothyroidism - continue lithium and add levothyroxine

stem: A 56-year-old man on lithium for 22 years for bipolar I disorder reports increasing nocturia, drinking >4 L of water daily, and waking 4 times overnight to urinate. He is on lithium 1000 mg daily with stable mood. His most recent lithium level is 0.8 mmol/L. He has no fever, no dysuria, and no haematuria. Random glucose is 5.6 mmol/L; HbA1c 5.4%.

data_table.Examination: Well, no oedema, no signs of dehydration.
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.8 mmol/L, Na 145 mmol/L, K 4.0, creatinine 110 micromol/L (baseline 80 five years ago), eGFR 60, glucose 5.6 mmol/L, urinalysis bland, urine osmolality 280 mosm/kg with serum osmolality 295 mosm/kg.

lead_in: Which is the single most likely diagnosis and best management approach?

options.text: Lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; manage with multidisciplinary review (psychiatry + nephrology), consider amiloride 5-10 mg daily and dose reduction or formulation change; assess overall lithium continuation decision against relapse risk

Type 2 diabetes mellitus with osmotic diuresis; commence metformin 500 mg twice daily, refer to diabetes service for HbA1c and renal review at 3 months, and continue lithium 1000 mg daily with quarterly level monitoring while glycaemic control improves

Primary polydipsia driven by anticholinergic dry mouth and habit; restrict fluid intake to under 2 L per day, recheck serum sodium and urine osmolality at 1 week, and continue current lithium with psychiatry review for any contributing anxiety symptoms

Central diabetes insipidus from pituitary involvement; commence desmopressin 100 microgram intranasally at bedtime, arrange pituitary MRI, and continue lithium 1000 mg daily as antidiuretic response will distinguish central from nephrogenic aetiology

Chronic kidney disease causing solute diuresis; reduce lithium dose to 750 mg daily, repeat eGFR and lithium level at 2 weeks, refer to renal medicine for staging, and continue without addition of any diuretic given concerns about solute load

subtopic_detail: Long-term lithium nephrogenic diabetes insipidus management

stem: A 26-year-old man with a recent first episode of mania is being commenced on lithium for prophylaxis. He has no medical comorbidity.

data_table.Examination: Mood euthymic post-resolution of manic episode; weight 80 kg.
data_table.Investigations: None yet performed.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate baseline assessment before starting lithium?

options.text: FBC, UEC and eGFR, TSH, calcium, ECG, weight and BMI, pregnancy test if relevant, and discussion of contraception
Morning cortisol and serum prolactin only, with no other baseline testing prior to commencing lithium prophylaxis
No baseline investigations required if the patient is asymptomatic at the time of starting lithium prophylaxis
Transthoracic echocardiogram and 24-hour Holter cardiac monitor as primary baseline cardiac assessment before lithium
Bone mineral density (DEXA) scan as the principal baseline investigation given long-term lithium therapy is planned

stem: A 40-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, currently in maintenance phase having had two manic and one depressive episode in the past 5 years, is being established on lithium. Her psychiatrist wants you to titrate to a maintenance target. She tolerates the medication well so far on 500 mg orally bd. Her current level (12 h post-dose) is 0.55 mmol/L.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no tremor, no signs of toxicity.
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.55 mmol/L, eGFR >90, TSH 1.6.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate target lithium maintenance level?

options.text: 0.6-0.8 mmol/L (12 h post-dose)
Levels are not required if the patient feels well
0.8-1.2 mmol/L for all bipolar maintenance

stem: A 52-year-old woman on lithium for 14 years attends for routine review. She has noted increased tiredness, mild constipation, and 'brain fog' for several months. Routine bloods show calcium 2.85 mmol/L (corrected, reference 2.10-2.60), albumin 38 g/L, phosphate 0.75 mmol/L (low-normal). Lithium 0.7 mmol/L; TSH 1.8; eGFR 70.

data_table.Examination: Well, no neck mass.
data_table.Investigations: Corrected Ca 2.85 mmol/L, phosphate 0.75 mmol/L, albumin 38 g/L, lithium 0.7, eGFR 70.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Measure PTH and 24-hour urinary calcium, repeat corrected calcium, and refer to endocrinology if PTH is inappropriately normal or elevated
Stop lithium and recheck in 6 weeks
Commence cinacalcet without PTH measurement
Restrict dietary calcium to <500 mg/day
Order a bone marrow biopsy to exclude myeloma

stem: A 60-year-old man on lithium 1000 mg daily for bipolar I (stable for 12 years) is admitted for an elective total hip replacement. The orthopaedic team asks about perioperative lithium management. He is otherwise well; eGFR 75, last lithium level 0.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Examination: Well, no signs of toxicity.
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.8 mmol/L, eGFR 75, electrolytes within reference.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate perioperative lithium plan?

options.text: Withhold lithium 24-72 hours before surgery and recommence postoperatively once oral intake, hydration and renal function are restored; communicate with anaesthetic team about NSAID and IV fluid choice
Continue lithium 1000 mg daily up to and including the morning of surgery, with intraoperative isotonic crystalloid maintenance fluids and routine postoperative continuation without dose change
Withhold lithium for the full week before surgery and the full week after surgery, restarting at 1000 mg daily on day 8 postoperatively with a lithium level at 1 week to confirm steady state
Substitute intravenous lithium infusion during the nil-by-mouth perioperative period at a rate equivalent to the oral 1000 mg dose, transitioning back to oral once the patient is tolerating diet
Halve the lithium dose to 500 mg daily and continue through surgery with a lithium level on day 2 postoperatively, accepting a sub-therapeutic level to reduce risk of perioperative toxicity

stem: A 22-year-old woman not previously on lithium presents to a Central Coast LHD ED 3 hours after ingesting 80 lithium 250 mg tablets (a relative's medication) in an intentional self-poisoning. She is alert, GCS 15, nauseated, with mild tremor. HR 96, BP 120/72.

data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented, mild tremor.
data_table.Investigations: Initial lithium level (3 h post-ingestion) 2.0 mmol/L. Creatinine 70 micromol/L, eGFR >90. ECG sinus rhythm, no abnormalities.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next investigation/management step in the first hour of ED management?

options.text: Whole bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol via NGT for sustained-release preparation, IV fluids, serial lithium levels every 2 hours, and immediate consultation with NSW Poisons Information Centre and on-call nephrology for dialysis triage

Administer activated charcoal 50 g orally as the primary gastrointestinal decontamination strategy on the basis that the ingestion was within 3 hours and the patient is alert, then observe her in the emergency department over the next 4 hours

Take a single lithium level on arrival, discharge the patient home if she remains asymptomatic at 4 hours, and arrange GP review the following day for repeat sampling without further levels, rehydration or specialist consultation in the ED

Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol over 1 hour to alkalinise the urine to pH >7.5 and enhance renal lithium excretion in this overdose, with repeat dosing 6-hourly thereafter targeting ongoing urinary alkalinisation

Forced diuresis with intravenous furosemide 40 mg every 2 hours, without concurrent volume replacement, to enhance lithium excretion via the kidneys, with the patient observed in the resuscitation area pending haematological results

subtopic_detail: Acute lithium overdose - sustained-release preparation management

stem: A 35-year-old woman on lithium for 3 years (level 0.7 mmol/L) reports 8 kg of weight gain. She is otherwise stable. Her BMI has risen from 25 to 28. Diet and activity are reasonable. She is reluctant to stop lithium because previous mood episodes were severe.

data_table.Examination: Weight 80 kg, BMI 28, no goitre.
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.7 mmol/L, TSH 1.6 mIU/L, HbA1c 5.6%, eGFR >90, lipid panel within range.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management approach?

options.text: Continue lithium; reinforce dietary, exercise and behavioural weight-management strategies; monitor TSH, lipids and HbA1c at 6-monthly intervals; consider switching mood stabiliser only if obesity-related morbidity develops and switch is acceptable

Stop lithium and switch to olanzapine 10 mg orally nocte for ongoing mood stabilisation, accepting the change in pharmacological profile, relapse risk and the well-documented metabolic burden of olanzapine in patients with raised BMI

Add metformin 500 mg orally twice daily routinely to mitigate ongoing lithium-related weight gain, irrespective of HbA1c, fasting glucose or insulin-resistance markers, alongside the current lithium dose and 6-monthly metabolic monitoring

Halve the lithium dose from 750 mg to 375 mg orally daily to reduce weight gain, accepting the risk of subtherapeutic plasma levels and mood relapse, with repeat lithium level and weight check at 4 weeks after the dose change

Switch from lithium to sodium valproate 500 mg orally twice daily for ongoing mood stabilisation, without discussion of reproductive contraindications, the TGA Pregnancy Prevention Program or alternative agents with lower teratogenic risk

stem: A 38-year-old man on lithium 750 mg orally daily in divided doses (250 mg morning + 500 mg evening) for 5 years asks about switching to once-daily nightly dosing. He is stable and tolerating the medication well.

data_table.Examination: Well.
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.7 mmol/L, eGFR 75, TSH 1.5.

lead_in: Which is the single best rationale for offering once-daily nightly lithium dosing?

options.text: Once-nightly dosing produces a higher single peak and lower trough than divided dosing, with evidence of reduced renal tubular exposure and potentially reduced long-term renal effects; adherence may also improve
Once-daily nightly dosing eliminates the need for routine 12-hour trough lithium level monitoring at steady state because peak-to-trough variation is reduced
Once-daily nightly dosing increases lithium bioavailability by approximately 50 per cent compared with divided dosing, allowing dose reduction without loss of efficacy
Once-daily nightly dosing requires switching to a sustained-release lithium preparation only and is not appropriate with immediate-release tablets at any dose
Once-daily nightly dosing eliminates lithium-induced thyroid side effects after 12 weeks of consistent administration in patients with normal baseline TFTs and adequate iodine intake

subtopic_detail: Once-daily nightly lithium - rationale and renal-sparing effect

stem: A 55-year-old man recovered from a documented episode of lithium toxicity (peak level 2.8 mmol/L) 8 weeks ago. He now reports persistent cerebellar ataxia, mild dysarthria and impaired short-term memory. His lithium has been stopped since the episode and current level is undetectable. Recent MRI brain shows cerebellar volume loss disproportionate to age.

data_table.Examination: Wide-based gait, dysarthria, intention tremor, impaired tandem walking, mild dysmetria.
data_table.Investigations: Lithium undetectable, MRI cerebellar atrophy, B12 350 pmol/L, TSH 2.0, full metabolic panel within range.

lead_in: Which is the single best diagnostic label and management implication?

options.text: Syndrome of Irreversible Lithium-Effectuated NeuroToxicity (SILENT); supportive multidisciplinary rehabilitation, do not rechallenge with lithium, document permanent contraindication, and consider alternative mood stabiliser after psychiatric review

Post-toxic transient cerebellar dysfunction expected to resolve within weeks; rechallenge with lithium at a lower 250 mg daily dose once symptoms have settled and serial trough levels normalise, with neurology and psychiatry review in 6 weeks

Vitamin B12 deficiency causing subacute combined degeneration with cerebellar features; commence oral cyanocobalamin 1 mg daily and intramuscular hydroxocobalamin loading, then 3-monthly maintenance injections with repeat clinical and imaging review

Hashimoto encephalopathy presenting with cerebellar features; commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily after thyroid antibody testing (anti-TPO, anti-thyroglobulin), neurology review, and consideration of intravenous immunoglobulin if no early response

Bilateral cerebellar ischaemic strokes from posterior circulation thromboembolism; arrange magnetic resonance angiography, dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel, and stroke service review for secondary prevention work-up

subtopic_detail: SILENT - persistent neurotoxicity after lithium toxicity

stem: A 30-year-old man on lithium 750 mg daily presents to his GP for the annual flu vaccine. He asks what he should do if he becomes unwell with a vomiting illness over the summer.

data_table.Examination: Well.
data_table.Investigations: Last lithium 0.7 mmol/L.

lead_in: Which is the single best 'sick day' advice for him to remember?

options.text: Maintain hydration and salt intake; avoid NSAIDs; if vomiting/diarrhoea persists more than 24 hours or he cannot keep fluids down, stop lithium and contact his GP or attend ED for a lithium level and assessment
Continue lithium at the usual 750 mg daily dose throughout the gastroenteritis regardless of vomiting, diarrhoea, oral intake, or how long the illness lasts, without seeking review

Double the lithium dose to 1500 mg daily during illness to compensate for any vomited or unabsorbed medication, irrespective of hydration status, urine output, or measured lithium level on arrival to the practice

Restrict total fluid intake to less than 1 litre per day during the vomiting illness to reduce gastrointestinal symptoms, ongoing diarrhoea and the perceived risk of overhydration during the gastroenteritis episode

Add regular ibuprofen 400 mg orally three times daily as needed for fever during the gastroenteritis episode, alongside the usual lithium 750 mg dose and ongoing oral fluids, without seeking GP or ED review

stem: A 34-year-old man with schizophrenia has been psychiatrically stable on olanzapine 20 mg daily for 8 months since his first episode. He attends a routine metabolic review. Reduce olanzapine to 10 mg daily and monitor metabolic parameters at 6 weeks

Refer for bariatric surgery assessment given his BMI exceeds 30 kg/m2

stem: A 42-year-old woman with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been stable on clozapine 450 mg daily for 3 years. She has gained 22 kg since initiation. Continue clozapine, initiate metformin with lifestyle intensification and monitoring
Reduce clozapine to 300 mg daily and repeat fasting glucose in 4 weeks
Continue clozapine and refer to endocrinology before initiating any treatment
Continue clozapine and commence a GLP-1 receptor agonist as first-line therapy

stem: A 28-year-old woman with schizophrenia has been stable on risperidone 4 mg daily for 14 months. She presents reporting 6 months of amenorrhoea and bilateral galactorrhoea. data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 2680 mIU/L (reference <500), TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.5-4.0), beta-hCG negative, FSH 2.1 IU/L (low), LH 1.8 IU/L (low)

Add cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly to directly lower prolactin levels
Switch to aripiprazole with a gradual cross-taper over 4 weeks
Add low-dose aripiprazole 5 mg daily as adjunct to current risperidone
Continue risperidone and initiate combined oral contraceptive for bone protection

stem: A 22-year-old man has been started on quetiapine 400 mg daily for a first episode of psychosis 6 weeks ago. He had normal baseline metabolic parameters. He presents for his scheduled 6-week metabolic review with no symptoms and feels well.

At 3 months from initiation as per standard monitoring protocol schedule
At 6 months from initiation with weight checks monthly in between
At 12 weeks from initiation with weight measured at each clinical contact
At 12 months from initiation if these 6-week parameters remain within range

stem: A 38-year-old man on clozapine 500 mg daily for treatment-resistant schizophrenia presents with 2 days of nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. He has no prior history of diabetes. His last fasting glucose 4 months ago was 5.6 mmol/L. He appears dehydrated with deep rapid breathing.

Continue clozapine throughout the acute illness to prevent psychotic relapse
Switch immediately to aripiprazole as clozapine is permanently contraindicated
Halve the clozapine dose and add long-acting insulin to prevent further episodes
Temporarily hold clozapine, treat DKA per protocol, plan rechallenge with diabetes management

stem: A 56-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium 900 mg daily for 12 years with no relapses. At annual review, her eGFR has declined from 72 mL/min/1.73m2 last year to 58 mL/min/1.73m2. Her lithium level is 0.7 mmol/L. She has no toxicity symptoms. data_table.Investigations: eGFR 58 mL/min/1.73m2, creatinine 96 micromol/L, lithium 0.7 mmol/L, urine PCR 22 mg/mmol (normal <30), calcium 2.48 mmol/L, TSH 5.8 mIU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to nephrology and continue lithium with renal monitoring every 3 months
Cease lithium immediately and switch to valproate to prevent further renal decline
Reduce lithium dose to achieve a level of 0.4 mmol/L to slow renal deterioration
Repeat eGFR in 2 weeks to confirm decline before taking any further action
Add amiloride to reduce lithium-associated nephrogenic diabetes insipidus

stem: A 44-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium 750 mg daily for 5 years. At routine monitoring, her TSH is 12.4 mIU/L with free T4 of 8.2 pmol/L. Previous TSH 6 months ago was 6.8 mIU/L. She reports fatigue and cold intolerance over 3 months. No goitre on examination. Lithium level is 0.72 mmol/L and mood is euthymic.

data_table.Investigations: TSH 12.4 mIU/L (0.5-4.0), free T4 8.2 pmol/L (10-20), lithium 0.72 mmol/L, anti-TPO antibodies positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease lithium and switch to lamotrigine for mood stabilisation
Initiate levothyroxine 50 mcg daily and continue lithium at current dose
Reduce lithium dose to 500 mg daily and recheck TSH in 6 weeks
Monitor TSH at 3-monthly intervals and treat only if TSH exceeds 20 mIU/L
Initiate levothyroxine 100 mcg daily for rapid correction given symptomatic state

stem: A 32-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is 28 weeks pregnant on lithium 600 mg daily maintained throughout pregnancy after careful risk-benefit discussion. Her mood has remained stable with monthly lithium monitoring. She asks about management approaching delivery.

data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.68 mmol/L (12h post-dose), eGFR >90, TSH 2.8 mIU/L, fetal growth scan normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for lithium management around delivery?

options.text: Cease lithium at 36 weeks to avoid neonatal toxicity and restart postpartum
Continue lithium unchanged through delivery with neonatal lithium level at birth
Withhold lithium at labour onset, monitor levels postpartum, restart at pre-pregnancy dose

Halve lithium dose at 34 weeks and maintain the reduced dose through delivery

stem: A 62-year-old man with bipolar I disorder on lithium 1000 mg daily presents with 3 days of diarrhoea from viral gastroenteritis. He continued taking lithium as usual. data_table.Vital signs: BP 102/64 mmHg, HR 92 bpm, temperature 37.1 degrees C

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 50 g orally to reduce ongoing lithium absorption
Commence haemodialysis given severe toxicity with neurotoxicity signs
Administer sodium polystyrene sulfonate to enhance lithium elimination
Cease lithium, withhold hydrochlorothiazide, and commence aggressive IV normal saline
Administer IV sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise urine and enhance lithium excretion

stem: A 24-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on sodium valproate 1500 mg daily for 2 years. She is in a new relationship and uses condoms inconsistently. She has no current pregnancy plans but might want children in the future. Her last pregnancy test was negative 3 months ago.

data_table.Investigations: Valproate level 85 mg/L (therapeutic 50-100), pregnancy test negative, LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management regarding her valproate use?

options.text: Continue valproate and provide written information about reliable contraception options
Continue valproate with pregnancy prevention program and annual acknowledgment form
Cease valproate immediately and commence lamotrigine at 200 mg daily

stem: A 26-year-old woman with bipolar II disorder is being transitioned from valproate to lamotrigine due to pregnancy planning. data_table.Vital signs: Temperature 36.9 degrees C, HR 72 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Widespread maculopapular rash on trunk and upper limbs, no mucosal involvement, no blistering, no facial oedema, no target lesions

options.text: Reduce lamotrigine to 25 mg daily and reintroduce more slowly at 12.5 mg steps
Cease lamotrigine immediately and consider alternative agents for mood stabilisation
Continue lamotrigine at 50 mg daily with close monitoring as benign rash is common
Add prednisolone 25 mg daily and continue lamotrigine with dermatology review
Pause lamotrigine for 1 week then rechallenge at the same 50 mg dose

stem: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 90 minutes after ingesting approximately 3 grams of amitriptyline. He is drowsy but responds to voice with dry mucous membranes, dilated pupils, and urinary retention. GCS is 13.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 94/58 mmHg, HR 128 bpm, RR 18 bpm, temperature 37.8 degrees C, SpO2 97% RA

Sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol IV bolus for QRS widening exceeding 100 ms
Phenytoin 1 g IV loading dose to prevent seizures and narrow the QRS complex
Lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus as rescue therapy for cardiovascular collapse

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents 2 hours after ingesting approximately 2 grams of dosulepin. She was initially alert but develops a generalised tonic-clonic seizure in the emergency department ongoing for 2 minutes. IV access is established. Pre-seizure ECG showed QRS 112 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pre-seizure: BP 106/62 mmHg, HR 136 bpm, SpO2 94% during seizure
data_table.Investigations: Pre-seizure ECG: QRS 112 ms, sinus tachycardia, R in aVR 4 mm

options.text: Phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV loading as first-line anticonvulsant for drug-induced seizures
Levetiracetam 2 g IV over 15 minutes as it avoids cardiac conduction effects
Diazepam 10 mg IV with concurrent sodium bicarbonate bolus administration

Thiopentone 3 mg/kg IV for immediate seizure termination and airway protection

stem: A 19-year-old woman presents 45 minutes after ingesting 20 tablets of amitriptyline 25 mg (500 mg total) in an impulsive act during an argument. She is fully alert with normal examination except mild tachycardia. She denies coingestants.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 102 bpm, RR 16 bpm, temperature 36.8 degrees C, GCS 15
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia 102 bpm, QRS 86 ms, QTc 420 ms, normal axis, no R in aVR

lead_in: What is the minimum observation period before medical clearance for psychiatric assessment?

options.text: Immediate clearance as the dose is sub-toxic and the ECG is normal now
4 hours post-ingestion observation with repeat ECG if still asymptomatic then
12 hours post-ingestion with continuous cardiac monitoring regardless of symptoms
24 hours cardiac monitoring as standard for all deliberate TCA ingestions

stem: A 35-year-old man has a 10-year history of recurrent episodes. He has had 4 manic episodes and 2 depressive episodes each lasting 4-8 weeks. During manic episodes he develops grandiose and persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations. Between mood episodes, he experienced persistent auditory hallucinations and referential delusions for 6 months while documented euthymic. He currently presents euthymic with no psychotic symptoms.
lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis based on the longitudinal history?

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder of bipolar type
Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features
Schizophrenia with comorbid mood features

Add lamotrigine titrated slowly to 200 mg daily for depressive stabilisation
Switch risperidone to quetiapine 600 mg daily for combined antipsychotic-antidepressant effect
Add lithium 450 mg daily as augmentation for treatment-resistant depression
Increase risperidone to 6 mg daily to achieve better overall symptom control

stem: A 27-year-old woman is admitted with a 3-week episode of elevated mood, decreased sleep, pressured speech, grandiosity, and auditory hallucinations. Schizophreniform disorder with mood features given 3 weeks duration currently
Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic with psychotic features
Recurrent brief psychotic disorder with concurrent hypomanic symptoms
Delusional disorder grandiose type with comorbid cyclothymic disorder

stem: A 52-year-old man is referred for assessment. His wife reports 2 years of conviction that their neighbour is conducting surveillance on their home. He has contacted police multiple times and installed security systems. He works as an accountant with no performance issues and maintains friendships. lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management approach?

options.text: Olanzapine 20 mg daily given the chronic and fixed nature of the delusional beliefs
Cognitive behavioural therapy focused directly on delusional beliefs with medication deferred
Therapeutic alliance building with gradual introduction of low-dose antipsychotic
Engage with the patient's concerns about safety and build therapeutic alliance first
Involuntary admission for assessment given persecutory beliefs and police involvement

stem: A 23-year-old woman with no psychiatric history presents with 10 days of disorganised speech, persecutory delusions, and visual hallucinations following a relationship breakdown. She has no drug use. Medical workup including MRI brain, autoimmune encephalitis antibodies, and urine drug screen are negative. She is commenced on risperidone 2 mg daily and symptoms resolve completely within 5 days.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnosis and antipsychotic duration plan?

options.text: Schizophreniform disorder with plan for 6 months minimum antipsychotic treatment
First-episode psychosis with plan for 12-24 months minimum antipsychotic treatment
Acute stress reaction with psychotic features requiring immediate antipsychotic cessation
Schizophrenia prodrome requiring indefinite antipsychotic maintenance therapy
Brief psychotic disorder with short-term antipsychotic and gradual taper after 1-3 months

stem: A 34-year-old woman presents requesting ADHD assessment. She reports lifelong difficulty with organisation, frequently losing belongings, inability to complete work tasks, and relationship difficulties from interrupting others. options.text: Neuropsychological testing showing executive function deficits on computerised assessment
A validated screening questionnaire score exceeding the diagnostic threshold value

Positive response to a stimulant medication trial confirming the underlying diagnosis
Genetic testing confirming dopaminergic pathway variants associated with ADHD phenotype

stem: A 31-year-old man with confirmed ADHD combined type requires pharmacotherapy. He works as a long-haul truck driver needing 12-14 hours daily symptom coverage. Extended-release methylphenidate with dose titration to adequate symptom coverage
Atomoxetine 40 mg daily as it provides continuous around-the-clock coverage
Dexamfetamine immediate-release 10 mg twice daily for strongest symptom control
Lisdexamfetamine 30 mg daily given its 12-14 hour duration of action

stem: A 29-year-old man with confirmed ADHD (childhood diagnosis, lost to follow-up) presents seeking treatment. Guanfacine extended-release as the safest option for substance use comorbidity
Stimulant medication is permanently contraindicated given methamphetamine use disorder

stem: A 26-year-old man with known schizophrenia is brought to the emergency department by police. He is highly agitated, pacing, shouting, and has thrown a chair. He refuses oral medication. Droperidol 10 mg IM with continuous cardiac monitoring for minimum 2 hours

stem: A 26-year-old man admitted with a severe depressive episode has barely spoken for three days. Staff report that he resists being moved and will not eat. He is afebrile.

stem: A 33-year-old man with schizophrenia was admitted 10 days ago for psychotic relapse and commenced on haloperidol 10 mg daily. Commence bromocriptine 2.5 mg three times daily as specific NMS dopamine agonist treatment
Continue haloperidol as cessation could worsen psychosis and features may represent EPS
Administer dantrolene 1 mg/kg IV with concurrent lorazepam and reassess trajectory
Urgent ECT consultation as it is equally effective for both malignant catatonia and NMS

stem:
A 34-year-old primary school teacher attends her GP reporting six weeks of persistent low mood after the end of a 9-year relationship. She describes early morning waking at 0400 (two hours before her alarm), profound diurnal mood variation with mornings worst, weight loss of 4 kg without dieting, marked psychomotor retardation noted by her partner, and complete loss of mood reactivity even when her two cats greet her or her best friend visits.

She is no longer able to plan lessons and has been on personal leave for three weeks. She denies hallucinations, sustained elevated mood, or any prior hypomanic episodes lasting more than a day. She drinks two standard drinks weekly, uses no other substances, and takes no regular medications. She reports passive thoughts of being better off dead but no plan or intent. Her TSH, FBC and UEC last month were unremarkable. PHQ-9 today is 23.

data_table.Examination: Tearful, congruent affect, slowed thought tempo, no thought disorder, no psychotic features.
data_table.Investigations: K-10 score 32. TSH 1.4 mIU/L, Hb 132 g/L, Na 139 mmol/L (all within reference).

lead_in: Which DSM-5 classification and specifier most accurately captures her presentation?

options.text: Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) with intermittent major depressive episodes
Adjustment disorder with depressed mood, severe
Major depressive disorder, single episode, moderate severity, no specifier
Major depressive disorder, single episode, severe, with melancholic features
Bipolar II disorder, current episode depressed with melancholic features

stem:
A 22-year-old apprentice electrician presents with an 8-week history of moderate major depression (PHQ-9 16). He has had no manic episodes, no psychotic symptoms, and denies suicidal ideation. He smokes 10 cigarettes daily, drinks 4 standard drinks weekly, and uses cannabis socially once a month. His chief functional complaints are early morning waking at 0430, fatigue at work and a recent 3 kg weight loss.

He is sexually active with his girlfriend and explicitly raises concerns about sexual side effects after reading about them online. He has no past medication trials, no allergies, no QTc concerns on a recent ECG (QTc 405 ms), and bloods including TSH, FBC, EUC, LFTs and B12 are unremarkable. His older sister had moderate depression that remitted well on sertraline. He and his GP agree to commence an antidepressant today alongside a Mental Health Treatment Plan for CBT.

data_table.Examination: Flat affect, no psychomotor agitation, no psychotic features, MSE otherwise unremarkable.
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 16, K-10 28, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, Hb 145 g/L, ALT 22 U/L, B12 360 pmol/L (all reference).

lead_in: Considering the eTG Psychotropic selection factors (efficacy, tolerability profile, sleep effect, sexual side-effect burden, family-history match), which is the single most appropriate first-line antidepressant?

Sertraline 50 mg orally daily
Venlafaxine XR 75 mg orally daily
Citalopram 20 mg orally daily
Fluoxetine 20 mg orally daily

stem:
A 42-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her partner with 6 hours of agitation, sweating and shivering. She was started on sertraline 100 mg daily six weeks ago for moderate depression. Two days ago she was prescribed tramadol 50 mg QID by another GP for acute lower back pain, and yesterday she began linezolid for a complicated skin infection at a sexual health clinic.

On arrival she is restless and diaphoretic. She has spontaneous clonus in both ankles which is more pronounced on the right, mild rigidity in the lower limbs, hyperreflexia, mydriasis 5 mm bilaterally and an oral temperature of 38.6 deg C. There are no rashes, no neck stiffness and no focal neurological deficits. She has had no haloperidol or other antipsychotics, no recent anaesthetic and no head injury. She has not used St John's wort, MDMA or any other serotonergic agent her partner can identify. Her observations and bloods are recorded below.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 158/96 mmHg, HR 122 bpm, T 38.6 deg C, RR 22, SpO2 98% RA, GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6).
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, mydriasis 5 mm, lower-limb hyperreflexia, spontaneous clonus right > left, mild rigidity legs > arms, bowel sounds hyperactive.
data_table.Investigations: Na 138 mmol/L, K 4.1, creatinine 78 micromol/L, CK 540 U/L, WCC 11.2 x10^9/L, lactate 2.1 mmol/L. ECG: sinus tachycardia, QTc 430 ms.

IV dantrolene with empirical intubation and ICU transfer
IM haloperidol 5 mg for agitation with cardiac monitoring
Withhold sertraline only and continue tramadol with oral paracetamol
Lumbar puncture and empirical IV ceftriaxone for suspected encephalitis

stem:
A 48-year-old woman with a 9-month episode of MDD attends her psychiatrist for review. She started sertraline at 50 mg and titrated to 200 mg daily over 12 weeks with full adherence confirmed by webster pack; she completed an adequate trial with only partial response (PHQ-9 22 to 16). She was then switched to venlafaxine XR titrated to 225 mg daily over a further 10 weeks, again with partial response (PHQ-9 14).

She has engaged consistently with a clinical psychologist for CBT throughout both trials. There has been no hypomania, no psychotic features and no substance use. She has hypertension treated with perindopril 5 mg daily (BP today 128/82) and recent fasting lipids and HbA1c are normal. She has not had ECT or rTMS. She and her psychiatrist agree she meets criteria for treatment-resistant depression and discuss next steps. She is keen to avoid hospital admission. Her TSH is 1.6 mIU/L and B12 is 410 pmol/L. There are no acute suicidal features today.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/82 mmHg, HR 78, weight 72 kg, BMI 25.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

Add tranylcypromine 10 mg twice daily to her current venlafaxine therapy
Augment venlafaxine with aripiprazole 2 to 5 mg orally daily

stem:
A 71-year-old retired engineer is admitted involuntarily with severe major depression with psychotic features. He has held a fixed nihilistic delusion that his bowels have rotted for the past 5 weeks, refuses food and fluids, has lost 9 kg, and has required IV rehydration. He has had two adequate trials of antidepressants (sertraline 200 mg for 8 weeks, then mirtazapine 45 mg for 6 weeks with olanzapine 10 mg added for 4 weeks) without meaningful response, and his consultant proposes electroconvulsive therapy.

He has well-controlled hypertension on amlodipine, an old uncomplicated inferior STEMI six years ago treated with primary PCI (most recent stress echo unremarkable), and a remote history of TIA with normal carotid imaging. He has no intracranial mass, no recent stroke, and no aneurysm. He is currently considered to lack capacity to consent to ECT and his adult daughter is the substitute decision-maker. Routine pre-ECT bloods are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82 mmHg, HR 76, T 36.7 deg C, SpO2 97% RA.

lead_in: Which is the most accurate statement regarding ECT in this patient?

options.text: ECT is absolutely contraindicated because of his prior inferior myocardial infarction
ECT is first-line for severe MDD with psychotic features and food refusal

All antidepressants must be ceased before ECT to avoid serotonin syndrome
Cognitive screening is unnecessary because he has no documented dementia diagnosis

stem:
A 27-year-old man presents to the emergency department at 0200 brought by police after his housemate found him writing letters to family members and packing personal effects into labelled boxes. He recently separated from his fiancee and was dismissed from his job in mining 3 weeks ago. He has a 6-month history of worsening depression treated by his GP with escitalopram 20 mg daily.

Tonight he tells you he obtained his late father's licensed firearm from his mother's garage on the weekend and stored it under his bed. He has researched suicide methods online for the past fortnight, has selected a remote bush location, and has chosen tomorrow as the day. He denies prior attempts, has no current intoxication (breath alcohol 0.00), and identifies his younger sister and his dog as the only things keeping him alive at present. data_table.Investigations: Bloods unremarkable. Risk assessment summarised in stem.

lead_in: What is the single most important immediate intervention?

options.text: Discharge home with a written safety plan and beyondblue helpline contact details
Increase his escitalopram to 30 mg daily and reassess in clinic in one week
Remove the firearm via police and admit involuntarily under the Mental Health Act
Administer IM olanzapine 10 mg for chemical restraint and continued observation
Have him sign a no-suicide contract and discharge to housemate supervision overnight

stem:

She describes three previous depressive episodes since age 22, each lasting 3 to 4 months and treated symptomatically. Her partner confirms these episodes are clearly different from her baseline, are noticeable to friends, and recur every 6 to 9 months. She has never been hospitalised for mental health issues, has never been psychotic, and has never required time off work during these elevated periods, which she actually finds productive. She uses no substances. TFTs, FBC and EUC are normal. She has no medical comorbidities and is not pregnant.

data_table.Examination: Currently euthymic-to-mildly low mood, reactive affect, no psychomotor change, no psychotic features, MMSE 30/30.
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.5 mIU/L, Hb 132 g/L, urine beta-hCG negative. Urine drug screen negative.

lead_in: Which diagnosis best fits her presentation?

Bipolar II disorder, currently depressed phase
Cyclothymic disorder with depressive features
Recurrent major depressive disorder, moderate severity
Borderline personality disorder with affective instability

stem:
A 38-year-old man with known bipolar I disorder is brought to the emergency department by his wife and police after 6 days of escalating behaviour. He has slept 90 minutes per night, has not eaten meaningfully for 3 days, has spent over $40,000 on cryptocurrency, has been propositioning strangers in shopping centres, and tonight stripped naked in the front yard while preaching to neighbours.

In the ED he is loud, intrusive and grandiose, claiming to have been appointed Pope by direct revelation. He stopped taking his lithium 750 mg nocte six months ago because he felt better. He uses no illicit substances and a urine drug screen is negative. His wife reports that during previous severe episodes a mood stabiliser plus an antipsychotic worked well.

He has no medical comorbidities and no antipsychotic allergies. He has been placed on an emergency assessment order under the state Mental Health Act and a bed on the acute psychiatric ward is being arranged.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

options.text: Sertraline 100 mg daily plus oral diazepam 10 mg TDS for agitation

stem:
A 29-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stabilised on olanzapine 10 mg nocte and valproate 1000 mg daily following an inpatient admission for acute mania three months ago. She wishes to come off valproate because she and her partner plan to conceive in the next year, and her psychiatrist proposes substituting lithium for long-term maintenance. She has no renal disease, no cardiac history, and is on no other medications.

She drinks one cup of coffee per day and no alcohol. The psychiatrist plans to commence lithium carbonate 250 mg nocte and titrate to a serum level of 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L for maintenance. She has read patient information about lithium and is concerned about tremor, weight change and the impact of dehydration on her dose. She and her partner are also discussing how she will manage acute illness with vomiting in future, and she has asked her psychiatrist to write a sick-day plan once treatment is established. Pre-initiation tests are now ordered.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/74 mmHg, HR 70, weight 64 kg, BMI 22.
data_table.Examination: MSE: euthymic, reactive affect, no psychomotor change, no psychotic features.
data_table.Investigations: Pre-lithium baseline pending.

lead_in: Which combination of baseline investigations is most appropriate before commencing lithium?

options.text: Echocardiogram, 24-hour urinary creatinine clearance and dexamethasone suppression test

FBC, UEC/eGFR, calcium, TFTs, pregnancy test and resting ECG
