FBC and UEC alone, with thyroid and calcium reviewed only after one year

stem:
A 64-year-old woman maintained on lithium carbonate 500 mg nocte for bipolar I disorder for 12 years is brought to the emergency department by her daughter after 4 days of worsening coarse hand tremor, unsteady gait with two falls, slurred speech and confusion. Her usual psychiatrist documented her last lithium level 4 months ago as 0.7 mmol/L with normal renal function.

Two weeks ago her GP commenced indapamide 2.5 mg daily for newly diagnosed hypertension and naproxen 500 mg BD for an osteoarthritic knee flare. She has been drinking less water than usual during a current heatwave (37 deg C ambient). She has no fever, no diarrhoea, and no chest pain. On arrival she is drowsy but rousable and has a coarse postural tremor, ataxic gait and mild dysarthria.

There is no clonus, no rigidity. ECG shows sinus rhythm with T-wave flattening. Initial bedside lithium level returns at 3.8 mmol/L, creatinine has risen from baseline 70 to 168 micromol/L and sodium is 142 mmol/L with no anion-gap acidosis.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82 mmHg, HR 62, T 36.7 deg C, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA, GCS 14 (E3 V5 M6).
data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor, mild dysarthria, broad-based ataxic gait, hyporeflexia bilaterally, no clonus, no rigidity.
data_table.Investigations: Lithium level 2.4 mmol/L. Na 134 mmol/L, K 3.6, urea 9.4 mmol/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 78), eGFR 38. TSH 2.1 mIU/L. Calcium 2.42 mmol/L. VBG: pH 7.39, lactate 1.8. ECG: sinus rhythm, T-wave flattening, QTc 420 ms.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g orally and reduce lithium to half dose tonight
IV sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg and observation on the ward overnight
Continue lithium and recheck a 12-hour post-dose level in 6 hours
Withhold lithium and naproxen only, continue indapamide and IV fluids
Withhold all three drugs, IV 0.9% saline, urgent dialysis with nephrology

stem:

This morning she said the baby was sent by spirits and should be returned to them. She has not been violent but is intermittently dishevelled. She has no past psychiatric history but her older sister has bipolar I. There are no infective symptoms, no headachebstetric review and bloods are unremarkable. data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78 mmHg, HR 92, T 36.8 deg C, RR 18, SpO2 99% RA.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

Lumbar puncture and empirical IV aciclovir for suspected postpartum HSV encephalitis
Oral diazepam 10 mg and discharge home overnight with the partner supervising
Admit to a Mother-Baby Unit, start antipsychotic, plan infant safety with partner

stem:

She describes feeling wound up most days, broken sleep with onset insomnia from rumination, muscle tension, irritability noted by her partner, and difficulty concentrating at work where her billable output has fallen by 25 percent. data_table.Examination: MSE: mildly anxious, no psychomotor change, no psychotic features, insight good.

stem:

Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with associated anxiety

stem:
A 35-year-old paramedic presents to a psychologist for assessment. She describes spending 2 to 3 hours each evening repeatedly checking that the front door is locked, the gas is off, and that her ambulance bag is fully stocked. She acknowledges that the checking is excessive and irrational, finds the urge intensely distressing, and the rituals interfere with her sleep and family life.

She also describes recurrent intrusive images of a fatal paediatric resuscitation she attended 18 months ago, occasional flashbacks triggered by sirens, and avoidance of certain suburbs where the call occurred. She no longer enjoys her work and has been on light duties for 4 months. She is not perfectionistic at baseline, does not collect lists or rules, is socially warm and flexible.

She has no past psychiatric history, drinks 4 standard drinks per week, no illicit substances. Sleep is broken by both nightmares and rituals; mood is low but secondary to the above.

data_table.Examination: MSE: anxious, congruent affect, intrusive thoughts and avoidance, insight preserved, no psychotic features.
data_table.Investigations: K-10 27, PCL-5 49 (above clinical threshold). Bloods unremarkable.

lead_in: Which combination of diagnoses best fits her presentation?

options.text: Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder as a single diagnosis explaining all features
Generalised anxiety disorder with intrusive rumination as the unifying construct
Obsessive-compulsive disorder AND post-traumatic stress disorder, both meeting criteria
Post-traumatic stress disorder alone, with compulsive checking as a coping behaviour
Adjustment disorder with anxious mood and work-related stress as the trigger

subtopic_detail: OCD vs OCPD vs PTSD discrimination

stem:
A 41-year-old former soldier presents to his GP 14 months after returning from a deployment where he witnessed a fatal IED incident. He describes nightly nightmares, intrusive images on most days, marked avoidance of news and crowds, persistent negative beliefs that the world is dangerous, hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, insomnia and irritability. He has a PCL-5 score of 54 (above clinical threshold).

He is not currently suicidal, is engaged in work part-time, drinks 6 standard drinks per evening (AUDIT 16) and uses no illicit substances. He is engaged with Open Arms Veterans and Families Counselling and is keen to consider trauma-focused therapy. He has not previously had pharmacotherapy or psychological treatment for PTSD. He has hypertension treated with amlodipine 5 mg daily (BP 132/82).

He has no allergies, no cardiac disease and no significant past psychiatric history He has read about SSRIs for PTSD but is keen to try psychological treatment first if available.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/82 mmHg, HR 76, BMI 28.
data_table.Examination: MSE: anxious, hypervigilant, mood low, no psychotic features, no current SI.
data_table.Investigations: PCL-5 54, AUDIT 16, K-10 31, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, LFTs ALT 38 (normal).

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg as required for nightmares and hypervigilance episodes
Trauma-focused CBT or EMDR with concurrent alcohol use disorder management
Sertraline 50 mg orally daily as first-line monotherapy with weekly GP review
Quetiapine 25 mg nocte for sleep and lifestyle advice only at this visit
Critical incident stress debriefing within the next two weeks as single session

stem:
A 24-year-old violinist auditioning for an orchestral position presents to her GP 4 weeks before her audition. She describes intense fear of trembling hands, sweating and a quavering voice during public performance, but is socially comfortable in everyday interactions, meeting new people, and giving casual presentations at her teaching work. She has never had a panic attack outside performance situations, and has no avoidance of social settings, no generalised worrynd no trauma history.

She has previously taken a beta blocker borrowed from a colleague before one audition with good effect but is unsure of the dose. She has no asthma, no diabetesllergies. She has access to a psychologist through a Mental Health Treatment Plan and is open to longer-term therapy after the audition. Resting HR 78, BP 116/74, ECG sinus rhythm with normal PR interval.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/74 mmHg, HR 78, RR 14, SpO2 99% RA, BMI 22.
data_table.Examination: MSE: mildly anxious about audition, otherwise normal. Cardiorespiratory exam normal.
data_table.Investigations: Resting ECG sinus rhythm rate 78, PR 152 ms. TSH 1.6 mIU/L, EUC normal.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management for the audition?

options.text: Propranolol 10-40 mg orally pre-event PRN, with CBT referral for longer-term care
Diazepam 5 mg orally one hour before the performance as a single dose
Sertraline 50 mg orally daily commencing immediately for ongoing daily use
Quetiapine 25 mg orally as required prior to performance for anxiolysis
Cannabidiol oil orally prior to the performance as an alternative anxiolytic

subtopic_detail: Social anxiety disorder - performance subtype management

stem:
A 36-year-old man presents to his GP 4 days after stopping venlafaxine XR 150 mg daily, which he had taken for 8 months for moderate depression. He stopped abruptly while on a 5-day camping trip after forgetting to pack his medication. Over the past 48 hours he has developed flu-like symptoms with no fever, dizziness on standing, brief electric-shock sensations in his head when he turns it (brain zaps), nausea, insomnia with vivid dreams, low mood, irritability and anxiety.

He has not had any new infectious contacts, no head trauma, no headache and no neurological deficit. He has no chest pain, no palpitations. He still has his original venlafaxine prescription at home. His depression had remitted well on treatment and he had not yet discussed planned cessation with his GP. He has no other medications, no allergies and no significant past medical history.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 120/78 mmHg lying, 108/70 standing, HR 80 lying, 96 standing, T 36.6 deg C, RR 16, SpO2 99% RA.
data_table.Examination: Mildly tremulous, normal neurological exam, no neck stiffness, no rash.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, CRP unremarkable. ECG sinus rhythm QTc 410 ms.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure as depressive relapse and start mirtazapine 30 mg nocte tonight
Lumbar puncture and empirical IV ceftriaxone for suspected meningitis
Admit for IV fluids and treat empirically as viral gastroenteritis overnight
Restart venlafaxine XR 150 mg daily and plan a gradual taper with GP
Increase venlafaxine to 225 mg daily once restarted and review in two weeks

stem:
A 74-year-old retired accountant is brought to clinic by his daughter with a 4-month history of progressively worsening low mood, total loss of interest in his lifelong hobby of bridge, marked early morning waking by 0330, 8 kg unintentional weight loss, profound guilt that he is ruining the family financially despite stable superannuation, and pervasive slowing of speech and movement noted by family. He describes his mood as distinctly worse in the morning, lifting somewhat by afternoon.

He has had passive suicidal thoughts but no plan. He has not had hallucinations or delusions. He has had two previous depressive episodes in his 50s, both responding to escitalopram. His current medications are ramipril 5 mg, atorvastatin 20 mg, and metformin 1 g BD. Bloods including TSH, FBC, EUC, LFTs, B12, folate, calcium and HbA1c are unremarkable. MMSE today is 27/30 (lost 2 on serial sevens, 1 on recall, attributed to concentration not cognitive decline).

His daughter is highly engaged and able to provide reliable collateral history covering the last 6 months His daughter notes he had no reactivity to a recent visit from his grandchildren and ate nothing at the family dinner.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/82 mmHg, HR 64, weight 68 kg (down from 76).
data_table.Examination: MSE: severe psychomotor retardation, monotone speech, depressed affect, mood-congruent worthlessness; no psychosis. MMSE 27/30.
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.6, B12 410, folate 18, calcium 2.38, HbA1c 6.8%, eGFR 78. ECG sinus 60 QTc 420 ms.

lead_in: Which feature most specifically supports an MDD specifier of melancholic features?

options.text: Past responsiveness of his prior depressive episodes to escitalopram therapy
Hyperphagia and hypersomnia accompanied by leaden paralysis sensation
Patient demographic factors including age over 65 and recent retirement
Anhedonia plus AM-worse diurnal mood, early waking, retardation and guilt
Presence of passive suicidal ideation without any specific plan or intent

subtopic_detail: MDD with melancholic features in older adult

stem:
A 28-year-old woman has had recurrent depression since adolescence. She describes that her mood lifts noticeably when good things happen (a friend visits, she gets praised at work) but plunges back within hours. She sleeps 11 hours daily including a 2-hour afternoon nap, has gained 12 kg in 9 months, experiences a profound leaden paralysis sensation in her limbs that makes physical activity feel impossible, and is acutely sensitive to perceived criticism or rejection (a tone of voice from her supervisor preoccupies her for days).

She has had two prior trials of antidepressants: sertraline 100 mg for 10 weeks (PHQ-9 16 to 12) and escitalopram 20 mg for 12 weeks (no further improvement). She has no manic or hypomanic episodes, no psychotic features. She has well-controlled hypothyroidism on thyroxine 75 mcg with TSH 1.8.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/78 mmHg, HR 72, weight 84 kg, BMI 30.
data_table.Examination: MSE: depressed mood with episodic brightening, weight gain, hypersomnolence, leaden affect; no psychotic features. MMSE 30/30.
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 18, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, FBC, UEC, LFTs unremarkable, fasting BSL 5.2, HbA1c 5.6%.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Add nortriptyline 50 mg orally nocte to her current escitalopram therapy
Increase escitalopram beyond licensed maximum and add bupropion adjunct
Cross-taper to phenelzine MAOI with washout, dietary restriction and specialist care
Substitute mirtazapine 30 mg orally nocte for her current escitalopram dose
Add levothyroxine 25 mcg orally daily to her current escitalopram as a thyroid-augmentation strategy for treatment-resistant depression

subtopic_detail: Atypical depression - feature recognition and MAOI escalation

stem:
A 24-year-old hospitality worker self-presents to a community mental health team after an overdose of 12 paracetamol tablets last night following an argument with her current partner of three weeks. During the assessment interview she tells the registrar that her partner is the only person who has ever truly understood her, and that the team nurse who saw her on arrival was 'cold and judgemental', in stark contrast with 'you, the first to really listen'.

She reports two prior emergency presentations in the past year following similar low-lethality overdoses, longstanding cutting of her forearms since age 15, recurrent feelings of emptiness, and intense difficulty being alone. She denies sustained elevated mood, persistent psychotic symptoms, and has no current diurnal mood variation, no early morning waking, no anhedonia outside relationship distress, and her mood reactively brightens when discussing her partner.

Father describes lifelong rapid shifts between idealising and devaluing close friends since adolescence. Serum paracetamol below the treatment line at 8 hours; LFTs normal. She has had no episodes of pervasive low mood lasting beyond a few days.

data_table.Examination: Alert, mildly tearful then bright affect within the same interview, no thought disorder, no perceptual disturbance, multiple superficial healed and recent linear scars to bilateral forearms.
data_table.Investigations: Serum paracetamol below Rumack-Matthew treatment line at 8 hours. ALT 24 U/L, INR 1.0, K-10 32.

lead_in: Which clinical feature most strongly supports a primary diagnosis of borderline personality disorder OVER major depressive disorder in this presentation?

options.text: Rapid splitting of the treating team within a single assessment, in the context of lifelong pattern of idealisation/devaluation since adolescence
Multiple low-lethality self-harm episodes recurring since adolescence in the context of chronic interpersonal stressors
Two emergency department presentations in the past month after acute relationship arguments with her current partner
Chronic subjective feelings of emptiness reported over many years, present across multiple interpersonal contexts
Mood reactivity observed during the interview, with tearful affect that brightens markedly in response to supportive engagement

stem:
A 30-year-old man is reviewed in a community mental health clinic after release from a 12-month custodial sentence for aggravated assault. Documented history: truancy from age 11, cruelty to a neighbour's cat at age 13, fire-setting at 14, multiple arrests for fraud and driving offences as a young adult, pattern of brief sexual relationships ended by him without distress. He is referred because his probation officer is concerned about his mental state.

On interview he is articulate, charming, shows little remorse for the assault and frames it as the victim's fault. He denies persistent low mood, sustained elevated mood, hallucinations, recurrent self-harm, chronic emptiness, fear of abandonment, or rapid shifts in his view of others (no splitting pattern on collateral). Collateral from his sister confirms longstanding deceitfulness, irritability and callous disregard for the welfare of partners and family across at least the past decade. He drinks heavily on weekends, uses cocaine intermittently and is on no regular medications.

data_table.Examination: Calm, oriented, no thought disorder, no perceptual disturbance, MSE notable for shallow affect and lack of remorse.
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for cocaine metabolites and cannabinoids. FBC, EUC, LFTs, TSH unremarkable.

lead_in: Which feature most specifically supports antisocial personality disorder OVER borderline personality disorder in this man?

options.text: Cocaine and heavy episodic alcohol use without any documented evidence of childhood conduct disorder or criminal disregard for others
Multiple short-lived sexual relationships ended by the patient without any documented exploitation, aggression or callous disregard for others
Evidence of conduct disorder before age 15 (truancy, cruelty to animals, fire-setting) followed by adult callous disregard for the welfare of others and lack of remorse
Irritability and verbal aggression toward family members without any documented evidence of childhood conduct disorder or adult criminality
Articulate self-presentation and use of charm during interview without any documented childhood conduct disorder or adult exploitation history

stem:
A 45-year-old corporate lawyer is referred by his GP after his wife of 12 years left him last month. He attends reluctantly, stating he expects to be seen by 'the head of the department' and finds the waiting room beneath him. He describes his career in detail, refers to himself as one of the best litigators in the country and as misunderstood by colleagues who he believes envy him.

He reports that his wife 'failed to appreciate his achievements' and that her departure has caused mild low mood but no anhedonia, no neurovegetative symptoms and no suicidal ideation. He has no history of self-harm, no chronic emptiness, no fear of abandonment, no impulsive risk-taking and no history of conduct disorder, criminal behaviour or callous disregard for others' rights. Collateral from his sister describes a lifelong (since early adulthood) tendency to demand admiration, exploit junior staff to advance his cases, and react to mild criticism with prolonged contemptuous anger. He drinks 8 standard drinks weekly and is on no regular medications.

data_table.Examination: Well dressed, expansive manner, reactive affect, no thought disorder, no perceptual disturbance, K-10 18.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, EUC, LFT, TSH all within reference range.

lead_in: Which DSM-5 personality disorder best fits this clinical pattern, and what most reliably distinguishes it from a closely related diagnosis?

options.text: Histrionic personality disorder - excessive emotionality and attention-seeking; distinguished from narcissism by dramatic emotionality without grandiose self-importance
Borderline personality disorder - identity disturbance, unstable relationships and self-harm; distinguished by affective instability rather than grandiose self-importance
Antisocial personality disorder - exploitation, lack of remorse and disregard for others' rights; distinguished by childhood conduct disorder before age 15
Narcissistic personality disorder - grandiose self-importance, need for admiration, exploitativeness and rage at criticism; distinguished from ASPD by absence of childhood conduct disorder
Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder - preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism and control; distinguished by rigidity rather than admiration-seeking grandiosity

stem:
A 38-year-old accountant is referred by his GP for psychiatric review at his wife's insistence. He works 11-hour days, refuses to delegate work because no one else does it correctly, keeps meticulous spreadsheets of household expenditure, and becomes irritable when family members leave items out of place. His wife reports he is rigid about routines, hoards old work documents 'for completeness', and is reluctant to spend money even when finances are comfortable.

He sees these behaviours as appropriate professional standards and is not distressed by them; rather, he is troubled by his family's resistance to his system. He denies intrusive unwanted thoughts, denies ritualised compulsions performed to neutralise anxiety, and has no history of contamination fears, checking compulsions or symmetry-driven rituals. His mood, sleep, appetite and concentration are unremarkable and he has no history of self-harm. His MSE is unremarkable except for circumstantial speech and a markedly orderly presentation.

data_table.Examination: Punctual, suit pressed, papers arranged precisely, K-10 14, no anxiety on observation.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, EUC, LFT, TSH within reference.

lead_in: Which feature most strongly supports obsessive-compulsive personality disorder rather than obsessive-compulsive disorder?

options.text: Rigid preoccupation with order and control
Hoarding of work documents at home
Reluctance to delegate tasks to others
Long working hours with high productivity
Behaviours felt as appropriate, not intrusive

subtopic_detail: Safety planning vs admission decision in BPD
stem:
A 23-year-old woman with established BPD attends the emergency department after taking 8 paracetamol tablets following a fight with her current partner. This is her fourth low-lethality presentation in the past 6 months. Serum paracetamol is below the treatment line at 8 hours and LFTs are normal. On interview she is engaged, has agreed to handover of remaining medication to a relative, identifies her older sister as a strong protective factor able to stay with her tonight, and has a current outpatient DBT clinician who can see her tomorrow morning.

She denies current plan or intent for further self-harm, denies psychotic features, and her K-10 is 28. She has previously had a 4-week voluntary admission that she describes as destabilising, with an increase in self-harm in the week after discharge. Her treating team has a documented care plan recommending brief, focused community management for low-lethality presentations.

data_table.Examination: Alert, reactive affect, no thought disorder, no perceptual disturbance, multiple healed and recent linear forearm scars.
data_table.Investigations: Paracetamol below Rumack-Matthew treatment line, ALT 22 U/L, INR 1.0, K-10 28.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discharge with a structured safety plan and next-day DBT review
Brief admission for 48 hours to monitor for further self-harm
Apply Mental Health Act involuntary admission criteria
Commence olanzapine 5 mg nocte and discharge
Refer for inpatient DBT program as next-day transfer

stem:
A 78-year-old woman is admitted with a community-acquired pneumonia and started on intravenous benzylpenicillin and oral doxycycline. On day 2 the nursing staff call you because she is restless, climbing out of bed, picking at the bed sheets and intermittently shouting at staff she has known well during the admission. Her daughter, who lives with her, says her cognition was normal at baseline last week and she manages her finances independently.

On interview her attention fluctuates: she can count backwards from 20 to 10 with multiple errors and her conversation drifts mid-sentence. She is not orientated to date or place. Six hours earlier on the morning ward round she had been calm and orientated. Vital signs show T 37.9, HR 102, BP 128/72, SpO2 95% on 2 L NP, RR 22. CXR confirms a right lower lobe consolidation. Sodium is 132 mmol/L, urea 8.2 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, WCC 14.2 x10^9/L.

data_table.Examination: Restless, picking at sheets, fluctuating attention, disoriented to date/place, no focal neurology, RLL crackles
data_table.Investigations: Na 132 mmol/L, urea 8.2, Cr 88, WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, CXR RLL consolidation
data_table.Medications: Benzylpenicillin IV, doxycycline PO, paracetamol PRN

lead_in: Which clinical tool finding best confirms a diagnosis of delirium in this patient?

options.text: MMSE score of 18 today compared with prior 28
Acute onset and fluctuation PLUS inattention PLUS disorganised thinking or altered consciousness
MoCA score of 17 with deficits across multiple cognitive domains
GCS of 14 with mild reduction in eye opening
Geriatric Depression Scale score of 9 of 15

stem:
An 84-year-old woman is admitted from a residential aged care facility with a urinary tract infection. On day 3 of intravenous ceftriaxone the nursing staff are concerned that she is withdrawn, eating poorly, sleeping during the day and unable to engage with the ward physiotherapist. Her usual GP letter from 2 weeks ago documents independent ADLs with walking aid, no prior mood disorder, and stable cognition with an MMSE of 27 at her last GP review.

On examination she is drowsy but rousable, slow to respond, attention is markedly impaired on backwards-counting, and her thinking is disorganised when she does engage. She has no thoughts of suicide and her affect is flat rather than clearly sad. Sodium is 128 mmol/L, urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 102 micromol/L, WCC 12.6 x10^9/L, CRP 84 mg/L. She is on paracetamol regularly and was started on oxycodone 5 mg PRN for hip pain two days ago.

data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, markedly impaired attention, disorganised thinking, flat affect, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Na 128 mmol/L, urea 12, Cr 102, WCC 12.6, CRP 84, MSU growing E. coli sensitive to ceftriaxone
data_table.Medications: Ceftriaxone IV, paracetamol regular, oxycodone 5 mg PRN (commenced day 1)

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence sertraline 25 mg daily for late-life depression
Commence haloperidol 0.5 mg BD for behavioural disturbance
Stop oxycodone, correct sodium and treat the urinary infection
Arrange CT brain to exclude an acute infarct
Refer to consultation-liaison psychiatry for ECT consideration

stem:
A 79-year-old man is brought to his GP by his wife who reports a 12-month gradual decline in short-term memory with two recent episodes of getting lost in a familiar suburb, slowly worsening word-finding difficulty, and recent difficulty managing his medications and bills. He denies low mood, anhedonia or suicidal ideation. He sleeps well, eats adequately, and his interest in lawn bowls is preserved when his wife sets out the equipment for him.

Over the past three months his cognition has plateaued without further sudden deterioration, his attention on serial 7s is mildly impaired but not fluctuating, and his MMSE today is 22 of 30 with deficits in delayed recall and orientation. Examination is unremarkable with no focal neurology. CT brain shows generalised cortical atrophy without infarcts or mass. Sodium, urea, B12, TSH, calcium, liver function, MSU and FBC are all within reference range. He is on perindopril and metformin only.

data_table.Examination: Pleasant, attentive at interview, mild word-finding pauses, MMSE 22/30, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Na 138, urea 5.2, Cr 82, B12 380, TSH 1.6, Ca 2.32, ALT 24, MSU negative, FBC normal, CT brain: generalised cortical atrophy
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily, metformin 500 mg BD

lead_in: Which feature most strongly favours dementia over either delirium or late-life depression?

options.text: Preserved interest in usual hobbies when supported
MMSE of 22 with deficits in delayed recall
Generalised cortical atrophy on CT brain
Gradual progression over 12 months without acute fluctuation
Wife's observation that he gets lost in familiar areas

stem:
An 82-year-old woman with moderate Alzheimer dementia is reviewed in her residential aged care facility after staff request medication for behavioural disturbance. Over the past two weeks she has become more agitated in the late afternoon, calling out for her late husband, attempting to leave the unit, and resisting personal care. There is no change in her usual medications, no fever days, and a recent MSU was negative.

She is eating and drinking adequately and her sleep is broken with daytime napping. A pain assessment using the Abbey Pain Scale is 3 of 18, but staff have noticed she grimaces when transferred from chair to bed. The behavioural disturbance is not associated with risk of physical harm to herself or staff. Her family is willing to be involved with care.

data_table.Examination: Restless in late afternoon, calling for husband, mild grimace on transfers, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: MSU negative, FBC, EUC, CRP unremarkable, no fever
data_table.Medications: Donepezil 10 mg daily, paracetamol PRN, perindopril 4 mg daily

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Risperidone 0.25 mg BD for behavioural symptoms
Lorazepam 0.5 mg BD scheduled for agitation
Increase donepezil from 10 mg to 23 mg daily
Citalopram 10 mg daily as adjunct for agitation
Scheduled regular paracetamol plus structured environmental measures

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic risk in elderly with dementia
stem:
A 79-year-old man with moderate Alzheimer dementia has had three weeks of distressing persistent persecutory delusions that staff are stealing from him, with intermittent verbal aggression toward his wife. Non-pharmacological measures including environmental modification, regular toileting, scheduled analgesia for known knee osteoarthritis, family attendance and a structured daily routine have been trialled for two weeks with limited effect. There is no delirium screen positive: he is alert, attention is not fluctuating, and his usual cognitive performance has not changed over the past three months.

He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidaemia and previous TIA. His current medications are perindopril, metformin, atorvastatin and aspirin. He has no QT-prolonging medications and his recent ECG showed QTc 432 ms. The family asks whether medication is now appropriate and how long any antipsychotic would be continued.

data_table.Examination: Alert, attention preserved, persistent persecutory delusions, no neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: FBC, EUC, LFT, CRP, MSU all unremarkable, ECG QTc 432 ms
data_table.Medications: Perindopril, metformin, atorvastatin, aspirin

lead_in: Which prescribing approach best balances benefit and harm?

options.text: Risperidone 0.25 mg BD reviewed at 12 weeks for ongoing clinical need
Olanzapine 10 mg nocte continued indefinitely without scheduled review
Haloperidol 2 mg BD for ongoing delusional content and agitation
Quetiapine 100 mg BD as first-line treatment for psychosis
Lorazepam 1 mg TDS scheduled regularly for ongoing agitation

stem:
A 74-year-old man is brought to the GP by his daughter with 6 months of fluctuating attention and cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations of small children in his lounge room, and 4 months of mild bilateral cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia and a slow shuffling gait. He has had two unexplained falls in the past two months. He has no resting tremor of note.

He has no prior psychiatric history, no alcohol or substance use, and his medications are perindopril and metformin only. Bloods, B12, TSH, sodium and CT brain are unremarkable. MMSE is 22 of 30 with prominent fluctuation between assessments two weeks apart. There are no features of stroke, no acute infectionation. The daughter asks what should be done about the visual hallucinations which are now distressing him in the evenings.

data_table.Examination: Bradykinesia, bilateral cogwheel rigidity, shuffling gait, fluctuating attention, well-formed visual hallucinations
data_table.Investigations: FBC, EUC, B12, TSH, MSU, CT brain all unremarkable, MMSE 22/30 (fluctuating)
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily, metformin 500 mg BD

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step for the distressing visual hallucinations?

options.text: Commence haloperidol 0.5 mg BD
Trial rivastigmine titrated to 6 mg BD oral
Commence risperidone 0.25 mg BD
Start levodopa-carbidopa at low dose
Lorazepam 0.5 mg PRN for distress

stem:
A 72-year-old retired engineer presents to his GP at his wife's prompting with 9 months of subjective forgetfulness, including occasional missed appointments and a tendency to repeat questions in conversation. His wife agrees there has been a noticeable decline compared with two years ago. Crucially, he remains independent with all instrumental activities of daily living: he drives safely on familiar routes, manages the household finances and his self-administered medications, prepares meals and uses his computer for hobbies.

He has no mood symptoms and his K-10 is 12. He has no fluctuation in attention, no hallucinations and no Parkinsonism. His MMSE is 28 of 30 with mild deficits in delayed recall, but a MoCA is 23 of 30, with deficits across delayed recall, visuospatial function and abstraction. Sodium, B12, folate, TSH, calcium, FBC and CT brain are within reference. He asks what the diagnosis is and what to do next.

data_table.Examination: Pleasant, attentive, mild word-finding pauses, no Parkinsonism, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: MMSE 28/30, MoCA 23/30, Na 139, B12 410, folate 18, TSH 1.8, Ca 2.34, FBC normal, CT brain mild atrophy
data_table.Medications: Atorvastatin 20 mg nocte

lead_in: Which classification and next step is most appropriate?

options.text: Major neurocognitive disorder - commence donepezil
Normal ageing - no review needed
Mild cognitive impairment - monitor with annual cognitive review
Vascular dementia - commence aspirin and statin
Subjective cognitive decline only - no investigations indicated

stem:
A 79-year-old woman with mild Alzheimer dementia is admitted with a displaced intracapsular fractured neck of femur after a fall at home. The orthopaedic team plan a hemiarthroplasty within 48 hours. On interview she is alert and conversant, oriented to person and place, knows the year but not the date. She knows she has broken her hip and that the doctors want to do an operation to put it back together.

She can repeat back, in her own words, that the operation involves replacing part of the bone, that risks include bleeding, infection and clots, and that without surgery she would be bed-bound with significant pain. She says she wants to have the surgery so she can walk again. Her MoCA today is 22 of 30 with deficits in delayed recall and visuospatial domains.

data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented to person/place, MoCA 22/30, conversant, no acute confusion
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118, EUC unremarkable, INR 1.0, ECG NSR, AP pelvis: displaced intracapsular NOF fracture
data_table.Medications: Donepezil 10 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, paracetamol 1 g QID

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate determination of capacity for this surgical consent?

options.text: She lacks capacity because her MoCA is below 26
She lacks capacity because of her dementia diagnosis
Defer to her son to provide substitute consent
She has capacity for this specific decision at this time
Request a Mental Health Act assessment for involuntary treatment

stem:
A 78-year-old woman is reviewed by her GP for a 10-week history of low mood, anhedonia, early morning waking, 4 kg weight loss, poor concentration and pervasive guilt about being a burden on her daughter. She has had passive thoughts of being better off dead with no plan or intent. She meets criteria for a moderate major depressive episode with K-10 of 34 and PHQ-9 of 17.

She lives alone, mobilises with a walking stick after a previous hip fracture, has a documented falls risk and an annual fracture risk on FRAX. Her comorbidities are hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and stage 3a CKD with eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her current medications are perindopril, metformin, atorvastatin and hydrochlorothiazide. Sodium is 134 mmol/L, normal otherwise. She has no prior antidepressant trial. Her ECG QTc is 432 ms. After discussion of psychological therapy and lifestyle measures, she agrees to commence an antidepressant.

data_table.Examination: Tearful, mild psychomotor slowing, no psychotic features, gait with stick, K-10 34, PHQ-9 17
data_table.Investigations: Na 134, K 4.2, Cr 96, eGFR 52, ALT 22, TSH 1.6, ECG QTc 432 ms
data_table.Medications: Perindopril, metformin, atorvastatin, hydrochlorothiazide

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial antidepressant?

options.text: Amitriptyline 25 mg nocte titrated weekly
Citalopram 40 mg daily as initial dose
Venlafaxine XR 150 mg daily as initial SNRI
Mirtazapine 45 mg nocte to address sleep and appetite
Sertraline 25 mg daily, monitor sodium and falls

stem:
A 31-year-old woman is reviewed at her 6-week postnatal visit. She had a normal vaginal birth of a healthy term infant; the pregnancy was planned and uncomplicated. Over the past 3 weeks she has experienced persistent low mood, anhedonia, broken sleep beyond what is explained by the baby's feeds, tearfulness, guilt about her mothering and difficulty bonding. Her EPDS is 16 with item 10 negative for self-harm.

She has no prior major depressive episodes, no bipolar history, no psychotic features, and no current thoughts of harm to herself or the baby. She is exclusively breastfeeding and prefers to start with a psychological therapy before considering medication. She has a supportive partner and family, no current significant stressors beyond the role transition to parenthood, no relationship grief or recent bereavement. She works in clerical administration and has private health insurance covering psychology sessions.

data_table.Examination: Tearful, reactive affect, no psychotic features, bonded enough to feed and care for the baby, no thoughts of harm
data_table.Investigations: EPDS 16, TSH 1.8, Hb 124, ferritin 38, B12 380

lead_in: Which structured psychological therapy is best supported as first-line for her presentation per the COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline?

options.text: Acceptance and commitment therapy as first-line for perinatal depression in this primiparous woman with mild-to-moderate symptom severity today
Interpersonal therapy (IPT) - structured 12-16 sessions focusing on role transitions and interpersonal conflict, with the strongest perinatal-specific RCT evidence base
Long-term psychodynamic psychotherapy with weekly sessions over 12-18 months focusing on early attachment patterns and developmental themes
Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR) targeting any incidental trauma history rather than the perinatal mood presentation itself
Dialectical behaviour therapy with weekly group skills training plus individual sessions over a 12-month treatment program as first-line

subtopic_detail: Motivational interviewing and stages of change
stem:
A 52-year-old man attends his GP at his wife's request after a recent admission with alcoholic gastritis. He drinks 8-10 standard drinks daily, has done so for at least 10 years, and acknowledges that his drinking 'might be a bit too much' but feels he could cut down on his own if he wanted to. He has not made any concrete plans to reduce, has not removed alcohol from the house, has not engaged with treatment, and does not yet identify himself as having a problem requiring help.

He has no current severe withdrawal symptoms (no tremor, no autonomic instability), no current suicidal ideation, AUDIT 22. PMH: T2DM, hypertension, macrocytosis on FBC. The GP plans a longer follow-up consultation to address the drinking through a structured behaviour-change framework.

data_table.Examination: Mild epigastric tenderness, no encephalopathy, no asterixis, no jaundice
data_table.Investigations: AUDIT 22, MCV 102 fL, GGT 220 U/L, ALT 64 U/L, HbA1c 7.4 per cent

lead_in: Which stage of change does this man most clearly demonstrate, and what is the best-matched evidence-based intervention plan today?

options.text: Precontemplation - provide brief structured information about risks; do not raise treatment options today as he is not yet ready to change
Preparation - schedule a quit date within 30 days, start naltrexone today, and provide a brief intervention focused on the AUDIT score and end-organ damage
Contemplation - motivational interviewing for ambivalence, brief intervention with FRAMES, and OFFER naltrexone or acamprosate given AUDIT and end-organ damage
Action - initiate naltrexone today, refer to a relapse-prevention group, and arrange weekly clinic follow-up for the first three months
Maintenance - relapse-prevention planning even though he has not yet achieved any reduction in drinking or made a quit attempt yet

subtopic_detail: Psychodynamic vs supportive vs CBT matching
stem:
A 42-year-old man is reviewed in a community mental health team after a third presentation in 12 months with recurrent moderate depressive episodes, prominent self-criticism, longstanding difficulty in close relationships, and a pattern of leaving jobs when feedback feels critical. He has had two previous structured 12-session CBT courses with modest short-term improvement that has not been sustained, and he describes finding the homework-driven structure of CBT useful but feels that 'something deeper isn't shifting'.

He is psychologically minded, articulate, and curious about understanding patterns from his upbringing. He has no current suicidal ideation, no substance use, and is currently on sertraline 100 mg with partial response. He works part-time and his health fund covers extended psychology sessions. He is asking what to try next that is not another medication change.

data_table.Examination: Reactive affect, no thought disorder, no perceptual disturbance, K-10 24
data_table.Investigations: FBC, EUC, LFT, TSH all unremarkable
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 100 mg daily

lead_in: Which structured psychological therapy is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Another 12-session course of cognitive behavioural therapy
Supportive counselling alone
Dialectical behaviour therapy
Time-limited psychodynamic psychotherapy
Acceptance and commitment therapy

subtopic_detail: Complex elderly - delirium superimposed on dementia + capacity
stem:
An 84-year-old woman with moderate Alzheimer dementia (premorbid MMSE 22 documented 6 weeks ago) is admitted from her home with a urinary tract infection and dehydration after her daughter found her drowsy. On day 4 of intravenous ceftriaxone the infection has clinically resolved with CRP falling from 156 to 24 mg/L, MSU now sterile, and sodium corrected from 122 to 137 mmol/L.

Her attention this morning is back to baseline on backwards-counting, her CAM is negative, her behaviour has settled, and the family-nurse and OT report she is at the cognitive level documented before this admission. Today she tells the team she wants to go home and refuses to engage with proposed residential aged care assessment. Her daughter, who is the documented enduring guardian, disagrees and is pushing strongly for nursing home placement.

data_table.Examination: Alert, attention preserved on backwards-counting, MMSE 22 (back to documented baseline), CAM negative
data_table.Investigations: Na 137, urea 6.4, Cr 88, CRP 24, MSU sterile, FBC normal
data_table.Medications: Donepezil 10 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Override her refusal because the daughter is her enduring guardian
Apply Mental Health Act involuntary admission to keep her in hospital
Discharge immediately because the delirium has resolved
Continue antibiotics for another 7 days while debate continues
Reassess decision-specific capacity for the discharge destination

subtopic_detail: Baseline metabolic workup before olanzapine initiation
stem: A 26-year-old man with a first episode of schizophrenia commenced olanzapine 10 mg nocte two weeks ago after baseline metabolic monitoring (BMI 24.3, waist 92 cm, BP 124/78, fasting glucose 4.8, lipids within range, ECG normal). His father has T2DM diagnosed at 58 and his mother has dyslipidaemia. He is a non-smoker, drinks two standard drinks on weekends, and is on no other medications. He has gained 1.8 kg in two weeks. The team plans to follow the RANZCP/Lambert metabolic-monitoring schedule for second-generation antipsychotics.

data_table.Observations: BP 124/78 mmHg, HR 76, weight 78 kg, BMI 24.3, waist 92 cm.
data_table.Bloods: Not yet taken at this visit.

lead_in: Per the RANZCP-endorsed metabolic monitoring schedule for second-generation antipsychotics, what monitoring should occur at the 12-week post-initiation review?

options.text: Weight and BMI only; bloods are scheduled at 6 months and annually thereafter
Weight, BMI, waist circumference, BP, fasting glucose (or HbA1c), and fasting lipids; repeat ECG only if symptoms or risk-factor change
Oral glucose tolerance test, fasting insulin and HOMA-IR in addition to anthropometry
Repeat ECG, prolactin, and 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure as a 12-week metabolic panel
Defer all repeat metabolic bloods until the 12-month anniversary review

stem:
A 34-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been on clozapine for 12 weeks, titrated to 350 mg nocte with good symptomatic response (PANSS reduced from 96 to 68 over the period). He had failed adequate trials of risperidone and olanzapine in the preceding two years. He attends the community clozapine clinic for his scheduled 12-week review and is accompanied by his case manager.

Baseline values 12 weeks ago were weight 82 kg, BMI 26.4 kg/m2, waist 96 cm, BP 122/78 mmHg, fasting glucose 5.1 mmol/L, HbA1c 35 mmol/mol (5.4%), total cholesterol 4.6 mmol/L, LDL 2.8 mmol/L, HDL 1.1 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.4 mmol/L. Today he weighs 91 kg (BMI 29.3, waist 106 cm), BP 134/86 mmHg, fasting glucose 6.2 mmol/L, HbA1c 41 mmol/mol (5.9%), total cholesterol 5.9 mmol/L, LDL 3.6 mmol/L, HDL 0.9 mmol/L, triglycerides 2.8 mmol/L.

He reports no chest pain or dyspnoea. ANC today is 3.4 x 10^9/L. He is keen to continue clozapine because it has 'given him his life back'.

data_table.Baseline (week 0): Weight 82 kg, BMI 26.4, waist 96 cm, FG 5.1, HbA1c 35 (5.4%), TC 4.6, LDL 2.8, HDL 1.1, TG 1.4.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop clozapine immediately and switch to aripiprazole monotherapy
Continue clozapine and add structured lifestyle intervention, metformin, and arrange cardiometabolic review; repeat metabolic panel in 4-6 weeks

Continue clozapine unchanged at 350 mg nocte and defer the next metabolic and weight review until 12 months from baseline, treating the current panel as within expected limits for the first year of clozapine therapy
Halve the clozapine dose to 175 mg nocte to reduce metabolic load
Order an urgent echocardiogram and stop clozapine pending the result

subtopic_detail: Threshold for switching antipsychotic for metabolic reasons
stem:
A 41-year-old woman with chronic schizophrenia has been on olanzapine 20 mg nocte for 4 years with partial symptomatic response (residual negative symptoms, no positive symptoms). She lives independently with case-management support and attends a community mental health clinic three-monthly. Over the past 3 years her weight has risen from 76 kg to 102 kg (BMI 36.1 kg/m2), waist 112 cm.

Today's review shows BP 142/92 mmHg (confirmed on repeat 5 minutes apart), fasting glucose 7.2 mmol/L on two separate occasions, HbA1c 58 mmol/mol (7.5%), LDL 4.1 mmol/L, HDL 0.8 mmol/L, triglycerides 3.4 mmol/L. She has type 2 diabetes diagnosed 8 months ago (on metformin 1 g BD), and stage 1 hypertension (on perindopril 5 mg). She has had three trials of structured lifestyle intervention with no sustained weight loss across the past two years.

She has never been on clozapine and has not had treatment-resistance formally assessed. She prefers oral medication and has a documented history of akathisia on haloperidol but tolerated a brief aripiprazole augmentation trial 3 years ago without akathisia or activation.

data_table.Comorbidities: T2DM on metformin 1 g BD; HTN on perindopril 5 mg.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next antipsychotic management step?

options.text: Continue olanzapine 20 mg nocte and add topiramate 50 mg BD for weight loss without addressing the obesogenic antipsychotic driver
Halve olanzapine to 10 mg nocte, continue current diabetes and BP therapy unchanged, and review weight, fasting glucose, lipids and BP in 3 months
Cross-taper olanzapine to chlorpromazine 200 mg twice daily as a first-generation antipsychotic alternative, continuing metformin and antihypertensive therapy
Cross-taper olanzapine to aripiprazole (or lurasidone), maintain metformin, continue diabetes and BP management, monitor closely for relapse risk
Refer for bariatric surgery and continue olanzapine 20 mg nocte without altering the underlying obesogenic antipsychotic at this metabolic review

subtopic_detail: Lithium interactions with NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, and dehydration
stem:
A 56-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, stable on lithium carbonate 900 mg nocte for 11 years (level 0.7 mmol/L at her quarterly check three months ago), presents to her general practitioner with a 5-day history of right knee pain after a long day of gardening. Her general practitioner is considering analgesia. She also has hypertension treated with perindopril 5 mg daily and indapamide 1.5 mg daily, and type 2 diabetes treated with metformin 1 g BD.

She is otherwise well and has had no recent vomiting or diarrhoea. The general practitioner is aware she is on lithium and wants to choose analgesia that minimises the risk of lithium toxicity. She weighs 72 kg, eGFR was 68 mL/min/1.73m2 last month, and she drinks 1.5 L of fluid per day. She lives alone and is travelling to a coastal holiday with predicted 36-degree temperatures next week, with several days outdoors planned.

data_table.Medications: Lithium 900 mg nocte, perindopril 5 mg, indapamide 1.5 mg, metformin 1 g BD.
data_table.Recent labs: Lithium 0.7 mmol/L (3 months ago); eGFR 68; HbA1c 51 mmol/mol.

lead_in: Which analgesic plan minimises the risk of precipitating lithium toxicity?

options.text: Ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for 7 days without recheck of lithium level during the analgesic course in this stable patient
Celecoxib 200 mg daily for 7 days as a COX-2 selective alternative considered safer for lithium co-prescription with no level recheck
Naproxen 500 mg twice daily with topical diclofenac for adjunctive local analgesia at the affected joint without lithium recheck
Switch lithium to sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for one week to allow ibuprofen 400 mg TDS, then return to maintenance lithium dose
Paracetamol 1 g four times daily PRN, with advice to maintain fluids especially in hot weather and avoid NSAIDs; recheck lithium if she becomes unwell

stem:
A 64-year-old man with bipolar I disorder, on lithium carbonate 1000 mg nocte for 14 years, is brought to a regional emergency department by his wife. Over the past 3 days he has become increasingly unsteady on his feet, with a worsening hand tremor and slurred speech. His wife says he has been 'not quite right', confused about the day of the week, and has fallen twice at home without losing consciousness.

He started ramipril 5 mg daily 10 days ago for newly diagnosed hypertension and has had reduced oral intake during a recent gastroenteritis episode. His usual lithium level taken 4 months ago was 0.75 mmol/L. On arrival he is afebrile, BP 138/82, HR 88, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6). He has a coarse irregular tremor, dysarthria, gait ataxia, hyperreflexia, and bilateral horizontal nystagmus.

No rigidity, no clonus, pupils equal and reactive. Bloods: Na 138 mmol/L, K 4.2, urea 9.8, creatinine 132 micromol/L (baseline 88), eGFR 48, lithium 1.6 mmol/L.

data_table.Neurological: Coarse tremor, dysarthria, ataxia, hyperreflexia, bilateral nystagmus, no rigidity, no clonus.
data_table.Bloods: Na 138, K 4.2, urea 9.8, creatinine 132 (baseline 88), eGFR 48, lithium 1.6 mmol/L.

lead_in: Which clinical feature is most specific for lithium neurotoxicity in this presentation?

options.text: Coarse tremor with hand-to-hand variation and intention component on finger-nose testing rather than ataxia
Cerebellar ataxia with dysarthria, nystagmus and hyperreflexia in the setting of a rising lithium level and falling renal function
Fever above 38.5 degrees Celsius with diaphoresis and tachycardia rather than focal cerebellar or dysarthric signs
Lead-pipe rigidity with autonomic instability typical of neuroleptic malignant syndrome rather than lithium toxicity here
Sustained inducible ankle clonus with ocular clonus, diaphoresis, mydriasis and hyperactive bowel sounds in a serotonergic pattern

stem:
A 24-year-old woman is reviewed at a community mental health clinic 6 weeks after a hospital admission for a severe manic episode that was her first lifetime presentation. She was discharged on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily and quetiapine 200 mg nocte, with good symptomatic resolution and a return to baseline function. She lives with her partner and works part-time as an early childhood educator.

She is sexually active in a stable relationship and uses condoms only as contraception. She is not currently planning pregnancy but says she might consider it in the next 2-3 years. She has no contraindication to hormonal contraception and no history of thromboembolism or migraine with aura. The Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) has issued repeated safety advisories about valproate in females of reproductive potential, and the medication carries a boxed warning regarding teratogenicity and neurodevelopmental harm in exposed offspring.

The treating team is reviewing whether her current prescription meets the Australian Pregnancy Prevention Program (PPP) framework for valproate and is asking about the next steps. She has no documented prior trials of alternative mood stabilisers.

data_table.Demographics: 24-year-old female, sexually active, condoms only, no current pregnancy plan but possibly in 2-3 years.
data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 1000 mg daily, quetiapine 200 mg nocte (commenced 6 weeks ago).

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step under the Australian valproate PPP framework?

options.text: Continue valproate 1000 mg daily with no change to condom-only contraception; document general teratogenicity counselling and treat as resolved
Continue valproate and document she has been counselled about teratogenicity; defer the contraception decision to her general practitioner at a separate visit
Discuss switching to a non-valproate mood stabiliser (lithium or atypical antipsychotic); if valproate retained, ensure LARC or combined hormonal contraception and annual specialist review
Stop valproate today without replacement and re-review in 4 weeks, accepting the risk of manic relapse during the unprotected mood-stabiliser-free interval
Halve the valproate dose to 500 mg daily on the assumption that lower doses are non-teratogenic and that full contraception is therefore unnecessary

subtopic_detail: Fetal valproate syndrome incidence and counselling
stem:
A 29-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been on sodium valproate 1200 mg daily for 5 years following two severe manic episodes requiring inpatient admission. She is now in stable remission for the past 30 months and consults her psychiatrist about planning pregnancy in the next 12 months. She lives with her husband and works full-time as a project manager.

Previous trials of lithium (terminated due to severe cystic acne and 12 kg weight gain at therapeutic levels) and quetiapine monotherapy (failed at 600 mg nocte with breakthrough mania at 4 months) are documented in her records. She uses a copper intrauterine device for contraception and is up to date on cervical screening. She wants to understand the absolute risks of staying on valproate during pregnancy versus switching to an alternative agent, and asks specifically about the rate of fetal valproate syndrome (FVS) and major congenital malformations.

Her general practitioner, treating obstetrician, and psychiatrist are jointly involved in the planning. The TGA boxed warning and Australian Pregnancy Prevention Program materials are on the table. She wants to know what the Australian evidence actually shows about exposure-related harm.

data_table.Background: Bipolar I, stable on valproate 1200 mg/day for 5 years.
data_table.Prior trials: Lithium (severe acne, weight gain) and quetiapine 600 mg monotherapy (failed).
data_table.Contraception: Copper IUD; plans pregnancy in next 12 months.

lead_in: Which counselling statement most accurately reflects the Australian evidence on valproate exposure in pregnancy?

options.text: Valproate carries an MCM rate of ~1%, comparable to background population risk in Australia; continuing valproate through pregnancy is reasonable without switching mood stabiliser
Valproate teratogenic risk applies only in the third trimester; first-trimester exposure is safe and does not require switching to an alternative mood stabiliser
Folic acid 5 mg daily eliminates the risk of fetal valproate syndrome and major malformations; valproate may be continued safely without other changes
Valproate carries about 10% MCM risk and 30-40% neurodevelopmental impairment risk; switch to a lower-risk mood stabiliser before conception, with overlap to maintain stability
There is no need to switch because fetal valproate syndrome is reversible after birth with early developmental intervention and folate supplementation

subtopic_detail: QRS widening and sodium bicarbonate therapy
stem:
A 27-year-old woman is brought to a metropolitan emergency department 90 minutes after intentional ingestion of approximately 50 tablets of amitriptyline 25 mg (estimated 1.25 g). She is drowsy but rousable, GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5), with mydriasis, dry mucous membranes, and warm dry skin. Observations: HR 122 sinus tachycardia, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius.

She has had one brief generalised tonic-clonic seizure on arrival, self-terminating. ECG shows sinus tachycardia, QRS 132 ms (baseline 90 ms), R wave in aVR 4 mm, terminal R/S ratio in aVR >0.7, QT 460 ms. Bloods: Na 138, K 3.8, HCO3 18, lactate 4.2, pH 7.28 on venous blood gas, paracetamol level negative. She has no prior cardiac history and is on no other medications. The team is in contact with the NSW Poisons Information Centre.

data_table.ECG: Sinus tachycardia, QRS 132 ms, R in aVR 4 mm, terminal R/S aVR >0.7, QT 460 ms.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Oral activated charcoal 50 g now (more than 90 minutes post-ingestion), continuous cardiac monitoring and serial ECGs every 30 minutes
Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg titrated to a Glasgow Coma Scale of 14 or above as an immediate reversal agent for the depressed conscious state
Intravenous flecainide 2 mg/kg load over 10 minutes for the wide-complex tachycardia, with continuous cardiac monitoring throughout the infusion
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 10 minutes as the primary agent for the wide QRS and tachycardia in this presentation
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate bolus with reassessment of QRS, airway protection and seizure precautions, in consultation with NSW Poisons

subtopic_detail: Use of the NSW Poisons Information Centre pathway
stem:
A 19-year-old man presents to a small rural emergency department 2 hours after ingesting an unknown quantity of dosulepin tablets (also called dosulepin) found in his mother's medicine cabinet. He is drowsy, GCS 13, HR 118, BP 102/64, RR 16, SpO2 98%. ECG shows sinus tachycardia, QRS 108 ms (no prior baseline), R in aVR 3 mm, QT 440 ms.

He has not had a seizure. Bloods are pending. The on-call rural physician is the most senior clinician on site and has not managed a tricyclic overdose in several years. The hospital has access to intravenous sodium bicarbonate, intralipid, intubation equipment, and a high-dependency bay. The nearest tertiary centre with an intensive care unit is 220 km away by road, with retrieval by aeromedical service possible. The patient's mother thinks the bottle contained 'maybe 30 to 60 tablets' but is not sure of the original count.

data_table.Setting: Rural ED, on-call physician most senior on site, ICU 220 km away.
data_table.Observations: GCS 13, HR 118, BP 102/64, ECG QRS 108 ms.
data_table.Resources: IV sodium bicarbonate, intralipid, intubation kit, HDU bay available.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step to guide management decisions?

options.text: Telephone the NSW Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26 for case-specific advice (TCA risk-stratification, sodium bicarbonate thresholds, retrieval criteria) and document the consult
Email the patient's GP for a verified medication list and prior overdose history, and wait for a reply before any antidote, intubation or further treatment
Search a general medical app for tricyclic overdose dosing and apply the first dose suggestion found without any specialist toxicology consultation today
Discharge home with mental health follow-up because QRS is under 120 ms and observed vital signs are currently stable in the emergency department
Administer intralipid 20% empirically before further assessment or specialist consultation given the wide-complex tachycardia on the current rhythm strip

stem:
A 37-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been on clozapine 400 mg nocte for 8 months, registered with an Australian clozapine monitoring service (e.g. CPMS or ClopineCentral). His weekly bloods through weeks 1-18 were unremarkable; he is now on 4-weekly haematological monitoring per the standard Australian schedule. Today's FBC: Hb 142, WCC 4.8, ANC 1.6 x 10^9/L (last month 2.4), platelets 218.

He has no fever, no sore throat, no mouth ulcers, and no other infective symptoms. He has not started new medications and has had no recent vaccinations. He is otherwise well, of European background (not associated with benign ethnic neutropenia), and has no prior neutropenia.
lead_in: Which combination of zone classification, dose action, monitoring frequency and registry action best fits the Australian clozapine haematological monitoring framework?

options.text: Green zone (ANC at or above 2.0 x 10^9/L) - continue clozapine at the current 400 mg nocte dose, maintain 4-weekly FBC frequency, and make no notification to the registered clozapine monitoring service

Amber zone (ANC 1.5-1.99) - continue clozapine at current dose, increase haematological monitoring to twice weekly, notify the registered clozapine monitoring service so the patient's status is updated
Red zone (ANC below 1.5 x 10^9/L) - cease clozapine immediately, admit for inpatient observation, notify the registered clozapine monitoring service, and document permanent rechallenge prohibition
Defer the next FBC for 4 weeks given the absence of infective symptoms, continue clozapine at 400 mg nocte, and arrange a routine clinic review at the next scheduled monitoring appointment
Continue clozapine at 400 mg nocte and add lithium 250 mg nocte as a neutrophil-stimulating adjunct, with weekly FBC monitoring and registry notification of the augmentation strategy

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation and clozapine level rise
stem:
A 45-year-old man has been on clozapine 450 mg nocte for 9 years, with steady-state clozapine level 480 mcg/L (therapeutic range 350-600) measured 6 months ago. He smokes 25 cigarettes per day. He is admitted overnight to a smoke-free general medical ward for a 5-day stay following a mechanical fall, and is offered nicotine replacement therapy (patch 21 mg/24 h plus PRN lozenges) but is not yet enrolled in a structured cessation program.

He has no current symptoms of clozapine toxicity (no sedation change, no hypersalivation increase, no tachycardia, no constipation worsening). The ward team contacts the community psychiatry team for guidance on clozapine dosing during the smoke-free inpatient period and any planned post-discharge cessation.

data_table.Background: Clozapine 450 mg nocte for 9 years; smokes 25/day.

lead_in: Which is the single best summary of the relevant pharmacokinetic mechanism and the appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Smoking induces CYP3A4; cessation will halve clozapine levels and require a dose increase of approximately 25 percent over the inpatient stay
Nicotine itself is the inducer; full nicotine replacement therapy on admission prevents any clozapine level change, so no dose adjustment is required
PAHs in tobacco smoke induce CYP1A2; cessation raises clozapine levels by 50-70% over 1-2 weeks; monitor for toxicity and consider pre-emptive 25% dose reduction
Smoking inhibits CYP1A2; cessation will lower clozapine levels and require a dose increase to maintain therapeutic plasma concentrations during admission
There is no clinically significant interaction between smoking and clozapine metabolism; routine clinical monitoring alone is sufficient for this admission

stem:
A 78-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter with a 4-day history of progressive lethargy, unsteadiness, two falls, and nausea. She was started on sertraline 50 mg daily 12 days ago for moderate depressive disorder after the death of her husband. She also takes amlodipine 5 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg, and atorvastatin 20 mg. She lives alone, drinks 2-3 cups of weak tea daily and about 1 L of water.

On examination she is afebrile, BP 138/76 (lying) and 124/72 (standing), HR 78, RR 14, SpO2 97%, GCS 14 (mildly drowsy but oriented), no focal neurological signs, mucous membranes moist, JVP normal, no oedema. Bloods: Na 121 mmol/L (baseline 138 four weeks ago), K 3.8, urea 4.1, creatinine 72 (baseline 70), glucose 5.4, TSH 2.0, serum osmolality 254 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 412 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 48 mmol/L. ECG shows sinus rhythm, QTc 432 ms.

data_table.Medications: Sertraline 50 mg (12 days), amlodipine 5 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg, atorvastatin 20 mg.
data_table.Bloods: Na 121 (baseline 138), K 3.8, urea 4.1, Cr 72, serum osm 254, urine osm 412, urine Na 48.

lead_in: Which is the single most likely mechanism of this hyponatraemia, and the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Thiazide-induced hyponatraemia alone; continue sertraline 50 mg as response is not yet established, stop hydrochlorothiazide only, restrict free water to 1 L/day, recheck sodium in 24 hours
Primary polydipsia from her depressive ruminations; restrict fluid intake aggressively to less than 500 mL/day without ceasing either contributing medication
Addisonian crisis from missed inhaled corticosteroid doses; give IV hydrocortisone 100 mg and broad fluid resuscitation rather than free water restriction
Cerebral salt wasting from occult subarachnoid haemorrhage; treat with hypertonic 3% saline and oral salt tablets rather than free water restriction here
SSRI-induced SIADH potentiated by thiazide; stop sertraline AND hydrochlorothiazide, fluid restrict to 1-1.2 L/day, recheck sodium in 6-12 hours, correction not exceeding 8-10 mmol/L/24 hr

subtopic_detail: Citalopram QT cap and discriminating serotonin syndrome from neuroleptic malignant syndrome
stem:
A 69-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance after his wife found him agitated, sweaty, and shaking in the lounge room of their home. Over the past 24 hours he has become progressively tremulous, restless, and confused, with deteriorating mental state through the morning. His usual medications include citalopram (recently up-titrated 5 days ago from 20 mg to 40 mg daily for persistent depressive symptoms despite a previously adequate response), risperidone 2 mg nocte (commenced 6 weeks ago for new psychotic features overlaid on depression), perindopril 5 mg daily for hypertension, and tramadol 50 mg up to four times daily started 4 days ago by an after-hours general practitioner for an acute lower back strain.

On arrival he is restless and agitated, GCS 13, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius, HR 124 sinus, BP 158/96, RR 22, SpO2 97% on room air. Examination shows mydriasis, profuse diaphoresis, hyperactive bowel sounds, tremor more pronounced in the lower limbs than the upper limbs, spontaneous sustained inducible clonus in both ankles (right > left), ocular clonus on lateral gaze, and globally brisk reflexes.

He is NOT rigid - tone is normal with no lead-pipe rigidity and no cogwheeling. ECG: sinus tachycardia, QTc 502 ms (baseline 6 months ago 432 ms). Bloods: Na 138, K 4.2, creatinine 86, CK 412 U/L, lactate 2.6, paracetamol level negative.

data_table.Medications: Citalopram 40 mg (up from 20 mg, 5 days ago), risperidone 2 mg (stable 6 weeks), perindopril 5 mg, tramadol 50 mg QID (4 days).
data_table.Examination: Diaphoresis, hyperactive bowel sounds, lower-limb-predominant tremor, sustained inducible ankle clonus (R>L), ocular clonus, hyperreflexia, NO rigidity.
data_table.Bloods/ECG: Na 138, K 4.2, Cr 86, CK 412, lactate 2.6, QTc 502 ms (baseline 432).

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate diagnosis and immediate management combination?

options.text: Serotonin syndrome from citalopram (above the over-65 dose cap of 20 mg) plus tramadol; stop both, give benzodiazepines for agitation and clonus, supportive cooling and fluids
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome from risperidone (started 6 weeks ago); stop risperidone, give IV dantrolene and bromocriptine, cooling and fluids, continue citalopram and tramadol
Sepsis with delirium and incidental clonus; commence broad-spectrum antibiotics and IV fluids only, with no change to current psychotropic or analgesic medication
Anticholinergic toxidrome from tramadol metabolites; give physostigmine slow IV push and stop all anticholinergic-burden medications immediately at this presentation
Acute ischaemic stroke recurrence with autonomic features; thrombolyse within the window without addressing the serotonergic medication interactions seen here

stem:
A 19-year-old male university student is brought to the ED by his parents after eight months of progressive social withdrawal, falling grades, and disorganised thinking. Over the past three weeks he has insisted his housemates are filming him through the smoke alarm and has stopped eating meals they prepare. He has had no prior psychiatric contact, denies suicidal ideation, and has used 1 to 2 cones of cannabis weekly for the past year (last use four weeks ago).

He drinks alcohol rarely. There is no family history of psychotic illness. On MSE he is guarded, makes fleeting eye contact, and describes 'the voice of an old teacher' commenting on his actions in the third person. He denies any plan to harm himself or others. Examination is unremarkable. Bloods including FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH, B12, and urine drug screen are all within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented, no neurological signs, weight 64 kg (down 5 kg over 6 months)
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, UEC normal, TSH 1.8 mU/L, B12 412 pmol/L, urine drug screen negative for amphetamines, cocaine, opiates; cannabinoids negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his care pathway?

options.text: Commence olanzapine 5 mg nocte and arrange routine GP follow-up in two weeks
Refer to the local early-psychosis (headspace / EPPIC-aligned) service for assertive multidisciplinary assessment
Diagnose cannabis-induced psychotic disorder and discharge with brief intervention on cessation
Arrange outpatient MRI brain and EEG before any psychiatric treatment is offered
Admit involuntarily under the relevant state Mental Health Act for assessment

stem:
A 23-year-old man with a confirmed diagnosis of schizophrenia after his second psychotic episode is being prescribed maintenance antipsychotic therapy following discharge. He has a BMI of 31 kg/m2, fasting glucose 5.9 mmol/L, HbA1c 41 mmol/mol, triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L and a strong family history of type 2 diabetes (mother and maternal uncle). He smokes 15 cigarettes daily and is sexually active in a stable relationship; adherence in his first episode was poor because of sedation and weight gain on olanzapine 15 mg nocte (he gained 9 kg in three months).

He works irregular nightfill shifts and reports that any morning dose 'knocks him out till lunchtime'. On MSE residual paranoid ideation is present but he is no longer responding to internal stimuli. Sexual side effects, akathisia history, and prolactin elevation were specifically asked about and were not problematic. He attends the early-psychosis service weekly He has read about the metabolic risks of olanzapine and clozapine and specifically asks for an antipsychotic with low weight-gain and sedation liability that can be given as a single morning dose so he can sleep through the day after his nightfill shifts. The early-psychosis psychiatrist is available for the prescribing decision today.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 132/82, BMI 31 kg/m2, waist 104 cm
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 5.9 mmol/L, HbA1c 41 mmol/mol, total chol 5.4 mmol/L, triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L, HDL 0.9 mmol/L, prolactin 280 mIU/L
data_table.Medications: Olanzapine 15 mg nocte (current), nicotine replacement patch 21 mg/24 h

lead_in: Which maintenance antipsychotic is most appropriate to switch to?

options.text: Aripiprazole 10 mg mane, titrating to 15 mg
Risperidone 2 mg orally twice daily titrated as needed
Quetiapine XR 400 mg nocte titrated over one week
Amisulpride 400 mg orally each morning titrated as required
Clozapine 12.5 mg nocte titrated by registered protocol

stem:
A 27-year-old man is brought to ED 18 hours after his first ever dose of intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg, which was given in a different ED for severe agitation related to methamphetamine intoxication. He has since received olanzapine 10 mg orally. He reports that his neck has 'twisted to the right and is stuck' over the past three hours and he cannot move it back; his eyes have rolled upwards intermittently.

He is distressed and clutching his jaw. He denies fever, rigidity elsewhere, or confusion. There is no past history of psychiatric illness. Examination shows sustained right-sided torticollis, intermittent oculogyric movements, and clenching of the masseters with normal power in the limbs and no rigidity. He is afebrile, alert and oriented. Urine drug screen earlier was positive for amphetamines only. ECG shows sinus rhythm, QTc 430 ms He has no known glaucoma and no urinary retention.

data_table.Examination: Sustained right torticollis, oculogyric crisis, jaw clenching, no limb rigidity, normal reflexes, GCS 15
data_table.Investigations: ECG QTc 430 ms, sodium 138, potassium 4.1, creatinine 78, CK 220, urine drug screen positive amphetamines

lead_in: What is the single best next intervention?

options.text: Intramuscular benzatropine 1 to 2 mg, repeated if no response in 20 minutes
Oral diazepam 10 mg and reassurance, expecting resolution within 24 hours
Oral propranolol 20 mg three times daily as monotherapy for the movement disorder
Intravenous dantrolene with active cooling for presumed malignant hyperthermia
Cease all antipsychotics and admit for 48 hours of observation without active treatment

stem:
A 34-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder was commenced on risperidone 2 mg BD seven days ago for an acute manic episode. She returns to the community mental-health team reporting intolerable inner restlessness for the past five days; she cannot sit through a meal or watch television and feels she 'must keep moving or jump out of her skin'. She paces during the interview and shifts weight from foot to foot when standing.

There is no involuntary contracture, no tremor at restidity. She is afebrile with normal vitals. She continues to take lithium 750 mg nocte (lithium 0.8 mmol/L last week) and is not on any anticholinergic. Suicidal ideation is now emerging, which she relates entirely to the restlessness and not to mood. MSE shows euthymic affect, no psychotic features, and full insight that 'the medication is causing this'.

data_table.Examination: Pacing, foot-tapping, no tremor, no rigidity, no dystonia, normal tone and power
data_table.Medications: Risperidone 2 mg BD (day 7), lithium 750 mg nocte (level 0.8 mmol/L last week)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add benzatropine 2 mg orally twice daily as anticholinergic monotherapy
Reduce risperidone dose and add propranolol 10 to 20 mg three times daily
Increase lithium dose to target a serum level above 1.0 mmol/L
Switch immediately from risperidone to clozapine under registered protocol
Reassure and continue current regimen, expecting tolerance within four weeks

stem:
A 41-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder is admitted to ED from a residential facility. Over the preceding four days haloperidol was uptitrated from 5 mg to 15 mg daily and depot zuclopenthixol acetate 100 mg IM was given two days ago. He has become progressively unwell over 48 hours with high fevers, marked rigidity, profuse sweating, and confusion. Staff report he was holding postures for several minutes earlier that day but is now stiff and barely interactive.

He takes no other regular medications and there is no over-the-counter or illicit drug use. On examination he is somnolent and only grunts in response. He has generalised lead-pipe rigidity, no clonus, and reduced deep-tendon reflexes. Pupils are mid-sized and reactive. He is profoundly diaphoretic. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with no acute ischaemia He is on no serotonergic medications, no SSRI's wort.

Bloods show creatine kinase 5400 U/L, urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 145 micromol/L, and white cell count 13.2. The medical and psychiatric teams are now debating whether this is neuroleptic malignant syndrome or serotonin syndrome, given the rigidity, hyperthermia and altered mental state.

data_table.Examination: GCS 10 (E2 V2 M6), generalised lead-pipe rigidity, no clonus, normal-mid pupils, profuse diaphoresis
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18 x10^9/L, Na 142, K 4.2, Cr 168 micromol/L (baseline 80), CK 8200 U/L, AST 220, lactate 3.1 mmol/L, urine myoglobin positive

lead_in: Which feature most strongly distinguishes neuroleptic malignant syndrome from serotonin syndrome in this presentation?

options.text: Documented core temperature greater than 40 degrees Celsius on presentation
Recent high-potency D2 antagonist escalation with lead-pipe rigidity and hyporeflexia
A markedly elevated creatine kinase with associated acute kidney injury
Altered conscious state with autonomic instability such as labile blood pressure
Sustained posturing earlier in the illness, raising suspicion of catatonia

stem:
