A 52-year-old woman is brought to ED two hours after a colleague found her shivering, agitated and unsteady at work. She was started on sertraline 50 mg daily eight weeks ago for major depression. Three days ago her GP added tramadol 50 mg up to four times daily for an acute lumbar strain; she has taken one tablet six-hourly. There is no history of recent illicit drug use.

She is alert but restless, sweating, and reports intermittent muscle twitching in her legs. Examination shows mydriasis, intermittent spontaneous clonus in the ankles, brisk patellar reflexes, and resting tremor of the upper limbs. She is afebrile at triage but on rechecking 30 minutes later her temperature has risen to 38.4 degrees. Pupils are 6 mm and reactive. She has no rigidity, no oculogyric movements, and her mental state is anxious but oriented and cooperative

data_table.Examination: Mydriasis 6 mm, spontaneous ankle clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor, shivering, no rigidity, GCS 15
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 138, potassium 4.0, creatinine 84, CK 480 U/L, lactate 1.8 mmol/L, urine drug screen negative
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 50 mg daily (8 weeks), tramadol 50 mg QID (3 days)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease serotonergic agents, give IV fluids, oral diazepam 5 mg, observe on monitored bed
Oral bromocriptine 2.5 mg three times daily with active cooling on the ward
Intramuscular benzatropine 2 mg as treatment for the movement disorder
Intravenous dantrolene with intubation and neuromuscular paralysis
Switch sertraline to venlafaxine and reduce the tramadol dose by half today

stem:
A 29-year-old man with schizophrenia has had persistent third-person auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions for the past 18 months despite engagement with the community team. He has completed an adequate trial of olanzapine 20 mg daily for 8 weeks (adherence confirmed by plasma level) with only minor reduction in symptoms and intolerable weight gain, followed by aripiprazole 30 mg daily for 7 weeks with adherence confirmed but minimal response.

He has been engaged in CBT for psychosis fortnightly. He has no medical comorbidities, an ECG shows normal sinus rhythm with QTc 410 ms, FBC is normal and he has no history of cardiac, haematological or seizure disorders. He lives with his parents who are willing to support a medication change, and he is currently in regular outpatient contact with his case manager He is willing to commit to weekly FBC monitoring and to admission for induction if needed.

He has no history of cardiomyopathy and an echocardiogram shows preserved ejection fraction He understands clozapine monitoring and is willing to commence today Augmentation strategies were considered and not chosen His parents support the change.

data_table.Examination: BMI 28 kg/m2, no neurological signs, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal (WCC 6.4, neutrophils 3.8 x10^9/L), UEC normal, ECG sinus rhythm QTc 410 ms, troponin not measured (asymptomatic)
data_table.Medications: Aripiprazole 30 mg daily (current, 7 weeks)

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Switch to clozapine, initiated under registered protocol with weekly FBC monitoring
Add a second oral antipsychotic, amisulpride 400 mg, to the current aripiprazole regimen
Trial a third oral antipsychotic, risperidone 6 mg daily, for 8 weeks first
Refer for electroconvulsive therapy as primary management of the persistent psychotic symptoms
Switch to a long-acting injectable formulation of aripiprazole given monthly intramuscularly

stem:
A 32-year-old woman has been on clozapine for 16 days, currently titrated to 200 mg nocte. She presents to the early-psychosis clinic feeling unwell for 36 hours with chest tightness on exertion, palpitations, a temperature of 38.2 degrees and a non-productive cough. There is no rash, no pleuritic pain, and no recent viral contact at home. She has no history of cardiac disease, no chest pain at rest, and observations show tachycardia.

Examination reveals a faint S3 gallop, no murmurs, clear chest sounds, and no peripheral oedema. Bloods today show WCC 7.8, neutrophils 4.6 x10^9/L (within normal), CRP 78, troponin I 380 ng/L (laboratory upper reference 26 ng/L), eosinophils 0.9 x10^9/L. ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 118, no ST elevation, no PR depression.

data_table.Examination: Faint S3 gallop, clear lung fields, no oedema, no rash
data_table.Investigations: WCC 7.8, neutrophils 4.6, eosinophils 0.9 x10^9/L, CRP 78, troponin I 380 ng/L (URL 26), ECG sinus tachycardia 118, no ST changes
data_table.Medications: Clozapine 200 mg nocte (day 16 of titration)

lead_in: What is the single best next intervention?

options.text: Continue clozapine, add aspirin and review in 48 hours with repeat troponin
Cease clozapine immediately, admit for cardiology review, and arrange urgent echocardiogram
Stop clozapine because the neutrophil count of 4.6 x10^9/L indicates impending agranulocytosis
Reduce clozapine to 100 mg and add atenolol 25 mg daily
Treat empirically for community-acquired pneumonia with oral amoxicillin and doxycycline

stem:
A 38-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been stable on clozapine 400 mg nocte for 4 years. His mother brings him to ED because he has not opened his bowels for nine days and has progressive abdominal distension, two episodes of vomiting today, and reduced oral intake. He has been on regular docusate and senna at home but his case manager added loperamide 1 week ago after he reported watery stools (in retrospect, likely overflow).

On examination he is mildly tachycardic, afebrile, and abdomen is distended, tympanic, with sluggish bowel sounds and diffuse tenderness without peritonism. He has no haematochezia. There is no past history of inflammatory bowel disease or abdominal surgery. He smokes 20 cigarettes daily. His clozapine FBC was normal three days ago His abdominal x-ray shows grossly dilated loops of large bowel with faecal loading and no free gas. The surgical registrar is reviewing him in ED.

data_table.Examination: Distended tympanic abdomen, sluggish bowel sounds, diffuse tenderness, no peritonism, no scars
data_table.Investigations: WCC 11.2, Hb 138, Na 138, K 3.6, creatinine 92, lactate 1.4 mmol/L; AXR: dilated colon with no rectal gas, no free gas
data_table.Medications: Clozapine 400 mg nocte, docusate 50 mg BD, senna 15 mg nocte, loperamide 4 mg/day (1 week)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease loperamide, admit for IV fluids, NG decompression, surgical review and escalated laxatives
Add an oral fibre supplement and arrange general practitioner follow-up in one week
Cease clozapine permanently because of constipation risk and switch to another antipsychotic
Order an urgent colonoscopy as the primary diagnostic investigation today
Prescribe oral metoclopramide as a single 10 mg dose and discharge home

stem:
A 56-year-old man is admitted to the medical ward after presenting with a fractured wrist sustained in a fall. He drinks approximately 25 standard drinks per day and his last drink was 36 hours ago. He has a history of two previous withdrawal seizures and one prior episode of delirium tremens. He is currently tremulous, diaphoretic and reports tactile hallucinations of insects on his skin.

He is oriented to person and place but disoriented to time. His CIWA-Ar score is 22. He has no head injury. He was given 100 mg IM thiamine in ED. He has no known liver decompensation; LFTs show AST 110, ALT 65, INR 1.2 and albumin 36. He has no respiratory disease.

data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor, diaphoresis, tactile hallucinations, oriented to person/place not time, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 5.6 mmol/L, Na 138, K 3.2, Mg 0.62 mmol/L, AST 110, ALT 65, INR 1.2, alcohol level 0
data_table.Medications: Thiamine 100 mg IM in ED, no regular meds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in managing his withdrawal?

options.text: Continue daily thiamine 100 mg orally and observe with hourly CIWA-Ar reassessment overnight
Symptom-triggered diazepam 10-20 mg PO 1-2 hourly titrated to CIWA-Ar plus IV Pabrinex
Commence oral carbamazepine 200 mg three times daily as the sole withdrawal agent
Use an intravenous propofol infusion in a ward-based setting with bedside monitoring
Restart small amounts of oral alcohol to taper consumption over 5 days at home

stem:
A 62-year-old homeless man is brought to ED after being found drowsy in a park. He has a 30-year history of heavy daily alcohol use and weighs 54 kg with a BMI of 18. He is hypothermic at 35.4 degrees and capillary glucose is 2.8 mmol/L. The triage nurse hangs an IV bag of 5% dextrose. Forty minutes later the resident notes ataxia, horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze, and ophthalmoparesis with bilateral abducens weakness.

He is intermittently confused but rousable. He has had no head trauma. CT brain shows no acute lesion. He has not received any thiamine yet. Sodium is 134, potassium 3.4, magnesium 0.58 mmol/L, INR 1.3, AST 95, ALT 50 The triage nurse asks whether the dextrose infusion should be paused before any thiamine is given, and whether IM 100 mg thiamine is sufficient He has no head trauma history.

data_table.Vital signs: T 35.4, HR 98, BP 108/62, RR 16, SpO2 98%, BSL 2.8 mmol/L
data_table.Examination: Ataxic, horizontal nystagmus, bilateral CN VI weakness, confused, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6)
data_table.Investigations: Na 134, K 3.4, Mg 0.58 mmol/L, INR 1.3, AST 95, ALT 50, CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: IV high-dose B-complex (Pabrinex 2 pairs IV TDS), correct magnesium, then continue dextrose
Continue dextrose, give a single 100 mg intramuscular dose of thiamine, then monitor
Hold any further IV glucose and commence intravenous magnesium sulfate as monotherapy
Arrange an urgent MRI brain before commencing any pharmacological replacement therapy
Commence oral thiamine 300 mg daily without any parenteral B-vitamin therapy

stem:
A 49-year-old teacher with alcohol use disorder presents to her GP seeking pharmacological help to stay abstinent. She completed a community-supported withdrawal three weeks ago and has been alcohol-free since then. Her main concerns are recurrent strong cravings and a high-risk family wedding in two weeks. She has chronic back pain managed with paracetamol only and no current opioid prescription.

She has no significant liver impairment (LFTs and INR normal), no renal impairment, and a normal ECG. She does not have a history of severe liver disease or active hepatitis. She is highly motivated, lives with a supportive partner, and attends weekly counselling. She has tried mutual-support groups previously without sustained benefit. She is otherwise well and not pregnant; she uses an IUD for contraception She has read about acamprosate, naltrexone and disulfiram and asks the GP to recommend the option most likely to help her control cravings, particularly given the high-risk family wedding in two weeks where alcohol will be present She has no opioid prescription and no current opioid use, and she does not want disulfiram because of the wedding.

data_table.Examination: BMI 24, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, normal mental state, no other comorbidities
data_table.Investigations: AST 28, ALT 24, GGT 38, bilirubin 12, INR 1.0, eGFR >90 mL/min, FBC normal
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol 1 g QID PRN, no opioids

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy is most appropriate as first-line maintenance treatment to support abstinence?

options.text: Naltrexone 50 mg orally daily
Acamprosate 666 mg three times daily
Disulfiram 200 mg daily
Diazepam 5 mg three times daily for ongoing craving
Topiramate 100 mg twice daily

stem:
A 58-year-old man has chronic alcohol use disorder and has failed adequate trials of naltrexone (compliance confirmed by his partner) and acamprosate over the past 12 months, with ongoing harmful drinking. He has well-compensated alcohol-related liver disease (Child-Pugh A; AST 80, ALT 55, INR 1.2, albumin 35, no ascites or encephalopathy). He has stable ischaemic heart disease with prior PCI two years ago and a normal ECG today.

He is highly motivated, lives with a supportive partner who can supervise daily dosing, and attends a specialist alcohol service. Echocardiogram shows preserved ejection fraction 58%. He has no respiratory disease. He understands and accepts the disulfiram-ethanol reaction The specialist alcohol clinician is keen to start a relapse-prevention pharmacotherapy today; the patient has consented to the disulfiram-ethanol reaction warning leaflet. The cardiology team has flagged that hypotension and arrhythmia risk are the main concern with disulfiram.

data_table.Examination: Stable, no signs of decompensated liver disease, normal mental state
data_table.Investigations: AST 80, ALT 55, INR 1.2, albumin 35, no ascites; ECG normal; EF 58%
data_table.Medications: Aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg, metoprolol 25 mg BD; naltrexone and acamprosate trialled previously

lead_in: Which factor most strongly contraindicates initiating disulfiram in this patient?

options.text: Pre-existing ischaemic heart disease with prior coronary intervention
Mild compensated liver disease with Child-Pugh A staging
Concurrent metoprolol therapy used for rate control
Patient age over 55 years at initiation of disulfiram
Concurrent atorvastatin therapy used for secondary prevention

stem:
A 31-year-old woman with a 6-year history of injecting heroin presents to a community OST clinic seeking opioid agonist treatment. She last used heroin 12 hours ago. She has tested positive for HCV antibody (RNA pending) and her LFTs show ALT 84, AST 60. She has no other psychiatric medications and no significant medical comorbidity. Her observations are normal. COWS score on assessment is 14 (moderate withdrawal) with pupil dilation, sweating, yawning, mild rhinorrhoea, anxiety and bone aches.

Urine drug screen is positive for opioids only. She is unable to attend a clinic for daily supervised dispensing because she works variable shifts but can attend twice weekly. She has no respiratory disease, no QT-prolonging medications, and an ECG today shows QTc 410 ms.

data_table.Examination: Mydriasis, diaphoresis, restless, no signs of overdose; venepuncture marks both antecubital fossae
data_table.Investigations: COWS 14, AST 60, ALT 84, ECG QTc 410 ms, urine drug screen positive opioids only, HCV antibody positive (RNA pending)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in induction?

options.text: Sublingual buprenorphine-naloxone 4 mg now, top-up 2 to 4 mg in 2 hours if withdrawal persists
Commence methadone 60 mg orally today as the safer first-day community induction dose
Wait until she has been opioid-free for 24 hours and then commence oral naltrexone
Give intramuscular naloxone now to confirm opioid dependence before any induction begins
Commence sublingual buprenorphine 16 mg as a single first dose to suppress withdrawal rapidly

stem:
A 45-year-old man on methadone 80 mg daily for 3 years presents to his GP with new-onset palpitations. He was admitted for community-acquired pneumonia 10 days ago and discharged on azithromycin 500 mg daily (now stopped) and oral fluconazole 200 mg daily (continuing) for oropharyngeal candidiasis. He has also been taking diphenhydramine for sleep. Resting ECG today shows sinus rhythm at 78 with QTc 510 ms (previously 430 ms before admission).

He has no chest pain, no syncope and no electrolyte derangement. Electrolytes are normal including potassium 4.1 and magnesium 0.85. He has not increased his methadone dose. He denies non-prescribed drug use and urine drug screen is positive only for methadone and benzodiazepines (he disclosed temazepam supplied by a friend)

data_table.Examination: No oedema, no murmurs, clear chest, no syncope
data_table.Investigations: ECG QTc 510 ms (was 430), K 4.1, Mg 0.85, eGFR >90, LFTs normal
data_table.Medications: Methadone 80 mg daily, fluconazole 200 mg daily, diphenhydramine PRN, temazepam (illicitly sourced)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Stop fluconazole and diphenhydramine, counsel against benzodiazepines, consider methadone dose reduction or switch
Continue the current regimen unchanged and review the patient in 4 weeks with a repeat ECG
Increase methadone to 100 mg daily to improve compliance and stabilise opioid receptors
Cease methadone abruptly today and commence naltrexone after 24 hours of opioid abstinence
Add an oral beta-blocker (atenolol 25 mg daily) to reduce torsades de pointes risk acutely

stem:
A 26-year-old man is brought to ED by police after acting bizarrely in a shopping centre, smashing a window and shouting at unseen individuals. He has used crystal methamphetamine for 18 months and admits to using last night. On arrival he is pacing, sweating, threatening staff verbally, and intermittently striking the wall. He has dilated pupils, marked tachycardia, hypertension and a low-grade fever.

He has not had any seizures, no head injury, and there is no other identified medical contributor. He is on no regular medication. Initial verbal de-escalation has failed and he is now attempting to leave. Capillary glucose is 6.8 mmol/L. Bloods are pending. The patient weighs approximately 80 kg, has no airway concerns at present, and continuous cardiac monitoring can be commenced in the high-acuity area

data_table.Examination: Mydriasis, diaphoresis, agitated, hyper-vigilant, no focal neurology, no head injury, no obvious overdose features
data_table.Investigations: BSL 6.8 mmol/L, urine drug screen pending, ECG sinus tachycardia, QTc 430 ms

lead_in: What is the single best initial pharmacological management of his acute behavioural disturbance?

options.text: IM droperidol 10 mg with cautious midazolam 2.5 to 5 mg titrated, in a monitored area
Oral diazepam 20 mg single dose, awaiting effect over the next 60 minutes
Intramuscular ketamine as first-line for acute behavioural sedation
Intravenous haloperidol 5 mg as a single dose without concurrent benzodiazepine
Physical restraint without any pharmacotherapy, awaiting natural resolution over hours

stem:
A 33-year-old woman is brought to ED by her partner. She has bipolar disorder and stopped lithium 3 weeks ago. Over the past 5 days she has slept 2 to 3 hours per night, has been spending savings on unnecessary purchases, and is now describing herself as 'chosen to save the city'. She has not slept in 36 hours and is pacing the ED.

There is no current suicidal ideation or thoughts of harming others. She has no medical comorbidity, and a UDS and bloods are unremarkable. On MSE she is dressed flamboyantly, pressured in speech, with flight of ideas and grandiose delusions. She insists she is not unwell and refuses any treatment, including reinstating lithium. Her partner is present and supportive, and the community mental-health team has a current case manager

data_table.Examination: Elevated mood, pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiose delusions, no current SI/HI, no psychomotor retardation
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH normal, urine drug screen negative, beta-hCG negative, lithium level <0.2 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Lithium ceased 3 weeks ago by patient; no current medications

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007 (or equivalent state Act)?

options.text: Detain under the MHA assessment schedule and admit to a declared mental health facility for review
Discharge home with her partner and arrange outpatient review with the case manager tomorrow
Apply common-law restraint and sedate her in the ED without using the Mental Health Act
Make a community treatment order today without proceeding to any inpatient admission
Document her refusal of care and allow discharge from ED against medical advice

stem:
A 58-year-old woman with schizophrenia has been treated with first-generation antipsychotics for 25 years (most recently haloperidol 10 mg daily) and is being reviewed in the outpatient clinic. She has new-onset chewing movements, lip-smacking and occasional protrusion of the tongue for the past 4 months, occurring while not consciously moving and persisting during conversation. She has no oculogyric movements, no postural instability.

AIMS examination scores her in the moderate severity range with involuntary orofacial movements. She is currently otherwise stable in her mental state. There is no history of cognitive impairment, and she has no recent change in medication. She has tried benzatropine in the past for these movements without benefit She remains on her depot haloperidol despite the tardive dyskinesia meeting AIMS criteria. The treating psychiatrist is reviewing whether to switch agents Her family is involved and supportive.

data_table.Examination: Orofacial dyskinesia, normal limb tone and reflexes, no tremor, no rigidity
data_table.Investigations: AIMS score elevated in oromandibular domain; FBC, UEC, LFTs normal
data_table.Medications: Haloperidol 10 mg daily, trial of benzatropine without benefit

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase oral benzatropine to 4 mg daily for the tardive movements
Switch from haloperidol to a second-generation antipsychotic, ideally clozapine
Add oral risperidone alongside the current haloperidol regimen
Increase haloperidol dose further to suppress the involuntary movements
Stop all antipsychotic therapy completely and observe over weeks

stem:
A 41-year-old man on clozapine 500 mg nocte for treatment-resistant schizophrenia missed 4 consecutive days of doses while travelling for a family funeral. He is asymptomatic, no longer psychotic, and feels well, but is keen to resume his usual dose tonight. He has a history of one previous generalised tonic-clonic seizure 5 years ago at clozapine 600 mg daily, which prompted dose reduction.

He has no other neurological history. His mother (a nurse) phones the clozapine service requesting advice. Bloods this morning show normal FBC (WCC 6.8, neutrophils 4.0). He takes no other regular medications, weighs 92 kg, has BMI 30, and smokes 20 cigarettes daily. He cannot easily reach the clozapine prescriber until 48 hours from now and his community pharmacy has his usual 500 mg tablet ready The clozapine service consultant on call confirms that any break of more than 48 hours in clozapine requires re-titration from 12.5 mg per the Australian Clozapine Protocols, because the rapid loss of receptor adaptation and the well-known dose-related seizure and cardiovascular risks make restarting at his previous maintenance dose hazardous.

She emphasises that this protocol applies even when the patient feels clinically well and asymptomatic, and that retitration is the same process used at first initiation, with monitoring of vital signs and observation for orthostatic hypotension, sedation, tachycardia and seizure activity during each step.

data_table.Examination: BMI 30, no neurological signs, no fever
data_table.Investigations: WCC 6.8, neutrophils 4.0, UEC normal, glucose 5.8 mmol/L; ECG sinus rhythm QTc 420 ms
data_table.Medications: Clozapine 500 mg nocte (4 doses missed), no other regular meds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Restart at the usual 500 mg dose tonight without any retitration
Resume retitration from 12.5 mg per the standard induction protocol
Halve the previous dose to 250 mg nocte tonight and resume usual schedule
Switch immediately from clozapine to olanzapine at the equivalent oral dose
Add prophylactic sodium valproate before restarting clozapine at any dose

stem:
A 64-year-old man admitted 3 days ago for orthopaedic surgery has not received scheduled benzodiazepine prophylaxis despite his documented daily alcohol intake of approximately 20 standard drinks. Last drink was 72 hours ago. He is now confused, agitated, picking at his bedding, and describing animals running across the ceiling. He has had two witnessed brief generalised tonic-clonic seizures in the past 4 hours.

He is febrile, tachycardic, hypertensive, and diaphoretic. CIWA-Ar is now uninterpretable due to confusion. He has a wound dressing intact, no neurological focal deficits, and CT brain is unremarkable. He has received total diazepam 30 mg over the past 6 hours with limited effect. He has known cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B), albumin 28, INR 1.6, AST 130, ALT 70, platelets 95

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, HR 140, BP 174/100, RR 28, SpO2 95% on room air
data_table.Examination: Confused, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), tremulous, diaphoretic, visual hallucinations, no focal neurology, post-op wound dressed
data_table.Investigations: Na 132, K 3.0, Mg 0.58, glucose 5.6, lactate 3.4, INR 1.6, albumin 28, AST 130, ALT 70, platelets 95, CT brain unremarkable
data_table.Medications: Diazepam total 30 mg PO over 6 hours, IV Pabrinex 2 pairs commenced

lead_in: What is the single best next step in management?

options.text: Transfer to ICU or HDU, escalate to IV diazepam (or lorazepam if hepatic impairment), correct electrolytes
Continue oral diazepam, increase the frequency and reassess his condition in 4 hours
Commence intravenous haloperidol 10 mg as the primary treatment for the agitated withdrawal state
Load with intravenous phenytoin 1 g as primary anti-seizure prophylaxis tonight
Administer intramuscular naloxone empirically in case of unrecognised opioid involvement

stem:
A 41-year-old woman is referred by her general practitioner to a community psychiatry clinic after 18 months of persistent abdominal pain and fatigue. She has had two normal colonoscopies, a normal gastroscopy, normal abdominal CT, normal coeliac serology, and a normal pelvic ultrasound across this period. She has consulted 11 different clinicians, frequently checks symptom-tracking apps and online forums for several hours each day, and reports that the uncertainty about what is wrong is so distressing that she has reduced her part-time bookkeeping work to one day per week.

She describes the pain as a constant 6 out of 10, worsening with stress, and is convinced something serious has been missed. She denies low mood pervading her day, denies anhedonia, sleeps 6 hours nightly with early waking only when pain is severe, and her K-10 is 24. She uses paracetamol most days and has no other regular medications. She has never had clear hypomanic, psychotic, or panic episodes.

data_table.Examination: Anxious, preoccupied with bodily focus, organised thought, no psychosis. Mild epigastric tenderness, otherwise unremarkable.
data_table.Investigations: K-10 24. FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH, coeliac serology, faecal calprotectin all within reference. Two prior colonoscopies and a gastroscopy normal.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate DSM-5 classification for this presentation?

options.text: Illness anxiety disorder with care-seeking behaviour
Somatic symptom disorder with persistent course
Generalised anxiety disorder with somatic predominance
Functional neurological disorder, mixed sensory type
Factitious disorder imposed on self

stem:
A 29-year-old graphic designer presents to the emergency department with sudden onset right leg weakness that began 3 days ago after a minor work argument. She has no headache, no visual change, no bowel or bladder symptoms, and no sensory level. She walks with a dragging right leg that appears to swing in a circumduction not typical of pyramidal hemiparesis.

Power in the right hip extensors is 2/5 when tested in isolation, but when she is asked to flex the left hip against resistance while lying supine, you feel strong downward pressure under her right heel. Right knee and ankle reflexes are normal and symmetric, plantar response is flexor, sensation is reported as patchy with a non-anatomical boundary at mid-thigh. Cranial nerves are intact. MRI brain and whole spine completed yesterday are normal. FBC, UEC, glucose, TSH, B12 and HIV serology are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% on air, afebrile.
data_table.Examination: Hoover's sign positive on the right (involuntary hip extension during contralateral hip flexion against resistance). Reflexes symmetric, plantars flexor, non-anatomical sensory boundary.
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain and spine normal. FBC, UEC, glucose, TSH, B12, HIV serology normal.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat MRI brain with stroke protocol and start dual antiplatelet therapy
Admit for high-dose IV methylprednisolone empirically for suspected multiple sclerosis
Tell the patient the scan is normal and there is nothing wrong, with GP follow up in 2 weeks
Explain the positive Hoover's sign as a rule-in diagnosis of functional neurological disorder and refer for FND-specific physiotherapy
Commence quetiapine 25 mg nocte for somatisation and arrange psychiatric admission

subtopic_detail: Illness anxiety disorder vs somatic symptom disorder
stem:
A 38-year-old IT consultant attends his general practitioner for the fourth time in 8 weeks requesting another full blood count and tumour marker panel. He is convinced he has pancreatic cancer despite a normal abdominal CT, normal CA 19-9, normal LFTs, and normal pancreatic enzymes obtained 3 weeks ago. He has minor occasional epigastric flutter and mild fatigue but no weight loss, no jaundice, and no anorexia.

He spends 3 to 4 hours daily on patient forums and oncology websites, has read three textbooks on pancreatic cancer staging, and asks colleagues to feel his abdomen for masses. His K-10 is 22. He acknowledges every reassurance gives him relief for around 24 hours before doubt returns. There is no family history of pancreatic cancer. He has no other regular medications. He sleeps 6 hours and his weight is stable. His functional decline at work is described as moderate.

data_table.Examination: Anxious, pressured speech around health topics, no thought disorder. Abdomen soft, non-tender, no masses.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, lipase, CA 19-9 all within reference. Abdominal CT 3 weeks ago: normal.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate DSM-5 diagnosis?

options.text: Somatic symptom disorder with predominant pain
Generalised anxiety disorder, severe
Illness anxiety disorder, care-seeking type
Obsessive-compulsive disorder with contamination obsessions
Delusional disorder, somatic type

stem:
A 45-year-old man presents to ED for the 7th time in 8 months with recurrent hypoglycaemia (plasma glucose 2.1-2.6 mmol/L, markedly elevated insulin and SUPPRESSED C-peptide each time). He has no diabetes, no insulinoma on prior CT and MRI. He is a former endocrinology nurse, currently unemployed, lives alone. He denies injecting insulin and becomes irritable when asked. He has no pending litigation, no Centrelink claim under reviewo active forensic process.

Staff have observed him discarding small objects in the sharps bin after symptom onset. Each admission has involved invasive investigations and extended stays during which he is highly engaged with treating teams who describe him as 'the most knowledgeable patient we've ever had'. He receives no financial benefit from admissions but openly enjoys the medical-team attention. K-10 is 30 with profound loneliness.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 128/82, RR 16, BSL 2.3 mmol/L on arrival.
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, oriented, no focal neurology.
data_table.Investigations: Plasma glucose 2.3 mmol/L, insulin 480 pmol/L (markedly raised), C-peptide 90 pmol/L (suppressed), sulfonylurea screen negative. CT and MRI pancreas previously normal.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate DSM-5 classification of his behaviour?

options.text: Malingering for secondary financial gain
Factitious disorder imposed on self
Somatic symptom disorder with predominant pain
Conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder)
Delusional disorder, somatic type

stem:
A 52-year-old woman is referred to community mental health by her general practitioner for a 4-month history of fatigue, low mood, weight gain of 5 kg, constipation, cold intolerance, and reduced concentration. She has stopped her weekly bushwalking group and finds her brain feels foggy. Her sister has Hashimoto thyroiditis and her mother had pernicious anaemia. She has no prior psychiatric history, no suicidal ideation, and her affect is flat with mildly slowed thought tempo.

She is not pregnant. She takes no regular medications and drinks 4 standard drinks weekly. Her general practitioner started sertraline 50 mg daily 6 weeks ago without baseline bloods, with no improvement, and has now sent her with K-10 of 28. On examination her skin is dry, reflexes show delayed relaxation phase, and there is a small diffuse non-tender goitre. HR is 52.

data_table.Examination: Slow speech, flat affect, dry skin, delayed reflex relaxation, small diffuse goitre.
data_table.Investigations: Not yet performed by mental health team.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next investigation before adjusting psychotropic therapy?

options.text: Switch sertraline to mirtazapine 30 mg nocte and review in 4 weeks
Dexamethasone suppression test for Cushing syndrome
Brain MRI to exclude frontal lobe lesion
TSH, free T4 and thyroid peroxidase antibodies
Empirical levothyroxine 50 microgram daily without bloods

stem:
A 22-year-old previously well university student is admitted to a psychiatric inpatient unit with 3 weeks of insomnia, paranoid delusions and disorganised behaviour. Over 48 hours her presentation has evolved: she now has orofacial dyskinesias, brief episodes of unresponsiveness with eyelid twitching, autonomic instability (HR oscillating 140 then 48, BP 165/95 then 95/55), and low-grade fever 38.1. She has had NO antipsychotic exposure to date (admitted before any were given).

Urine drug screen is negative. CK 320 U/L. No neck stiffness. Family report a brief flu-like illness 6 weeks ago. CT head normal. LP performed: mild lymphocytic pleocytosis (35 cells/microL), normal glucose, mildly raised protein, no organisms on Gram stain, viral PCR (including HSV-1/2 and enterovirus) pending.

data_table.Vital signs: Fluctuating HR 48-140, BP 95/55 to 165/95, T 38.1, RR variable.
data_table.Examination: Orofacial dyskinesias, intermittent unresponsiveness with eyelid twitching, no neck stiffness, no focal deficit.
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative. CK 320 U/L. CT head normal. CSF: WCC 35 (lymphocytic), protein 0.65 g/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L (paired plasma 5.0).

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next investigative AND empirical step in parallel?

options.text: Send serum AND CSF anti-NMDA receptor (and broader autoimmune encephalitis) antibodies, arrange MRI brain with contrast, request urgent neurology review, and start empirical IV aciclovir until HSV PCR returns negative
Increase olanzapine to 20 mg daily and add lorazepam for agitation while awaiting CSF PCR
Empirical IV aciclovir alone with no autoimmune antibody panel, on the assumption that lymphocytic pleocytosis is always HSV until proven otherwise
EEG and serial CK only, on the assumption this is neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Whole-body PET CT to exclude paraneoplastic origin as the first investigative step

stem:
An 84-year-old woman with Alzheimer disease (baseline MoCA 16/30, lives at home with daily community nursing) is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia and treated with IV ceftriaxone plus oral azithromycin. On day 3 her family report a change from baseline: drowsy in the morning, agitated and pulling at her cannula by evening, sees small children in the curtains, and cannot identify where she is.

Her usual mild forgetfulness has been replaced with fluctuating attention - cannot maintain a conversation >30 seconds. SpO2 95% on 2 L. No bowel motion in 4 days. Urinalysis: leucocytes only, no nitrites, asymptomatic. Recent additions to her chart include oxycodone 5 mg 4-hourly PRN (taken regularly), lorazepam 1 mg PRN nocte, and metoclopramide 10 mg TDS. CXR shows improving consolidation. CAM is positive for delirium.

data_table.Examination: Fluctuating attention, inattentive on months-of-year backwards, visual hallucinations, distractible.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, CRP improving. Glucose 6.4 mmol/L. Urinalysis mild leukocytes only. CXR improving. ECG normal.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate INITIAL management plan, per the Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care delirium clinical care standard?

options.text: Add scheduled risperidone 1 mg BD for delirium agitation; continue oxycodone, lorazepam and metoclopramide unchanged at their current doses today
Start donepezil 5 mg daily for worsening Alzheimer disease and discharge home with primary care follow-up arranged at 4 weeks after this admission
Transfer to a closed psychiatric ward under an involuntary order for management of presumed psychosis arising from his underlying dementia process
Deprescribe lorazepam, switch oxycodone to non-opioid analgesia, cease metoclopramide, address constipation and dehydration, optimise non-pharmacological care, do not treat asymptomatic pyuria
Commence IV ciprofloxacin empirically for presumed urinary tract infection based on the positive urinalysis nitrites and leukocytes

stem:
A 52-year-old man with recurrent major depressive disorder has not adequately responded to sertraline 200 mg daily for 10 weeks followed by venlafaxine titrated to 225 mg daily for 8 weeks (adequate dose, adequate duration, confirmed adherence by pharmacy records and partner observation). PHQ-9 has fallen from 22 to 19 only. He has no significant intolerance, no bipolar history, no psychotic features, is not catatonic, not refusing food, has no immediate suicide plan; K-10 today is 30.

Sleep 5 hours, weight loss 3 kg over 8 weeks. Bloods: FBC normal, UEC normal (eGFR 92), TSH 1.8, fasting glucose 5.2, LFTs normal. ECG QTc 410 ms. He is a non-smoker, drinks 4 standard drinks weekly, no chronic medical illness. RANZCP defines TRD as failure of two adequate antidepressant trials. He is willing to take additional medication and to engage with augmentation but prefers to avoid ECT if alternatives exist.

data_table.Examination: Low mood, congruent affect, no psychosis, no catatonia.
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 19. FBC, UEC (eGFR 92), TSH 1.8, fasting glucose 5.2, LFTs all within reference. ECG QTc 410 ms.
data_table.Medications: Venlafaxine 225 mg daily (current), sertraline 200 mg daily for 10 weeks previously.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next pharmacological step per the RANZCP CPG TRD pathway?

options.text: Add lithium augmentation titrated to trough 0.4-0.8 mmol/L with renal and thyroid monitoring at baseline, 6 weeks and 3-monthly thereafter
Switch venlafaxine to fluoxetine 20 mg daily monotherapy without augmentation
Add bupropion 150 mg daily as monoamine combination augmentation (not PBS-listed in Australia)
Add diazepam 5 mg BD as anxiolytic augmentation for six weeks
Refer urgently for ECT as the first-line treatment for resistant depression

stem:
A 47-year-old woman with treatment-resistant MDD with atypical features has been on fluoxetine 40 mg daily for 9 months (partial response, PHQ-9 21 to 16). Her psychiatrist plans to switch to phenelzine, a non-selective irreversible MAOI. She has no concurrent serotonergic medications, no St John's Wort, no tramadol, no triptans, no pethidine, no linezolid, and is not pregnant. Renal and hepatic function are normal.

Lives with supportive partner, no immediate suicide risk, agrees to weekly review during transition. She specifically asks why the wait between stopping fluoxetine and starting phenelzine is different to what her friend was told when switching from citalopram to phenelzine (2 weeks).

data_table.Examination: Mild psychomotor slowing, otherwise unremarkable, no autonomic instability.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH all within reference. ECG normal.
data_table.Medications: Fluoxetine 40 mg daily for 9 months, no other serotonergic agents.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate switching strategy and the underlying reason?

options.text: Direct switch: stop fluoxetine today and commence phenelzine 15 mg three times daily tomorrow, with weekly outpatient review for the first month
Cross-taper: reduce fluoxetine over two weeks while simultaneously titrating phenelzine upward to maintain antidepressant cover during the transition
Stop fluoxetine and wait at least 5 weeks before commencing phenelzine because norfluoxetine has a half-life of ~7-15 days and requires ~5 half-lives for clearance
Stop fluoxetine and wait only 5 days before starting phenelzine, ignoring the long active metabolite half-life of norfluoxetine in this washout
Continue fluoxetine and add low-dose phenelzine 7.5 mg daily as augmentation rather than switching agents entirely, accepting interaction risk

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome vs NMS vs anticholinergic discrimination
stem:
A 28-year-old man is brought to ED by ambulance 6 hours after his community team added tramadol 100 mg QID for back pain. He was already on escitalopram 20 mg daily and started linezolid 4 days ago for a soft tissue infection. He is agitated and shivering with sweating; intermittent myoclonus is most prominent in the LOWER limbs; pupils are dilated (6 mm) and reactive; he is markedly hyperreflexic with sustained inducible clonus at the ankles, and ocular clonus is present.

Skin is MOIST. HR 128, BP 168/92, RR 22, T 39.4. He is alert but agitated. CK 480 U/L. No recent antipsychotic exposure on review of his community team's chart. The ED registrar is choosing between the Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria, NMS criteria and an anticholinergic toxidrome.

data_table.Examination: Agitation, diaphoresis, dilated reactive pupils, lower-limb-predominant clonus, hyperreflexia, ocular clonus, moist skin.
data_table.Investigations: CK 480 U/L, FBC, UEC, glucose normal. Paracetamol level negative.
data_table.Medications: Escitalopram 20 mg daily, tramadol 100 mg QID (started today), linezolid for soft tissue infection.

lead_in: Which toxidrome best fits, and which is the most discriminating feature on examination?

options.text: Anticholinergic toxidrome - dry mucous membranes, absent bowel sounds, mydriasis and urinary retention are the deciding features in this drug-exposed patient
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome - lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, antipsychotic exposure and bradykinesia are the deciding features rather than clonus or hyperreflexia
Serotonin syndrome by Hunter criteria - the discriminating feature is spontaneous or inducible clonus with hyperreflexia in the setting of multi-serotonergic exposure
Sympathomimetic toxidrome from undisclosed stimulant intoxication - urine drug screen for amphetamines, cocaine or designer agents will confirm at presentation
Malignant hyperthermia from recent anaesthetic exposure - masseter rigidity and a rapidly rising end-tidal CO2 are the deciding features in this acute toxidrome

stem:
A 56-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder maintained on lithium carbonate 750 mg daily (trough level 0.7 mmol/L 6 weeks ago) presents to ED with 3 days of coarse tremor, ataxia, drowsiness, and vomiting. Over the past 2 weeks she has been treated for hypertension with newly added perindopril, has been taking ibuprofen 400 mg TDS for shoulder pain, and during a recent heatwave she has had reduced oral intake with no fluid replacement.

She has lost 2 kg in 10 days. Her usual sertraline 50 mg daily has been unchanged. She is alert but confused, with hyperreflexia, coarse tremor, and gait ataxia. There is no clonus and no fever. Her ECG shows T-wave flattening with QTc 460 ms. Her current lithium level is 2.1 mmol/L. Creatinine has risen from baseline 75 to 145 micromol/L (eGFR fallen from 78 to 38).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 142/86, RR 16, T 36.8, mild dehydration.
data_table.Examination: Confused, coarse tremor, gait ataxia, hyperreflexia, no clonus, no rigidity, no fever.
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 2.1 mmol/L, creatinine 145 (baseline 75), eGFR 38 (baseline 78), Na 138, K 4.2, ECG QTc 460 ms with T-wave flattening.
data_table.Medications: Lithium 750 mg daily, sertraline 50 mg daily, perindopril (new 2 weeks), ibuprofen 400 mg TDS (recent), no diuretics.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue lithium, give 1 L IV normal saline, recheck level in 24 hours
Continue lithium, withhold ACE inhibitor and ibuprofen, recheck level next week
Give 50 g oral activated charcoal to bind unabsorbed lithium acutely
Cease lithium and give IV furosemide 40 mg to enhance lithium excretion
Cease lithium, withdraw NSAID and ACE inhibitor, IV crystalloid, consult toxicology for haemodialysis

stem:
A 26-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has had two manic episodes in the past 18 months despite lithium 1000 mg daily (level 0.8 mmol/L, partner-confirmed adherence). She and her partner are planning a pregnancy within the next 12 months and have stopped contraception. She is otherwise well, takes no other medications, has normal renal/hepatic function, normal TSH, normal weight, no PCOS history.

Her predominant illness course is MANIC (no significant depressive episodes documented). She has no current depressive symptoms, no psychosis, no current suicide risk and has been adherent with stable lithium troughs. She asks specifically about adding sodium valproate (her sister with epilepsy takes it) and about lamotrigine.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic mood, no psychosis.
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.8 mmol/L, FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH all within reference. Pregnancy test negative.
data_table.Medications: Lithium 1000 mg daily; no contraception.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step in this preconception window?

options.text: Add sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily as an adjunctive mood stabiliser to her current lithium, with quarterly serum level monitoring
Add quetiapine extended-release titrated to 300-600 mg nocte with metabolic monitoring, continuing lithium at its current dose
Switch lithium to carbamazepine 200 mg twice daily as monotherapy, with baseline FBC and LFTs and review at 4 weeks
Stop lithium immediately given the pregnancy planning, with no replacement mood stabiliser and GP follow-up in 4 weeks for mental-state review
Switch lithium to lamotrigine 200 mg daily as monotherapy, with the standard 6-week dose-titration schedule and rash-monitoring counselling

subtopic_detail: TCA overdose - cardiac toxicity and sodium bicarbonate
stem: A 32-year-old woman with chronic depression is brought to ED 90 minutes after deliberate ingestion of approximately 50 amitriptyline 25 mg tablets with alcohol. She is drowsy but rousable (GCS 12), has had a single self-terminating generalised tonic-clonic seizure on arrival, pupils dilated, mucous membranes dry, catheter drained 200 mL. ECG: sinus tachycardia 132 bpm, QRS 140 ms, terminal R wave in aVR 4 mm, QTc 510 ms. BP 92/54. VBG: pH 7.28, lactate 3.4, Na 138, K 3.6. No paracetamol co-ingestion. No other regular medications.

data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, dilated pupils, dry mucosae, post-ictal.
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia, QRS 140 ms, terminal R in aVR 4 mm, QTc 510 ms. VBG: pH 7.28, lactate 3.4, Na 138, K 3.6. Paracetamol level negative.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate intervention, and what is the threshold guiding it?

options.text: IV sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg bolus, repeated to narrow QRS below ~120 ms and target pH 7.50-7.55; indicated for QRS >100-120 ms, hypotension or seizures
IV flumazenil 0.2 mg titrated to a Glasgow Coma Scale of 14 or above, followed by transfer to a monitored bed for ongoing observation
IV amiodarone 300 mg over 20 minutes for the wide-complex tachycardia, with continuous electrocardiogram monitoring during the infusion
Gastric lavage followed by oral activated charcoal 50 g at 90 minutes post-ingestion, with the patient nursed in the left lateral position
IV physostigmine 1 mg slow push as a targeted antidote for the anticholinergic features (mydriasis, dry mucosa, warm dry skin)

stem:
A 41-year-old woman who has been on venlafaxine XR 150 mg daily for 14 months for MDD agrees with her GP to reduce her dose. Within 48 hours of dropping to 75 mg daily she develops brief electric-shock sensations ('brain zaps'), dizziness, nausea, headache, insomnia and intermittent crying spells with irritability. PHQ-9 four days earlier on 150 mg was 4.

Her mood remains reactive, she still enjoys her usual activities, has no anhedonia, no early-morning waking, no suicidal ideation, no diurnal mood variation. She is still functioning at work and socially engaged. Symptoms began within 48 hours of the dose reduction. She has no other new medications, no infections, no thyroid symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Reactive affect, mild irritability, no anhedonia, no psychomotor change, no psychosis.
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 at 150 mg dose 4 days ago: score 4.
data_table.Medications: Venlafaxine 75 mg daily (reduced from 150 mg 48 hours ago).

lead_in: Which is the single most likely cause of her symptoms, and what is the most appropriate immediate response?

options.text: Recurrence of major depressive disorder; reinstate full venlafaxine dose and refer urgently for psychiatric review and ECT consideration today
Antidepressant discontinuation syndrome; resume venlafaxine 150 mg and taper more slowly (37.5 mg reductions every 2-4 weeks); venlafaxine's short half-life predisposes
Serotonin syndrome from a drug interaction; cease all serotonergic agents and commence cyproheptadine with active supportive cooling measures
Hypothyroidism from long-term SNRI use; commence thyroxine replacement and recheck TSH at 6 weeks before considering any further taper of venlafaxine
Serotonin withdrawal-induced generalised anxiety disorder; commence sertraline as an alternative SSRI with cognitive behavioural therapy referral today

subtopic_detail: Chronic vs acute risk factors and safety planning
stem:
A 38-year-old Aboriginal man presents to ED after an impulsive paracetamol ingestion of 8 tablets following an argument with his partner. He is medically cleared (no transaminitis, paracetamol level below the Rumack-Matthew nomogram line). History: one previous self-harm 4 years ago; harmful alcohol use (8 standard drinks/day currently); unemployment 12 months; recent eviction. He has chronic back pain and stopped his SSRI 3 months ago because he 'could not afford it'.

Tonight he says the argument was 'the last straw' and although he does not want to die now, he feels 'hopeless about anything getting better'. He has a legally-licensed firearm at home for pest control. His brother completed suicide 8 years ago. He has not yet been linked with the local Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Service. He agrees to attend follow-up if it is arranged for him.

data_table.Examination: Hopeless, mildly intoxicated, no psychosis, no agitation, no suicide plan at this moment.
data_table.Investigations: Paracetamol level non-toxic. LFTs normal. UEC normal. BAC 0.18%.
data_table.Medications: Nil current (stopped SSRI 3 months ago).

lead_in: Of the listed factors, which is the single most important MODIFIABLE acute risk factor to address before discharge planning under current Australian suicide-prevention guidance?

options.text: Brother's completed suicide 8 years ago
His Aboriginal identity as a demographic factor
Previous self-harm episode 4 years ago
Pervasive hopelessness about the future improving
Access to a firearm at home (means restriction)

subtopic_detail: Safety plan after self-harm (DBT chain analysis)
stem:
A 23-year-old woman with established borderline personality disorder presents to ED after superficial wrist cutting following a perceived rejection by a friend. She has had 6 similar presentations over 12 months. She is medically cleared after wound closure and tetanus update. She has an established treatment relationship with a community DBT-informed team; her case manager is contactable and has texted the ED to confirm she is engaged with treatment.

She declines admission. She is no longer acutely distressed and denies current suicidal intent. She agrees that she 'just snapped' when she saw the unread message. She has no alcohol or substances on board tonight. She lives with her supportive mother who is present in ED. She asks for help with what to do differently next time.

data_table.Examination: Calm, reactive affect, no current suicidal ideation, no psychosis, superficial laceration sutured.
data_table.Investigations: Wounds superficial, tetanus updated, paracetamol level negative, BAC zero.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step before discharge, per the National Health and Medical Research Council Clinical Practice Guideline for Borderline Personality Disorder?

options.text: Admit involuntarily under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007 for inpatient stabilisation, with handover to the inpatient team for ongoing dialectical behaviour therapy
Discharge with a 'no-suicide contract' signed by the patient and her mother without formal safety planning or any specific follow-up arrangement
Collaboratively develop a Stanley-Brown style safety plan (warning signs, coping, social support, means restriction), share with DBT team, arrange same-week DBT contact
Commence olanzapine 10 mg daily for affective instability and discharge home with primary care follow-up arranged in 2 weeks for medication review
Refer to the local drug and alcohol service for an outpatient assessment, with co-ordinated handover back to her current dialectical behaviour therapy team

stem:
A 68-year-old man is reviewed in stroke clinic 8 weeks after a moderate left middle cerebral artery ischaemic stroke. He has residual mild right-sided weakness and mild expressive dysphasia from which he is recovering. His wife reports that since week 3, he has been progressively withdrawn, has stopped attending physiotherapy sessions, cries during morning routines, has lost 4 kg, sleeps 9 hours but wakes unrefreshed, and says repeatedly 'I'm a burden'.

His PHQ-9 today is 17 (excluding his neurological items). He has no prior psychiatric history. His current medications are aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg, perindopril 5 mg, and a multivitamin. subtopic_detail: Postpartum mood disorder after pregnancy loss
stem:

No psychotic symptoms, no delusions or hallucinations. EPDS today is 18 with item 10 (self-harm) scored 1 (occasionally has the thought). No prior psychiatric history. She is not breastfeeding (no surviving infant). She would like to try again in the future. She lives with a supportive partner.

data_table.Examination: Tearful, congruent affect, no psychosis, no thought disorder.

stem:

subtopic_detail: B12 deficiency presenting as cognitive and mood symptoms
stem:

Past medical history includes autoimmune thyroiditis on stable levothyroxine (TSH 1.8 today) and 12 months of pantoprazole 40 mg daily for reflux. She has been a strict vegan for 25 years and takes no vitamin supplements. She drinks no alcohol. On examination she has glossitis with a beefy tongue, mild distal sensory loss to vibration and proprioception in both feet, brisk knee reflexes with absent ankle reflexes, Romberg positive, and MoCA 19 of 30. Skin is pale with a lemon-yellow tint. FBC and film: Hb 95 g/L, MCV 112 fL, hypersegmented neutrophils on film.

data_table.Examination: Glossitis, lemon-yellow pallor, reduced vibration and proprioception in both feet, brisk knee reflexes, absent ankle reflexes, Romberg positive, MoCA 19/30.

data_table.Medications: Levothyroxine, pantoprazole 40 mg daily (12 months).

stem: A 26-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder presents for the fifth time this year to a Central Coast LHD emergency department after superficial cutting. She arrived voluntarily, brought by her DBT therapist who is now in the waiting room. She is calm, denies acute intent to die, and asks to go home. There is no acute decompensation in her presentation compared with baseline, and her DBT therapist confirms continued engagement and an active safety plan.

options.text: Discharge to home with continuation of DBT and brief contact with her therapist tonight
Admit to the acute inpatient mental health unit for several days
Initiate involuntary detention under the NSW Mental Health Act

stem: A 31-year-old woman is being discharged from a Hunter New England LHD acute mental health unit following a 5-day admission for major depression with suicidal ideation. data_table.Examination: Euthymic, future-oriented, no current ideation.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is brought to a Central Coast LHD ED 4 hours after ingesting 30 tablets of paracetamol 500 mg following an argument with her boyfriend. She tells the psychiatry registrar she did not really want to die, has no plan to repeat, and would like to go home now. She has no past psychiatric history.

data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented, calm, no abnormality on MSE.

Wait until paracetamol level returns to determine psychiatric disposition

stem: A 38-year-old man presents to a Hunter New England LHD ED with suicidal ideation. He insists his family must not be told he is here, refuses consent for collateral history from his wife who has phoned the ED asking about him, and is otherwise engaging with assessment. He has a known history of recurrent MDD, no current substance use, and a previous near-fatal overdose 3 years ago. The ED registrar asks how to handle the family's call.

data_table.Examination: Withdrawn but cooperative; expressing passive death wish, no plan disclosed.

lead_in: Which response best balances confidentiality with safety obligations?

options.text: Acknowledge the patient's confidentiality preference, explore the reasons for refusal, and explain that information may be received from the family without breaching confidentiality, even if disclosure to them is restricted

Refuse to take any information from the wife at all in order to honour the patient's stated confidentiality preference, declining her phone call and asking her not to attend the ED until the patient has consented to family involvement

Disclose his presence in the ED and the full clinical details of his suicidal ideation to the wife immediately to enable her active involvement in safety planning, overriding the patient's explicit refusal to consent to family contact

Confirm to the wife only that the patient is present at the ED but withhold all clinical details, including the reason for presentation and any risk assessment, while documenting the limited disclosure in the clinical record

Defer the wife's phone call to the on-call psychiatry registrar to decide whether and how to respond, taking a verbal message but undertaking no further action until the registrar has reviewed the case in person

stem: A 24-year-old man with first-episode schizophrenia presents to a Hunter New England LHD ED accompanied by his case manager. options.text: Admit to an inpatient mental health unit for medication review and close observation

Wait for the on-call psychiatry consultant to ring back tomorrow
Switch to oral quetiapine in the ED before disposition

stem:
An 84-year-old man attends your general practice in Tamworth for a repeat prescription of his analgesia. His wife of 58 years died 4 months ago and he now lives alone on their farm. He has osteoarthritis of both knees and sleeps poorly because of pain. When you ask how he is managing, he says, 'I'm just tired of it all, Doc.' He keeps a rifle for pest control.

His daughter rang the practice last week to say he is 'just old and grumpy'.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach at this consultation?

options.text: Ask him directly today about suicidal thoughts, any plans and his access to means
Arrange a routine mood review in 3 months, as his age group is at low risk
Explore his mood in general terms first, as naming suicide may plant the idea
Refer him to the older persons' mental health team and leave that enquiry to them
Reassure him that this is expected grief and review him after the first anniversary

stem: A 47-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is reviewed in a Central Coast LHD outpatient psychiatry clinic. She is currently euthymic on quetiapine 400 mg nocte. She has had two prior episodes of suicidal ideation during depressive phases and the consultant is considering switching to lithium for maintenance, partly for mood stability and partly for anti-suicide effect. Lithium reduces suicide only because it stabilises mood; no independent effect has been shown
Lithium has no proven effect on suicide and is only indicated for acute mania
Lithium increases suicide risk due to its narrow therapeutic index
Lithium's anti-suicide effect is restricted to women with rapid-cycling presentations

stem: A 28-year-old woman attends her GP at a Hunter New England LHD community clinic for her 6-week postnatal review. Her Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) score is 17. On Question 10 ('The thought of harming myself has occurred to me') she has answered 'Sometimes'. She has a 6-week-old breastfed infant, is sleeping in 2-hour blocks, denies a plan to act, and her husband is supportive but works long hours.

data_table.Examination: Tearful, mood low, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features.
data_table.Investigations: TFT pending; ferritin pending; B12 pending.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Direct follow-up with structured suicide risk assessment, safety planning including infant care arrangements, and same-week perinatal mental health referral

Recommend ceasing breastfeeding to improve sleep and reassess

options.text: Admit to a perinatal or mental health unit immediately, ensure infant is not in her unsupervised care, and arrange urgent psychiatric review

Reassure that postpartum hormone shifts often cause transient psychotic symptoms
